Q893
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 74-year-old man has had trouble reading for 18 months. He underwent uncomplicated cataract surgery in both eyes with no noticed improvement. His family also reports some gradual cognitive decline over the past year. His visual acuity is normal at near and distance. The posterior chamber intraocular lenses are well centered, with clear posterior capsules, and fundus examination results are normal. Humphrey visual fields show a left homonymous hemianopia. The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) result is unremarkable. What diagnosis would explain his symptoms?
Correct answer: C. posterior cortical atrophy
Rationale
A patient presenting with normal visual acuity and ocular examination, but inability to read, is concerning for dementia, specifically the visual variant of Alzheimer disease or posterior cortical atrophy. Patients with posterior cortical atrophy may present early to an eye doctor with visual findings, including homonymous visual field defects.
Cancer-associated retinopathy and melanoma-associated retinopathy would not produce a homonymous hemianopia. Occipital stroke commonly produces a homonymous hemianopia but is unlikely in the setting of an unremarkable MRI.
MRI may show some generalized atrophy, and occasionally more so in the occipital lobes, but not always. The positron emission tomography (PET) scan usually would be abnormal, although it is still not always specific. In a patient with a homonymous hemianopia and an MRI scan that does not explain it (ie, no stroke or tumor), the considerations are either posterior cortical atrophy or Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. In this case, given the chronicity of symptoms, posterior cortical atrophy is quite likely.

Q894
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient has an inferior arcuate visual field defect in the right eye. Given the optic nerve appearance shown, what additional testing would you recommend to confirm your presumed diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. B-scan ultrasonography
Rationale
This patient has buried and visible optic disc drusen. The lack of hyperemia, surface microvascular abnormalities, and clear visualization of the retinal vessels at the disc margin distinguish drusen from papilledema. Visual field defects, including an enlarged blind spot and arcuate scotomas, are commonly present with disc drusen. Imaging modalities that can confirm the presence of drusen include B-scan ultrasonography, autofluorescence, and CT scan. Typical B-scan findings include focal high reflectivity from disc drusen calcification as shown. Spectral-domain-OCT of the nerve head may also be helpful.

Q895
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For what vision-threatening tumor is there an increased risk in a child with the findings shown in the figure?
Correct answer: C. optic nerve glioma
Rationale
The presence of Lisch nodules (shown on the iris in the Figure) raises suspicion for neurofibromatosis type 1. Children with neurofibromatosis type 1 are at increased risk for vision loss secondary to optic pathway glioma. Neurofibromatosis type 2 is associated with the development of acoustic neuromas, meningiomas, and retinal hamartomas. Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with the development of retinal hemangioblastomas, which commonly are multiple and bilateral.

Q896
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Lisch nodules in neurofibromatosis type 1 are composed of what type of abnormal cellular growth?
Correct answer: B. hamartoma
Rationale
Ocular findings in neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) include Lisch nodules (figure), prominent corneal nerves, and choroidal hamartomas. Lisch nodules are flat or dome-shaped iris nodules, usually less than 1 mm and tan to dark brown in color. They are hamartomas (tissue normally found at the site, but in increased amounts). Schwann cells, fibroblast-like cells, and mast cells have been identified in biopsies of Lisch nodules, supporting neural crest origin. Lisch nodules are present in 10% of children with NF1 at 1 year of age, but in nearly 100% by age 10. The presence of 2 or more Lisch nodules is one of the criteria for the diagnosis of NF1 (6 or more cafe-au-lait spots; 2 or more neurofibromas; intertriginous freckling; optic nerve glioma; Lisch nodules; distinctive osseous lesions; first-degree relative with NF1). The NF1 gene is located at chromosome 17 q11.20, and its product, neurofibromin, is a tumor suppressant. The loss of neurofibromin leads to cell and tumor growth. Lisch nodules differ from iris mamillations, which are smaller, diffuse nodules on the iris surface, but which are the same color as the iris.

Q897
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 44-year-old woman with a history of diabetes develops a third nerve palsy, which is diagnosed as microvascular by her local physician. She presents to an ophthalmologist 8 weeks later, with lid elevation on attempted downgaze of her affected eye. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
Correct answer: D. immediate neuroimaging to rule out a compressive lesion
Rationale
Lid elevation on attempted downgaze indicates aberrant regeneration of the third cranial nerve, which occurs as damaged axons regrow to innervate muscles other than those they originally innervated. This fiber misrouting produces synkinetic phenomena, including eyelid retraction with adduction or pupillary miosis with elevation, adduction, or depression. Aberrant regeneration may result after trauma or from compression of the nerve from tumor or aneurysm. Aberrant regeneration does not occur with microvascular ischemia. Even in a diabetic patient in whom third nerve palsy is initially consistent with ischemic vasculopathy, development of this finding should prompt urgent neuroimaging to rule out a compressive etiology that requires treatment.
Continued follow-up for 6 months to check for resolution would be appropriate in a complete non-pupil-involving third nerve palsy in a vasculopathic patient with no signs of aberrancy. While more aggressive treatment of diabetes may be appropriate in these patients, it will not address the immediate concern of a more dire cause of the palsy. A test of sedimentation rate and the initiation of steroid therapy are appropriate if giant cell arteritis is suspected as an etiology, but not for a compressive lesion.

Q898
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient reports oscillopsia while chewing. Examination shows reduced voluntary vertical eye movements. What is the most likely cause of these symptoms and findings?
Correct answer: B. Tropheryma whipplei infection
Rationale
Tropheryma whipplei infection

The patient is reporting symptoms of oculomasticatory myorhythmia, in which use of the muscles of mastication causes ocular oscillation. Vertical saccadic deficiencies may be seen in this condition as well. The infectious agent responsible for this condition is Tropheryma whipplei, which causes Whipple disease. Patients may not have characteristic gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms.
Midbrain degeneration is associated with progressive supranuclear palsy and vertical gaze deficiencies but not oscillopsia. Alcoholics may develop vitamin deficiencies and Wernicke encephalopathy, which includes ophthalmoparesis but not oscillopsia with chewing. Arnold-Chiari I malformation may result in downbeat nystagmus that is constant and not induced by mastication.

Q899
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 25-year-old man presents with episodes of sharp, ice-pick-like right eye pain, right eye redness and tearing. In the differential for epiphora what is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. cluster headache
Rationale
In the differential of epiphora, ectropion, canaliculitis, and acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction all could be painful, but the classic description of the pain is the key to the diagnosis. Cluster headache is a trigeminal autonomic cephalgia that is characterized by attacks of intense pain in 1 eye that can last up to 3 hours, ipsilateral tearing, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, and postganglionic Horner syndrome. This severe pain that leaves the patient unable to rest is in contrast to the irritative and foreign body sensation from entropion or ectropion, or for that matter canaliculitis or the localized pressure and tenderness of dacryocystitis and nasal lacrimal duct obstruction.

Q900
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient has jerk nystagmus worse in down and lateral gaze to either side. What structure is most likely to have a lesion?
Correct answer: A. flocculus of the cerebellum
Rationale
Downbeat nystagmus results from lesions that compromise the vestibulocerebellum (ie, the nodulus, uvula, flocculus, and paraflocculus of the cerebellum). Examples of other localizing forms of central vestibular nystagmus are upbeat nystagmus (medulla), Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain), and seesaw nystagmus (parasellar region/diencephalon).

Q901
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 75-year-old patient with eye pain and transient monocular vision loss is found to have episcleral injection, aqueous flare, hypotony, and midperipheral retinal hemorrhages. Following surgical treatment for this disorder, the ophthalmologist should be alert to what potential complication?
Correct answer: A. increased intraocular pressure (IOP)
Rationale
This patient has ocular ischemic syndrome, which is most commonly caused by ipsilateral carotid artery stenosis. Thus, treatment includes carotid endarterectomy or other revascularization procedure to restore ocular and cerebral blood flow. The rapid return of normal perfusion to the eye may result in a sudden rise in IOP that may need medical or surgical management. The other conditions listed (RRD, cortical cataract formation, total corneal decompensation) are complications of various ocular surgeries, not carotid endarterectomy for ocular ischemic syndrome.

Q902
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient develops a facial nerve palsy and vesicles on the pinna of the ipsilateral ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. herpes zoster
Rationale
Herpes zoster involving the seventh cranial nerve is called Ramsay Hunt syndrome. It is diagnosed by the identification of vesicles along the posterior aspect of the external auditory canal, over the tympanic membrane, or the pinna. Facial pain is typically severe, and postherpetic neuralgia may result. Lyme disease, caused by infection with the tick-borne spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi, can cause unilateral or bilateral facial palsies but is not associated with vesicles. Classic manifestations include a characteristic rash, arthritis, and meningopolyneuritis. Similarly, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) may initially present with isolated seventh nerve palsy, or other isolated or multiple cranial nerve palsies, but not with vesicles. Facial diplegia may occur in Guillain-Barré syndrome, especially in the variant known as Miller Fisher syndrome when ophthalmoplegia and ataxia are also present. Vesicles on the pinna are not characteristic of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Q903
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What percentage of patients with acute isolated demyelinating optic neuritis have normal-appearing optic nerves?
Correct answer: A. 65%
Rationale
Acute isolated demyelinating optic neuritis is the most common form of optic neuritis. It typically presents in young white females, and the history usually consists of subacute painful monocular visual loss over the course of 1-3 days, with the pain worse with eye movements. Examination findings include decreased visual acuity, visual field defects, severe dyschromatopsia (especially red-green) proportionally worse than the loss of visual acuity, and a relative afferent pupillary defect if unilateral. Optic neuritis can affect the anterior optic nerve, which appears as optic nerve edema (papillitis), or the posterior optic nerve, which has a normal optic nerve appearance (retrobulbar optic neuritis).
According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial, most cases of optic neuritis are retrobulbar (65%), with the remaining 35% being anterior papillitis. These proportions do not apply to atypical causes of optic neuritis.

Q904
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What structure in the brainstem is responsible for the excitatory burst in horizontal eye movements?
Correct answer: B. paramedian pontine reticular formation
Rationale
Ocular motility is mediated by specific structures within the brainstem. Excitatory burst cells are constantly firing nerves that generate the tone for extraocular movement. Omnipause cells tonically inhibit the excitatory burst cells, and cortical impulses (signals for saccades, smooth pursuit, or vestibular-ocular reflex [VOR]) inhibit omnipause cells, which results in conjugate extraocular movement. A neural integrator receives cortical and cerebellar input to determine the amount of tone needed (ie, how far the eyes should move).
For horizontal movement, the excitatory burst cells are found in the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF), located adjacent to the nucleus of cranial nerve VI. Damage to the PPRF results in ipsilateral gaze palsy. The nucleus prepositus hypoglossi (NPH) is the neural integrator for horizontal movement. The rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (riMLF) and interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC), respectively, are the excitatory burst cells and neural integrator for vertical/torsional movement.

Q905
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Pupil-sparing third cranial nerve palsies are usually caused by what condition?
Correct answer: A. ischemia
Rationale
When the pupil function is completely normal (ie, equal pupil size and reactivity) but there is complete loss of eyelid and ocular motor function of the third nerve, this represents a typical finding of ischemic (microvascular) cranial neuropathy. Other associated findings can include pain. Ischemic diseases associated with this include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or hyperlipidemia. Neuroimaging may not be required immediately, depending on comorbid conditions; however, failure to recover after 3 months warrants investigation to rule out other possibilities, such as a mass or infiltrative lesion.
If there is relative pupil sparing, the pupil may react normally with only minimal impairment of levator palpebrae and extraocular function. When this occurs, other fibers within the third cranial nerve are spared and usually related to compressive lesions and can later progress to involve the pupil. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits using a gadolinium contrast agent and with attention to the path of the affected third nerve should be obtained.

Q906
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient has a right eye adduction deficit with abducting nystagmus of the left eye, otherwise full motility, normal pupils, and no ptosis. Where is the pathologic lesion most likely to be found?
Correct answer: C. right medial longitudinal fasciculus
Rationale
This patient has findings consistent with right internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO), which is caused by a lesion (usually demyelinating in younger patients and ischemic in older patients) in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). The cardinal sign of a unilateral INO is slowed adducting saccadic velocity in one eye, usually associated with abducting nystagmus in the fellow eye. The eye with slowed adduction might have a full or limited range of adduction. The INO is named for the side with slowed adduction (i.e., a right INO refers to slowed adduction of the right eye secondary to a MLF lesion on the right side of the brainstem).
A lesion of the anterior cavernous sinus could affect the inferior division of cranial nerve III, but it would also affect the ipsilateral pupil and inferior rectus function.

Q907
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 22-year-old woman noted blurred vision while reading. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU at distance, J1+ OU at near, with brisk pupillary responses, no relative afferent pupillary defect, and the brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shown. What additional finding associated with this disorder could account for her symptoms?
Correct answer: B. downbeat nystagmus
Rationale
Downbeat nystagmus from distortion of her craniocervical junction would explain her blurred vision in downgaze (reading position). The sagittal MRI scan shows herniation of the cerebellum through the foramen magnum (Chiari malformation). Anatomic abnormalities at the craniocervical junction may cause downbeating nystagmus, which is often worse in downgaze to the right and left. Patients may be asymptomatic in primary position, but as they look down to read, the nystagmus worsens, causing symptoms such as oscillopsia or blurred vision. Accommodative insufficiency would be unlikely, because she can read with J1+ vision OU without correction. Convergence retraction is typically seen with midbrain lesions and as part of the dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome. Bitemporal visual field defects would not be expected, because the optic chiasm is normal in this MRI scan.

Q908
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 37-year-old woman is having trouble keeping her eyes open. She has no other visual complaints and states she is otherwise in good health. Her central and peripheral vision is normal (perimetry performed with the eyelids taped up). Her ductions are reduced in all directions. The ptosis does not worsen with effort. What diagnostic test will be most specific for the most likely disorder?
Correct answer: D. muscle biopsy and genetic testing
Rationale
This patient has classic signs and symptoms of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO). It is an inherited mitochondrial myopathy characterized by slowly progressive, symmetric ophthalmoplegia with or without ptosis. Patients often present with ptosis and, because the ophthalmoplegia is usually symmetric, do not generally complain of diplopia. Genetic testing is available for detection of abnormalities in the mtDNA. Histologic examination of muscle biopsy specimens shows characteristic “ragged red fibers.” Western blot for Borrelia burgdorferi evaluates for Lyme disease, which would not present in this way. Edrophonium (Tensilon) testing is used for diagnosis of myasthenia gravis, which would show fatigable ptosis. MRI will be normal in a patient with CPEO.

Q909
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 57-year-old man presents with sudden painless altitudinal visual field loss in the left eye and corresponding hyperemic swelling of the left optic nerve, consistent with nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). What additional systemic evaluation should be obtained?
Correct answer: D. overnight polysomnography
Rationale
Numerous risk factors for NAION have been investigated over the years, and a correlation between obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and NAION has been described in several studies. In addition, there may be utility to treating OSA to prevent fellow eye involvement. Coagulopathies are not usually present in patients with NAION, and cardiac emboli also are not thought to be causative. Neuroimaging is not indicated in NAION patients, since the disorder is thought to result from microvascular ischemia that would not be seen on such studies.

Q910
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 27-year-old woman who delivered a healthy child 2 days prior presents with acute onset of severe headache, nausea, vomiting, and diplopia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings are shown. What finding is expected on visual field testing?
Correct answer: C. bitemporal hemianopia
Rationale
Several neuro-ophthalmic abnormalities occur with greater frequency or can be exacerbated during pregnancy or the postpartum period. These disorders include cerebral venous thrombosis, pituitary apoplexy, pseudotumor cerebri, and lymphocytic hypophysitis. Bitemporal hemianopia suggests damage to the optic chiasm from pituitary compression, commonly seen in the postpartum female with pituitary apoplexy. Hemorrhage within the tumor causes acute, painful ophthalmoplegia by extension into the adjacent cavernous sinus and is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment.
Homonymous hemianopia in a postpartum woman could be suggestive of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). However, in this case, MRI would be expected to show T2-hyperintense vasogenic edema involving the white matter of the posterior cerebral regions.
Arcuate visual field defects and blind spot enlargement both could occur in the setting of papilledema associated with cerebral venous thrombosis or pseudotumor cerebri. While symptoms of headache, nausea, vomiting, and diplopia could be consistent with increased intracranial pressure, the MRI would not demonstrate a hemorrhagic pituitary lesion in these cases.

Q911
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 35-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes presents with a 4-month history of diplopia. She reports that she was seen in her local emergency department and had a normal computed tomography (CT) head scan 3 months ago. Her examination findings are shown. What is the best next step in management?
Correct answer: A. urgent MRI brain with contrast and noninvasive angiography (computed tomography arteriography [CTA] or magnetic resonance angiography [MRA])
Rationale
This patient has aberrant regeneration of the third nerve, in which nerve fibers that originally were destined for the right inferior rectus are now innervating the right levator muscle (thus producing the synkinetic elevation of the lid with depression of the eye). Aberrant regeneration is common after trauma or compression by an aneurysm or tumor but does not occur with microvascular ischemia. The most important etiology to exclude emergently is posterior communicating artery ("Pcomm") aneurysm. The 3rd cranial nerve courses from the brainstem to the cavernous sinus through the intersection of the posterior communicating artery and internal carotid artery in the Circle of Willis, which can best be seen by cerebral arterial imaging.
Giant cell arteritis can cause a third-nerve palsy but would not be expected in a patient younger than age 50. In a patient over age 50 presenting with a third-nerve palsy and other signs or symptoms concerning for giant cell arteritis, ESR, and CRP should be checked.
While an MRI with contrast would be the test of choice to evaluate for a tumor, noninvasive angiography is required to reliably evaluate for aneurysm.

Q912
Neuro-Ophthalmology
One day ago, a patient developed a vesicular rash in the V1 dermatome. His primary care doctor started him on acyclovir and referred him for ophthalmologic examination. He does not have uveitis, and his ocular examination is unremarkable. What should the ophthalmologist do next?
Correct answer: C. Tell the primary care doctor and patient that there is no iritis, but uveitis may develop over weeks and follow-up will be arranged.
Rationale
The vesicular rash in the V1 dermatome is typical for that of shingles or varicella-zoster virus (VZV). The anterior uveitis (iritis) associated with herpes zoster in the V1 dermatome can be mild or severe, but may develop weeks after the onset of disease. It can be associated with decreased corneal sensation, diffuse keratic precipitates (sometimes stellate), iris atrophy, and increased intraocular pressure (due to trabeculitis; these are common findings in viral anterior uveitis), but all these findings may or may not be found. It may be very long-lasting, and if mild and chronic, respond to very low doses of topical corticosteroids. Anterior uveitis secondary to VZV may occur without skin lesions (known as varicella-zoster sine herpete).
Acyclovir may decrease the rate of anterior uveitis, though not in all cases, even at appropriate doses given in a timely manner. The use of oral steroids is ineffective in preventing post-herpetic neuralgia.

Q913
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What percentage of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) initially present with optic neuritis?
Correct answer: D. 25%
Rationale
Optic neuritis is a presenting symptom in 25% of MS patients, and their first evaluation will be performed by an ophthalmologist. In the optic neuritis treatment trial (ONTT), 50% of patients with optic neuritis developed clinically definite MS over the next 15 years, although the risk was much less for those with no brain MRI lesions at presentation (25%) versus those with 1 or more brain MRI lesions at presentation (72%).

Q914
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 53-year-old woman reports worsening ability to keep her eyes open. Because of this, she has stopped driving and reading. The examining ophthalmologist observes forceful, episodic bilateral eyelid closure with simultaneous contraction of the corrugator and procerus muscles. What is the best next step in management?
Correct answer: D. botulinum toxin injection
Rationale
Essential blepharospasm consists of episodic contraction of the orbicularis oculi. Onset usually occurs between ages 40 and 60 years. Initially, the spasms are mild, but they may progress to the point that the patient’s daily activities are severely disrupted. The exact cause of benign essential blepharospasm is unknown, but increasing evidence using functional neuroimaging suggests that it is caused by basal ganglia dysfunction. Currently, the treatment of choice for essential blepharospasm is injection of botulinum toxin into the orbicularis oculi muscle.
Neuroradiologic studies are generally unrevealing and rarely indicated. Essential blepharospasm can be exacerbated by stress, but referral to psychiatry is typically not warranted. Myasthenia gravis does not cause forceful contracture of the facial muscles.

Q915
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An optic nerve mass in a 6-year-old patient is most likely to show what feature on orbital imaging?
Correct answer: D. fusiform or globular enlargement of the optic nerve
Rationale
A 6-year-old patient with an optic nerve mass is most likely to have an optic nerve glioma, which is a tumor of pilocytic astrocyte origin. Approximately 70% of optic pathway gliomas are detected in the first decade of life, though they can occur at any age. Classic neuroradiologic features include fusiform or globular enlargement, as well as kinking or buckling of the optic nerve itself.
In contrast, optic nerve sheath meningiomas (ONSMs) are more common in adults and have the classic features of diffuse, tubular enlargement of the optic nerve with sheath thickening and enhancement, sparing the optic nerve substance (coined the "tram track" or "railroad track" signs). They are associated with calcification of the nerve sheath and adjacent bony hyperostosis on computed tomography (CT) scan, whereas optic nerve gliomas do not cause bony changes.

Q916
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 32-year-old woman presents with gradual reduction in vision over 2 days. On examination, there is a relative afferent pupillary defect with reduced color vision in 1 eye. There is no swelling of the optic nerve on visual examination. If this is typical isolated optic neuritis, when would she expect to recover vision?
Correct answer: D. within 1 to 3 months of presentation
Rationale
Most cases of optic neuritis are either isolated or due to a demyelinating disorder.  Common features of isolated optic neuritis include young age (mean 32 years) and female sex (77%), with subacute monocular visual loss that occurs over several days. Ninety-two percent of patients complain of pain with eye movements, and 65% of cases have only retrobulbar involvement. In typical optic neuritis, most patients experience improvement of vision within 1 month and recover the majority of their vision within 1 to 3 months of onset.
Atypical features that should prompt further workup include older age, lack of pain, peripapillary hemorrhages, ocular inflammation such as uveitis, choroiditis, retinal changes, involvement of other cranial nerves, and lack of any improvement in vision after 1 month.

Q917
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 29-year-old man with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy experienced bilateral, sequential vision loss in his teens. He asks if he might pass the disease to any children. What information can the ophthalmologist provide?
Correct answer: A. He cannot pass on the disease because only women can transmit this disorder.
Rationale
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy results from a mutation in the mitochondrial DNA, most frequently at the 11778 (followed by 14484, then 3460) positions. Since the mutation is transmitted via mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited only from the mother, only women transmit the disease. Not all men with affected mitochondria experience vision loss, and affected women experience visual symptoms infrequently. The reasons for selective male susceptibility are unknown.
The incorrect answer that his children have a 50% risk of receiving the disease gene and may be more severely affected at an earlier age describes an autosomal dominant condition with anticipation.
The incorrect answer that he can pass on the disease only if the mother also is a carrier for the same gene mutation describes an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

Q918
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient develops tearing while chewing.  What nerve was previously damaged?
Correct answer: D. CN VII
Rationale
Lacrimation while chewing (crocodile tears) is caused by aberrant facial nerve regeneration, in which the fibers originally supplying the mandibular and sublingual glands reinnervate the lacrimal gland by way of the greater superficial petrosal nerve.  This syndrome usually develops after severe injury to the proximal CN VII.

Q919
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An 80-year-old hypertensive man presents with 3 episodes of binocular transient visual loss (TVL) over the last week. He describes a sudden blackout of his entire vision for 1 to 2 minutes and resolving as quickly as it started. What is the most likely cause?
Correct answer: A. occipital ischemia
Rationale
Episodes of complete binocular TVL may represent a transient ischemic attack (TIA) that involves the occipital lobes in the distribution of the basilar artery or the bilateral posterior cerebral arteries. These episodes are particularly common in older patients with vascular risk factors or cardiac anomalies. Patients with suspected occipital TIA must be referred immediately to an emergency department and evaluated by a neurologist.
Migraine is the most common cause of transient visual loss that is generally hemianopic, involving dynamic positive visual phenomena, such as zigzag flashes, and lasts in the 20- to 30-minute range, but can be seen outside this range. Occipital arteriovenous malformation or other mass may be suspected in a patient with hemianopic visual field loss in the same location repeatedly, especially with associated headache that worsens in frequency or severity. Occipital seizures may cause transient hemianopic field unformed hallucinations, such as grid patterns.

Q920
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents with intraocular inflammation and testing reveals a positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test. What is the next step in management?
Correct answer: C. serum FTA-ABS and if positive, lumbar puncture with CSF VDRL, followed by antibiotic therapy
Rationale
Syphilitic uveitis is considered a CNS disease and warrants a lumbar puncture in all cases. A positive CSF VDRL is diagnostic for neurosyphilis. Because syphilitic uveitis is a CNS disease, it requires a neurologic dosing regimen of penicillin and so a single intramuscular injection will not be sufficient. A series of IV or IM dosing is necessary. Serum FTA-ABS is also useful as there are a number of reasons RPR can be falsely positive. However, it does not supplant the need for LP in the case of uveitis. Topical prednisolone is insufficient treatment for neurosyphilis. Penicillin is always required in neurosyphilis, even in the presence of a penicillin allergy. In these cases, desensitization is performed prior to treatment.

Q921
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What term describes an oscillating eye movement characterized by irregular, brief bursts of rapid frequency and low amplitude with no slow phase?
Correct answer: B. voluntary flutter
Rationale
Voluntary flutter, sometimes misdiagnosed as nystagmus, is characterized by irregular, brief bursts of rapid frequency and low-amplitude eye movements with no slow phase. Voluntary flutter is usually seen in patients with nonorganic motility disturbances. End-gaze nystagmus has a fast and slow phase; spasm of the near reflex is characterized by episodes of intermittent convergence, increased accommodation, and miosis. Seesaw nystagmus is a form of disconjugate nystagmus in which one eye elevates and intorts and the other eye depresses and extorts, like a seesaw.

Q922
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 45-year-old man presents with vertical double vision when he tilts his head to the left or looks to the right. What sign or symptom indicates that the cause of the diplopia is longstanding or congenital?
Correct answer: D. presence of 8 prism diopters of vertical fusional amplitude
Rationale
This patient presents with vertical diplopia when tilting his head to the left and looking to the right, which suggests a left 4th nerve palsy. The presence of increased vertical fusional amplitude indicates a longstanding or congenital vertical deviation. A normal vertical fusional amplitude is typically less than 3 prism diopters, and therefore a vertical fusional amplitude of 8 prism diopters indicates that this patient’s left 4th nerve palsy is likely congenital.
Excyclotorsion and diplopia are expected for any cause of 4th nerve palsy. Eyestrain can occur with any cause of diplopia.

Q923
Neuro-Ophthalmology
The classic triad of spasmus nutans includes ocular oscillations, head nodding, and what other symptom?
Correct answer: C. torticollis
Rationale
The classic triad of spasmus nutans is nystagmus, head nodding, and torticollis. Spasmus nutans typically develops in the first year of life, manifesting as intermittent, binocular, very small amplitude, high-frequency, pendular nystagmus. The nystagmus may be dissociated, even monocular. Spasmus nutans is a benign disorder and disappears after several years. However, nystagmus of spasmus nutans can be virtually impossible to distinguish from more ominous conditions of nystagmus of childhood. Therefore, most patients with presumed spasmus nutans should undergo neuroimaging to exclude a glioma of the anterior visual pathway and other parasellar or hypothalamic tumors.
Patients with spasmus nutans can have strabismus, but this is not part of the classic triad. They would not be expected to have vertigo or reduced deep tendon reflexes.

Q924
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 39-year-old woman diagnosed with normal-tension glaucoma in her right eye is referred to an ophthalmologist for evaluation. She reports that colors have appeared "washed out" in that eye for the past several months. She is noted to have a right-sided relative afferent pupillary defect (rAPD), and the dilated examination reveals optic nerve rim pallor on the right. What is the most important next step in her evaluation and management?
Correct answer: D. neuroimaging
Rationale
Normal-tension glaucoma should be considered a diagnosis of exclusion. Findings that should cause the clinician to look for other etiologies include unilateral disease, decreased central vision, dyschromatopsia, young age, the presence of a relative afferent pupillary defect, and/or neuroretinal rim pallor.
Neuroimaging should be the next step in evaluation, because the patient's symptoms and examination findings do not correlate with glaucoma. Perimetry and OCT are diagnostic tests for evaluating optic neuropathies, including glaucoma and optic atrophy, that would further characterize the optic neuropathy but would not determine the presence of a retrobulbar lesion. ESR and CRP should be considered if temporal arteritis is in the diagnosis, which is not likely in this scenario.

Q925
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Over the past 5 years, a 60-year-old woman has had slowly worsening vision and increasing proptosis in her right eye. She reports no sudden changes or eye pain. Her visual acuity is 20/30 OD, with a right relative afferent pupillary defect, and her right optic disc is mildly pale. Given the visual fields and imaging shown, what is the next step in managing this patient's condition?
Correct answer: D. orbitotomy with surgical excision of the lesion
Rationale
Patients with intraorbital or intracanalicular compressive lesions typically present with slowly progressive vision loss, a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), and monocular visual field loss. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of this patient shows a well-encapsulated intraconal lesion compressing the right optic nerve. The next step in management would be orbitotomy with surgical excision of the lesion for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. This patient underwent endoscopic medial orbitotomy with tumor removal. The final pathology results showed cavernous hemangioma.
Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign neoplasm in the orbit in adults. Slowly progressive proptosis is usually the principal finding, although compressive optic neuropathy also can occur. Imaging typically demonstrates a homogeneously enhancing, well-encapsulated mass. Treatment is surgical excision, if the lesion is causing significant proptosis, compromising vision (as in this case), or growing significantly.
Fine-needle aspiration biopsy may provide the diagnosis, but it would not relieve the compression and could potentially make a cavernous hemangioma bleed. Stereotactic radiation would not provide a tissue diagnosis and is not the typical treatment for cavernous hemangioma, which was the most likely diagnosis based on the MRI. Continued observation with annual examination is not appropriate, because there is progressive worsening of vision from compressive optic neuropathy.

Q926
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What ocular complication may occur with use of fingolimod in the treatment of multiple sclerosis?
Correct answer: B. cystoid macular edema
Rationale
Fingolimod, an oral medication approved for treatment of relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis, is associated with a 0.5% risk of development of cystoid macular edema. The risk is increased in patients with diabetes or a history of uveitis. The macular edema typically resolves upon cessation of fingolimod therapy. It is important that cystoid macular edema be considered as a possible etiology for vision loss in patients receiving fingolimod treatment for multiple sclerosis. It is recommended that screening for macular edema with dilated funduscopic examination be performed at baseline and again 3 to 4 months after initiation of fingolimod treatment.

Q927
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What maneuver can be useful to diagnose a suspected nonphysiologic ptosis?
Correct answer: C. Ask the patient to look up.
Rationale
Patients who feign ptosis generally cannot simultaneously elevate the eye and maintain a drooping eyelid. Thus, with upward gaze, the ptosis will "resolve." Looking down is not as effective for this purpose. Asking the patient to look down for a few seconds and then refixate straight ahead is a way to evaluate the patient for Cogan lid-twitch sign, which can be present in patients with myasthenia gravis. Asking a patient to make horizontal saccades and measure the palpebral fissures is used for the evaluation of aberrant regeneration or Duane retraction syndromes.

Q928
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Trigeminal neuralgia can result from what artery coming in contact with the trigeminal root in the subarachnoid space?
Correct answer: C. superior cerebellar artery
Rationale
Within the subarachnoid space, the trigeminal root may come in contact with the superior cerebellar artery and cause trigeminal neuralgia. Trigeminal neuralgia presents with unilateral facial pain described as an electric shock-like sensation lasting seconds to minutes, usually in the CN V2 or V3 distribution. Microvascular decompression involves surgical placement of a spacer (often a sponge) between the trigeminal nerve and the superior cerebellar artery.

Q929
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Following an automobile accident, a young man complains of diplopia. In primary position he has 6 prism diopters (PD) of right hypertropia. In left gaze he has 12 PD of right hypertropia, and in right gaze 9 PD of left hypertropia. In primary position, the patient has 16 degrees of excyclotorsion. On right head tilt he has a right hypertropia, and in left head tilt he has a left hypertropia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. bilateral fourth cranial nerve palsies
Rationale
Bilateral fourth cranial nerve palsy should always be considered whenever a unilateral fourth nerve palsy is suspected, especially after head trauma. Bilateral cranial fourth nerve palsy presents with:
  • crossed hypertropia (ie, the right eye is higher on left gaze, and the left eye is higher on right gaze)
  • excyclotorsion of 10 degrees or greater (best measured with double Maddox rod testing)
  • a large (≥25 prism diopters) V pattern strabismus
  • habitual chin down position
This patient demonstrates both crossed hypertropia and high amounts of excyclotorsion following head trauma, which is indicative of bilateral fourth nerve palsies.
The presence of a third nerve palsy alone or in combination with a fourth nerve palsy would result in horizontal misalignment. Entrapment of ocular muscles is not variable in gaze positions and is not affected by head tilt.

Q930
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 42-year-old woman presents with photophobia worsening over the last 6 months. On examination, the ophthalmologist notices anisocoria with a large right pupil. The difference in pupil size is greater in light. When re-fixating from near to distance, her right pupil is slow to re-dilate. On slit-lamp examination her iris shows sectoral palsy of the pupillary sphincter. What is her most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. Adie tonic pupil
Rationale
This patient has Adie tonic pupil. The sectoral palsy and slow vermiform iris contraction are typical signs of Adie tonic pupil. Cranial nerve III involvement would give a fixed dilated pupil. Horner syndrome would present with anisocoria in dim illumination. Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome patients may have an irregular pupil contour and size with scarring between iris and endothelium.

Q931
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Microscopy of the irregular myocytes ("ragged-red" fibers) from a muscle biopsy as shown is most characteristic of what disease?
Correct answer: C. mitochondrial myopathy
Rationale
Mitochondrial myopathies are associated with abnormal mitochondria. Histologically, one sees irregular or ragged red fibers and inclusion body abnormalities on electron microscopy of muscle. Myasthenia gravis is associated with blockage of acetylcholine receptor sites by immune complexes. Congenital Horner syndrome is caused by pathology elsewhere along the oculosympathetic pathway. Myotonic dystrophy is associated with typical myotonic discharges, which can be demonstrated with electromyography.

Q932
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A woman presents with the findings below after a motor vehicle accident. What finding might be seen in this patient?
Correct answer: C. elevated IOP in the right eye
Rationale
This patient has dilated and arterialized conjunctival vessels on the right from a traumatic carotid cavernous fistula. Supporting this diagnosis is the fullness of the right superior sulcus and a right abduction deficit. This patient's esotropia might be due to sixth nerve palsy or to congestive orbitopathy. The vascular congestion caused by the fistula leads to elevated IOP and might cause dilation and enlargement, not thinning, of the right cavernous sinus. The retinal venous system becomes dilated, and not attenuated, as the venous system becomes filled with arterial blood. Angiography would be helpful to determine the site of the fistula. This patient has an abduction deficit in right gaze, so an esotropia, not exotropia, is present.

Q933
Neuro-Ophthalmology
During what decade of life is a diagnosis of optic pathway glioma most likely?
Correct answer: A. first decade
Rationale
Optic pathway glioma is a slow-growing tumor that typically affects children. Ten to seventy percent (10%-70%) of patients have associated NF1, and those patients have a better prognosis. Patients with optic pathway gliomas most frequently present in the first decade of life. Malignant gliomas (glioblastoma) are rare; they almost always occur in adult males, and they have a very poor prognosis, including almost certain death within 1 year. Optic pathway gliomas constitute about 1% of all intracranial tumors.

Q934
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 45-year-old woman reports bilateral eyelid twitching for the past 3 months. She has noticed that is has gotten worse, and on occasion has made it difficult to read and perform her job in data entry. She reports no new external stressors. How would her condition typically be managed?
Correct answer: A. episodic injections of botulinum toxin type A
Rationale
Benign essential blepharospasm (BEB) is a form of bilateral facial dystonia. It is more common in middle-aged women. Characterized by increased blinking and involuntary spasms of the muscles around the eyes, the spasms usually start as twitches and progress to forceful contractures. This condition can be severe in some individuals, causing difficulty with activities of daily living. It may even render these patients functionally blind due to episodic sustained contracture. Diagnosis is made clinically, and neuroimaging is rarely indicated. The exact cause of BEB is unknown, but is believed to originate in the basal ganglia. BEB must be differentiated from hemifacial spasm.
Hemifacial spasm involves the contracture of the entire side of one’s face and is almost always unilateral. Hemifacial spasm is due to vascular compression of the facial nerve at the brain stem by enlarged vessels. Magnetic resonance imaging/magnetic resonance angiography (MRI/MRA) can be useful in visualizing this vascular abnormality. Unlike benign cases of blepharospasm, hemifacial spasm can occur at any time, even during sleep. Treatment options for hemifacial spasm may include surgical decompression of the brain stem, as well as temporizing treatments such as Botox injections. Management of BEB can include injection with Botox, surgical myectomy, and ablation of the facial nerve. Episodic injection of Botox type A is the first line of treatment and is usually very effective at relieving symptoms. Injections start working after several days and typically last for up to 4 months. As the effect wears off, re-injection is required. Botox type B can also be used, but in general, injections are less tolerated and less effective. However, treatment failure with injection with Botox type A may be followed by a trial of injection with Botox type B.
Complications of Botox injection usually result from medication spread to adjacent muscles and can include blepharoptosis, epiphora, diplopia, lagophthalmos, and ectropion. For patients unresponsive to Botox therapy, subtotal myectomy of the orbicularis oculi is the next option for treatment. This may also make the patient more responsive in the future to Botox injection, which should be re-attempted if myectomy is not completely effective. For those still severely debilitated by spasms, total myectomy can be a permanent solution of last resort. In the past, partial ablation of the facial nerve had been a treatment for people with severe blepharospasm, but recurrence rates were high, as was the risk of hemifacial paralysis. Of note, medical treatment with muscle relaxants and sedatives has little use. Also, psychotherapy has been unsuccessful in treating this disease.

Q935
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 39-year-old woman with a history of polycystic kidney disease presents with sudden onset of severe headache, nausea, vomiting, and blurred vision, which started 30 minutes ago. She has no prior history of migraine headaches and believes her symptoms are from nicotine withdrawal. On examination, she has preretinal and intraretinal hemorrhages in both eyes, with mild optic disc swelling. What management is most appropriate at this time?
Correct answer: D. computed tomography (CT) of head with CT angiography of head and neck
Rationale
This patient has new severe headaches with cerebral aneurysm risk factors, including cigarette smoking and polycystic kidney disease. Other predisposing factors include hypertension, arteriovenous malformations, coarctation of the aorta, and connective tissue diseases. Examination findings indicate either suddenly increased intracranial pressure or subarachnoid hemorrhage (perhaps both). This presentation is an emergency that requires immediate imaging. CT is preferred for detection of acute intracranial hemorrhage, and CT angiography can be performed at the same time to look for aneurysm. This patient should be sent to the nearest emergency department for this assessment.

Q936
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Myasthenia gravis is closely associated with what immune system-mediated disorder?
Correct answer: B. thyroid eye disease
Rationale
Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder associated with antibodies directed against the acetylcholine receptor antibody at the neuromuscular junction. It is associated with other autoimmune disorders, particularly thyroid orbitopathy. Thyroid eye disease is present in 5% of patients with myasthenia gravis.

Q937
Neuro-Ophthalmology
If a lesion affects the right and left occipital lobes, resulting in alexia, what structure must also be involved if the patient also has agraphia?
Correct answer: B. dominant angular gyrus
Rationale
Patients with damage to the dominant occipital lobe (and splenium of the corpus callosum) can have interruption of information passing from the left visual field (right occipital lobe) to the left angular gyrus where it is processed. These patients can write but are unable to read. If the left angular gyrus is damaged, then both reading and writing will be affected (alexia with agraphia).
Occipitotemporal lesions often cause hallucinations and may result in inability to recognize faces (prosopagnosia) or object agnosia. Occipital ventromedial cortex lesions may cause hemiachromatopsia or achromatopsia, depending upon their extent with associated superior homonymous visual field loss. Lesions of the cingulate gyrus may result in hemispatial neglect.

Q938
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What assessment may best distinguish between a retinopathy and an optic neuropathy?
Correct answer: B. electrophysiology
Rationale
Determining if vision loss is related to retinal disease or optic neuropathy is a common question, especially when the clinical findings and history are nonspecific. Optical coherence tomography is helpful for visualizing the retina or optic nerve anatomy and quantifying thickness of the retina or retinal nerve fiber layer, respectively. However, many retinopathies will eventually result in thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer (and can even cause optic atrophy), and primary optic neuropathies can result in thinning of the retina around the macula.
Fluorescein angiography may be helpful in distinguishing between pseudoedema and true edema of the optic nerve, and can also reveal certain retinal vascular and anatomic defects. However, fluorescein angiography alone does not differentiate between all retinopathies and optic neuropathies. For example, macular edema may be present in optic neuropathies (such as neuroretinitis or severe papilledema). Decreased color vision out of proportion to visual acuity may suggest optic neuropathy, but in cases where there is decreased visual acuity and color vision, it may not be as clear-cut: Maculopathies can also cause decreased color vision. Electrophysiologic studies (electroretinogram [ERG] and visual evoked potentials [VEP]) can be very specific in localizing the etiology of the vision loss to the retina or optic nerve. For example, an abnormal ERG and VEP would be consistent with retinopathy, whereas a normal ERG and abnormal VEP is highly suggestive of an optic neuropathy.

Q939

A vasculopathic patient presents with sudden onset facial weakness, diminished ipsilateral hearing, and vestibular dysfunction. What test is most appropriate?
Correct answer: B. neuroimaging of the posterior fossa
Rationale

Q940
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 77-year-old man presents with subacute vision loss in the right eye, pain with eye movements, a right relative afferent pupillary defect, and the clinical findings shown below. For this condition, what is the clinical finding and its most likely etiology?
Correct answer: B. vasculitis
Rationale
This patient has herpes zoster ophthalmicus involving the first distribution of cranial nerve V on the right side. The disorder is thought to occur from reactivation and replication of herpes virus within the trigeminal ganglion. The skin lesions begin as vesicles that then crust; they are not related to bacterial infection. Anterior uveitis may occur and is thought to be related to inflammation and not ischemia. Cranial nerve palsies, including cranial nerves III, IV, and VI, are believed to occur from inflammation or vasculitis; a concurrent compressive lesion is extremely unlikely. In some cases, optic neuritis may occur and is typically a result of vasculitis.

Q941
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient with severe vision loss due to advanced glaucoma experiences hallucinations that he recognizes are not real. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. Charles Bonnet syndrome
Rationale
Charles Bonnet syndrome is a condition in which severe visual impairment, as is possible with advanced glaucoma, leads to hallucinations. Patients are aware the hallucinations are not real.
Uhthoff phenomenon refers to worsening of vision in multiple sclerosis patients when their bodies become overheated. It happens in patients with a history of optic neuritis.
Anton-Babinski syndrome is a condition in which patients who are cortically blind do not recognize their vision loss.
Muir-Torre syndrome is an autosomal dominant cancer syndrome associated with both a sebaceous carcinoma and an internal malignancy.

Q942
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Damage to what part of the visual system is responsible for the loss of color vision in cerebral achromatopsia?
Correct answer: B. area V4, within the lingual and fusiform gyrus
Rationale
Area V4, within the lingual and fusiform gyrus, seems to be particularly sensitive to color. Damage to this area is probably responsible for most cases of cerebral achromatopsia. Area V1, within the striate cortex, is also known as the primary visual cortex, or Brodmann area 17. It is arrayed along the horizontal calcarine fissure and holds the terminal cortical neurons mediating primary detection of visual stimuli. Area V3, which lies primarily in the posterior parietal lobe, receives direct input from V1 and is involved in visual integration. Area V5, within the medial temporal region, holds neurons that encode the speed and direction of moving stimuli. This sensory area is likely the origin of pursuit movements and thus connects the afferent and efferent pathways.

Q943
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 19-year-old man has drooping eyelids that do not change position during the day. The ophthalmic examination is remarkable for chin-up positioning, limitation of ocular motility in all directions, and pigmentary changes in the peripheral retina. Orbital imaging shows thin, atrophic extraocular muscles. What abnormality would be expected to be found on muscle biopsy?
Correct answer: B. "ragged red fibers"
Rationale
The combination of constant, bilateral ptosis; pigmentary retinopathy; and extraocular muscle thinning in a young man is most likely to be from chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO). The chin-up posture is characteristic, and the patient may be unaware of both the ptosis and head position because they develop very slowly. Muscle biopsy demonstrated "ragged red fibers."
Non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of sarcoidosis. IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration of tissues is characteristic of IgG-4-related disease. Bland-appearing epithelial cells arranged in a "Swiss cheese" pattern are characteristic of adenoid cystic carcinoma.

Q944
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 70-year-old man presents with complaints of seeing a red flash in his right eye for 1 year, every time he hears his doorbell ring. What clinical history would be consistent with his symptom?
Correct answer: B. long-standing optic neuropathy of the right eye
Rationale
Patients with subacute or long-standing optic neuropathy may experience sound-induced photisms (sensations of color or light induced by a loud noise). These photisms are attributed to discharges from the lateral geniculate nucleus, which is also responsive to sound. In general, lesions affecting the anterior optic radiations (ie, temporal lobe) typically cause formed hallucinations, whereas more posterior lesions (ie, parietal and occipital lobes) typically produce unformed hallucinations, there are many exceptions. Temporal lobe lesions most often produce olfactory and gustatory hallucinations, but they can also can cause complex, formed hallucinations in either the ipsilateral or the contralateral visual field. Patients with occipital lobe lesions may describe white or colored flashes of light, kaleidoscopic colors, moving discs, flickering, or a hexagonal array (eg, chicken-wire or honeycomb patterns). Retinal vasospasm can cause transient loss of vision due to transient retinal ischemia, but it is not triggered by sound.

Q945
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 30-year-old man presents with the finding shown in the figure. His visual function is normal at the time of the examination. What is the expected clinical course in this case?
Correct answer: D. stable course with no significant vision loss
Rationale
The figure depicts myelinated nerve fibers. Myelination of the optic nerve normally stops at the lamina cribrosa. However, sometimes myelination inappropriately extends anterior to the lamina and can be seen at the optic nerve head margins. Myelinated nerve fibers can obscure the retinal vessels, thus mimicking papilledema. However, the dense white appearance of myelinated nerve fibers can be differentiated from the partially translucent, grayish appearance of true edema. With myelinated nerve fibers, vision loss is rare unless there is macular involvement. Myelination is stable and does not progress.
Acute onset of vision loss, with variable levels of recovery, may occur in optic neuritis (among other causes). Progressive vision loss may occur in compressive optic neuropathy (among other causes). Acute onset of vision loss, with minimal recovery, may occur in arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (among other causes).

Q946
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 47-year-old man complains of difficulty in reading. His visual acuity is 20/20 and J1, OU. His ocular examination is unrevealing except for the visual fields shown. What test or intervention step is indicated next?
Correct answer: B. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain
Rationale
The patient has a right inferior homonymous scotoma causing difficulty in reading. The homonymous nature indicates a retrochiasmal lesion. The first step would be an MRI to evaluate for a structural cause, such as a prior stroke or tumor. An MRA of the carotids would not evaluate the retrochiasmal pathway. Gonioscopy would be in order if one were to suspect a Bjerrum scotoma from normal tension glaucoma, but glaucoma would not be expected to cause a homonymous scotoma. The patient is 47 and therefore may have some presbyopia, but in this case, he is able to read J1, and therefore his difficulty in reading is most likely from the homonymous scotoma.

Q947
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most likely diagnosis for a 10-year-old girl who has bilateral optic disc pallor, 20/60 vision with mild dyschromatopsia, and family history of visual loss in her father and brother?
Correct answer: B. autosomal dominant optic atrophy
Rationale
Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy, with an estimated prevalence of 1:50,000. It is caused by mutations of the OPA1 gene on chromosome 3, producing a protein that interrupts mitochondrial membrane integrity and function. ADOA causes maculopapular bundle defects and temporal optic atrophy, with resulting central vision loss and central or cecocentral visual field loss. The question stem describes a typical ADOA patient who has a dominant inheritance pattern, a color vision defect (often tritanopia), and moderate vision loss in the first decade of life.
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is also a mitochondrial optic neuropathy, but it has a mitochondrial DNA inheritance pattern (transmitted only by women) affecting primarily boys and men age 10 to 30 years. Although B12 vitamin deficiency is in the differential of central vision loss, it is much more common in older patients with intestinal malabsorption or malnutrition and no family history of vision loss. Stargardt disease would affect this age group, but instead of optic disc pallor on examination, one would expect to find a bull's-eye lesion and pisciform flecks in the macula, and inheritance is most commonly autosomal recessive, not autosomal dominant as in ADOA.

Q948
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 23-year old obese female presents with worsening headaches, pulse-synchronous tinnitus, and transient visual obscurations. A dilated fundus examination reveals bilateral disc edema. What is the most common motility abnormality in this patient?
Correct answer: C. abduction deficit
Rationale
This young obese female has signs and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure (ICP). Given her age and obesity, the patient likely has idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), but this diagnosis requires a MRI to rule out a structural cause and a lumbar puncture to evaluate the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and to measure the opening pressure. Patients with raised ICP have bilateral papilledema, which leads to an absence of spontaneous venous pulsations. The most common visual field defects from raised ICP are enlarged blind spots and nasal step defects. Patients with raised ICP can have diplopia due to abducens palsy. Raised ICP would not be expected to cause an adduction deficit, upgaze paralysis, or nystagmus.

Q949
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 72-year-old man is admitted to the neurology department due to acute stroke. His eyes both tonically deviate to the left. Doll's head maneuver produces full ocular motility. What is the most likely location of his lesion?
Correct answer: A. left cortex
Rationale
Gaze preference is an acute inability to produce gaze contralateral to the side of a cerebral (supranuclear) lesion. It is accompanied by a tendency for the eyes to tonically deviate toward the side of the lesion. The doll's head maneuver generates a full range of horizontal eye movements because the vestibular-ocular pathways are intact. Stroke is the most common etiology.
Gaze palsy is a symmetric limitation of movements of both eyes in the same direction. Sixth nerve nuclear lesions producing a horizontal gaze palsy disrupt eye movements toward the side of the lesion. Since sixth nerve nuclear lesions damage the final common site for supranuclear innervation of horizontal eye movements, the doll's head maneuver does not cause movement of the eyes toward the side of the lesion.

Q950
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What examination finding would suggest functional rather than organic vision loss in a patient with apparent no light perception (NLP) vision in both eyes?
Correct answer: A. inaccurate finger-touching test
Rationale
Even complete vision loss should not affect proprioception, and just as finger-touching testing should be accurate with the eyes closed, it should also be normal with NLP vision. The near triad of accommodation, convergence, and pupillary miosis may be preserved in patients with vision loss. For example, patients with NLP vision from organic disease may show pupillary constriction and convergence when asked to "look" at an object they know is close to them. This pupillary reaction should not be taken as evidence of vision. A normal a-wave on ERG does not preclude organic vision loss from inner retinal or ganglion cell pathology. Exodeviation may occur from inattention or vision loss and is not evidence for either functional or organic vision disturbances.

Q951
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the "gold standard" imaging study to exclude a cerebral aneurysm?
Correct answer: C. conventional angiography
Rationale
The definitive method to exclude a cerebral aneurysm is conventional angiography. The other choices (CT with contrast, MRI with IV gadolinium, MRA), are less-invasive methods to evaluate the orbital vasculature, and can be helpful, but are not the best way to exclude an aneurysm.

Q952
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What cranial nerve palsy is most commonly associated with idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
Correct answer: A. cranial nerve VI
Rationale
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is characterized by signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (headaches, nausea, vomiting, transient visual obscuration, and papilledema). Patients are awake and alert and show no localizing neurologic signs other than unilateral or bilateral abducens nerve palsy (cranial nerve VI). Headaches are not a neurologically localizing finding. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure is elevated, with normal CSF cytology and chemistry. Neuroimaging studies are normal except for small ventricles or empty sella. No other cause of intracranial hypertension is present. Localizing neurologic signs such as seizures or IV palsies suggest a tumor, not a pseudotumor.

Q953
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What clinical test best quantifies torsional strabismus?
Correct answer: A. double Maddox rod
Rationale
The double Maddox rod test helps identify and quantify torsional misalignment when vertical diplopia is present. The alternate cover test, cover-uncover test, and red glass test are used to identify and quantify horizontal and vertical misalignment, but not torsional misalignment.

Q954
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 49-year-old patient has right eye paracentral visual field loss found on routine examination. Cup to disc ratio is mildly elevated with pallor of the right optic disc noted on examination. Intraocular pressure is 24 mm Hg in both eyes. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient's condition?
Correct answer: A. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain and orbits with gadolinium contrast
Rationale
This patient has an asymptomatic visual field defect found on examination, with optic disc pallor in the affected eye. Although the intraocular pressure is elevated, the presence of pallor suggests that there is a nonglaucomatous optic neuropathy in addition to any glaucomatous damage. The patient may benefit from lowering the intraocular pressure, but an MRI brain/orbits must be obtained first to look for a possible compressive lesion giving the insidious visual field loss and pallor. Only in very advanced glaucoma can pallor be seen.
Repeat testing in 6 months without neuroimaging also is inappropriate, given that pallor is present. Screening for infectious or inflammatory disorders in the absence of active ocular inflammation or a swollen optic nerve is unlikely to be useful and should be done only if the neuroimaging is negative and there are other clinical or historical factors that raise the risk for one of these infections.

Q955
Neuro-Ophthalmology
In a patient with Horner syndrome, what additional finding would suggest an acute carotid artery dissection?
Correct answer: A. facial pain
Rationale
Painful Horner syndrome can be associated with internal carotid artery dissection. Pain from dissection is usually located around the temple and orbit and can extend to the throat. Internal carotid artery dissection is often accompanied by sympathetic dysfunction (Horner syndrome) due to involvement of the sympathetic fibers in the wall of the carotid artery. Patients with a possible carotid dissection must be recognized because, in the acute stage, stroke is a possible complication.
Hydroxyamphetamine testing can help localize a Horner syndrome to a postganglionic (third-order) neuron if the pupil does not dilate after instillation of hydroxyamphetamine 1%
Hemoptysis in the setting of a Horner syndrome is concerning for apical lung mass (Pancoast tumor).
Iris heterochromia in this setting suggests congenital Horner syndrome.

Q956
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What imaging technique is preferred to detect acute subarachnoid hemorrhage?
Correct answer: D. computed tomography (CT)
Rationale
CT is the preferred imaging modality to detect acute subarachnoid hemorrhage. MRI is not preferred for detecting acute hemorrhage, but it can clarify the evolution of intraparenchymal hemorrhage. CTA and MRA are preferred for detection of aneurysms and carotid stenosis.

Q957
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 68-year-old woman has a 2-month history of diplopia when she drives. She is otherwise healthy and denies fatigue, weight loss, nausea, and headache. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU, her pupils are equal, and the motility examination demonstrates full lateral excursion in both eyes with mild limitation of elevation of both eyes. She has deep superior sulci. There is an esotropia of 12 PD in primary and lateral gazes with orthophoria at near. Facial sensation is symmetric with no ptosis or eyelid retraction, and anterior and posterior segments are normal. What is the preferred treatment for the most likely cause of her diplopia?
Correct answer: B. base-out prism in her distance spectacles or strabismus surgery
Rationale
This case describes a woman with divergence insufficiency secondary to sagging eye syndrome. Sagging eye syndrome is caused by degeneration of the lateral rectus-superior rectus band, leading to inferior displacement of the lateral rectus muscle. Patients develop diplopia due to a comitant esodeviation greater at distance than at near vision (usually orthophoric at near). While lateral eye movements remain full, there may be some limitation of supraduction, which can be asymmetric in some cases. In addition to the divergence insufficiency pattern esotropia, sagging eye syndrome often is associated with deep superior sulci, high lid creases, and ptosis from levator dehiscence. Since the esotropia is comitant and no worse in abduction (which would suggest a sixth nerve palsy), as well as being found in isolation, it is likely benign and can be treated optically with base-out prism over distance spectacles. Strabismus surgery is another treatment option.
The incorrect answer choices address the differential diagnosis of new-onset esotropia: myasthenia gravis, which can be treated with pyridostigmine; Graves disease, in which the thyroid hormone abnormality can be treated by decreasing the thyroid antibody response with methimazole; and, in patients over 50 years old, giant cell arteritis, which is treated with high-dose steroid.

Q958
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An 87-year-old man presents with sudden complete and painless loss of vision in the left eye. What laboratory tests should be performed urgently?
Correct answer: B. erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and complete blood cell count
Rationale
An elderly patient presenting with a central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) has giant cell arteritis (GCA) until proven otherwise. Because of the potential for contralateral vision loss and systemic vascular complications, workup and treatment should be performed emergently. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) are nonspecific measures of inflammation. ESR increases with anemia and age. Most cases of GCA have markedly elevated ESR, although ESR can be normal in up to 16% of cases. CRP is less affected by age and anemia and, therefore, may be more specific for the diagnosis of GCA. Thrombocytosis may suggest active disease.
Factor V Leiden assay, homocysteine level, and lupus anticoagulant evaluate for causes of thrombophilia. While a hypercoagulable state also could be a cause for CRAO, GCA must be ruled out first, prior to pursuing further work up. Antinuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and rheumatoid factor are screening tools for autoimmune disorders. Again, GCA must be ruled out prior to pursuing further work up. Infectious diseases such as Lyme, Bartonella, and syphilis do not typically present with a CRAO.

Q959
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What pupillary abnormality may be present in an optic tract lesion?
Correct answer: B. contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect
Rationale
There is an asymmetric hemidecussation of the optic nerve axons at the chiasm, with more crossed (53%) than uncrossed (47%) fibers. Thus, each optic tract contains more axons from the contralateral eye than the ipsilateral eye. Pupillomotor fibers travel in the optic tract and exit just before the lateral geniculate nucleus for the brachium of the superior colliculus. When an optic tract lesion occurs, it can damage both pupillomotor and visual fibers, resulting in a contralateral visual field defect and relative afferent pupillary defect.
Light-near dissociation can occur with dorsal midbrain lesions. Sympathetic nerves do not travel in the optic tract, and a tract lesion does not cause a Horner syndrome. Fixed pupils are not a result of optic tract damage.

Q960
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 60-year-old woman presents with transient monocular vision loss that has now resolved. The history reveals recent weight loss, general malaise, and proximal joint pain. What test is essential and should be checked immediately in the evaluation of this patient?
Correct answer: A. erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Rationale
ESR is the correct answer. Give yourself full points if you wrote C-reactive protein (CRP) or temporal artery biopsy in challenge mode.
Symptoms of giant cell arteritis (GCA) usually present as headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, or malaise. Patients with GCA may also present with weight loss, proximal joint pain, or muscle aches. Up to 20% of patients present with occult symptoms. Older patients with transient monocular vision loss should be evaluated for GCA, as this condition has a significant mortality. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is markedly elevated in 90% of patients, and diagnostic confidence is increased if the C‑reactive protein level and the platelet count are elevated. This is a "do not miss" diagnosis, and ESR/CRP evaluation is critical.
RF is a useful test, especially in a patient with joint pain, but ESR is more critical.
Automated perimetry is useful to document vision loss, but in this case, because the symptoms are transient, the results will likely be normal. This test is reasonable to obtain, but is not critical on initial evaluation.
Glucose level would be used to check for diabetes, but less likely given the question stem and not immediately life threatening like GCA.
