Q961
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with a 3-hour history of severe headache, accompanied by altered mental status, and decreased vision in her right eye. Her medical history includes chronic hypertension. Her right eyelid is mildly ptotic, and she has limitations in adduction and infraduction in the right eye only. Her right pupil is dilated and unreactive; her left pupil is normal. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye reveals a vitreous hemorrhage obscuring the posterior pole. The peripheral retina appears normal. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic test in the management of this patient?
Correct answer: C. computed tomography (CT) and CT angiography (CTA) of the brain
Rationale
The presentation of acute-onset headache, altered mental status, third cranial nerve palsy and a vitreous hemorrhage is strongly suggestive of a subarachnoid hemorrhage from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm with Terson syndrome. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) accounts for nearly 50% of cases with intracranial hemorrhage. Its incidence increases with age, and it is more common in women. African American and Hispanic individuals have a higher incidence of SAH when compared with white individuals. Most SAHs result from saccular, or "berry," aneurysms. Only a minority of cases of SAH are nonaneurysmal in etiology. Approximately 85% of congenital saccular, or "berry," aneurysms develop in the anterior part of the circle of Willis. The origin of the posterior communicating artery from the internal carotid artery is the most common site. Such an aneurysm typically presents with headache and third cranial nerve palsy involving the pupil. Vascular malformations within and on the surface of the brain parenchyma constitute approximately 7% of cases of subarachnoid hemorrhage and arise from capillary telangiectasias, cavernous hemangiomas, venous angiomas, or AVMs.
SAH usually presents with abrupt onset severe headache that is typically described by patients as the "worst headache of my life." The headache occurs in 97% of  cases; 30% have symptoms lateralized to the side of the hemorrhage. The combination of vitreous hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage (Terson syndrome) portends a worse prognosis. Maintaining a high index of suspicion and evaluating the patient with noncontrast CT, followed by mandatory lumbar puncture if CT results are negative, are essential in making the diagnosis. Digital subtraction angiography is superior to CT or MRA for the detection of SAH due to aneurysm.
Terson syndrome is a vitreous and sub-ILM or subhyaloid hemorrhage caused by an abrupt intracranial hemorrhage. Although the exact mechanism is not known, it is suspected that the acute intracranial hemorrhage causes an acute rise in the intraocular venous pressure, resulting in a rupture of peripapillary and retinal vessels. Approximately one-third of patients with subarachnoid or subdural hemorrhage have associated intraocular hemorrhage, which may include intraretinal and subretinal bleeding. Terson syndrome occurs primarily in individuals between 30 and 50 years old, but it can occur at any age. In most cases, the visual function is unaffected once the hemorrhage clears. Spontaneous improvement generally occurs, although vitrectomy is occasionally required to clear the ocular media.
Pupillary dysfunction with CN III palsy results from loss of parasympathetic input and produces a mid-dilated pupil that responds poorly to light. Patients may present with variable dysfunction of the levator palpebrae or extraocular muscles. Aneurysms that arise at the junction of the posterior communicating artery (PCoA) and internal carotid artery (ICA) are juxtaposed to CN III and are, therefore, in a position to produce a CN III palsy as the initial manifestation of aneurysmal expansion or rupture. Pupillary involvement occurs because the pupillomotor fibers reside superficially in the medial aspect of the nerve adjacent to the PCoA. Thus, until proven otherwise, the clinician must assume that a nontraumatic CN III palsy with pupillary involvement or evidence of progression to pupillary involvement is secondary to an aneurysm.
If left untreated, subarachnoid hemorrhage has a high mortality rate (10% of aneurysmal SAHs die before they reach the hospital, 25% die within 24 hours, and 45% die within 30 days); as such, the most important diagnostic test is neuroimaging with noncontrast CT of the brain. A lumbar puncture is indicated for cases in which the initial CT results are negative but suspicion remains high. Although B-scan ultrasonography may be useful to evaluate the posterior pole, neuroimaging is the most important imaging study for the initial consideration. MRI is not as helpful as a noncontrast CT for detecting blood, and CTA is faster, which makes a CT and CTA slightly more optimal in the emergent management of this condition.

Q962
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 34-year-old woman in her 34th week of pregnancy develops pre-eclampsia. She is monitored successfully until she presents to the emergency department with acute-onset headache, altered mental status, and complete vision loss in both eyes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows increased fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) signal in the bilateral occipital lobes. After she is stabilized, how should the ophthalmologist counsel her family regarding her visual prognosis?
Correct answer: B. "She will likely recover most or all of her vision."
Rationale
This pregnant patient with pre-eclampsia is presenting with signs and symptoms of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). PRES is characterized by headache, altered mental status, seizures, and visual disturbances (blurred vision, homonymous visual field loss, cortical blindness, photopsias, and visual hallucinations). MRI shows T2-hyperintense vasogenic edema involving the white matter of the cerebral posterior regions, especially the parieto-occipital lobes; however, the frontal and temporal lobes, basal ganglia, and brainstem may be involved as well. Although vision loss can be bilateral and complete (cortical blindness), prognosis is excellent and patients usually recover all of their vision.

Q963
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most likely cause of the eyelid abnormality shown in downgaze in images below?
Correct answer: D. aberrant regeneration of the right CN III
Rationale
Eyelid retraction is seen in the right eye with downgaze. The right eye also has limited elevation and depression with ptosis in primary position. These findings are most consistent with partial right CN III palsy and aberrant regeneration. In this case of aberrant regeneration, damaged nerve fibers from the inferior rectus have been "misrouted" on regrowth and now innervate the levator palpebrae. This patient had a cavernous sinus meningioma that caused these findings. Importantly, while aberrant regeneration is common after trauma or compression by an aneurysm or tumor, it does not occur with microvascular ischemia.
MG and CPEO cause ptosis but not eyelid retraction on downgaze. Thyroid eye disease (TED) causes lagophthalmos but not a frank reversal of relative eyelid heights as seen here.

Q964
Neuro-Ophthalmology
In automated static perimetry, what is the difference between a 25 dB stimulus and a 35 dB stimulus?
Correct answer: B. The 35 dB stimulus is dimmer than the 25 dB stimulus.
Rationale
Stimulus size is kept constant in automated static perimetry, and the intensity of the stimulus is varied at each tested point to determine the detection threshold. The value is displayed in decibels (dB), which is a logarithmic scale of intensity, measuring attenuation from the maximum stimulus of the perimeter. Thus, a stimulus detected at 35 dB is 10 times dimmer than one detected at 25 dB. Stimulus size is not indicated by the dB value and must be supplied as a separate piece of information.

Q965
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 56-year-old male presents for evaluation of intermittent blurred vision. On examination, he has a normal head position. He is noted to have 4 prism diopters of right hypertropia in primary gaze, 5 prism diopters of right hypertropia in left gaze, 3 prism diopters of right hypertropia in right gaze, and 4 prism diopters of right hypertropia in right and left head tilt. He has right inferior oblique overaction, mild superior oblique underaction, and 5 degrees of right excyclotorsion. The rest of his examination is normal. What finding on his clinical examination most suggests a long-standing etiology for his condition?
Correct answer: A. comitance of deviation
Rationale
Patients with strabismus can present with minimal symptoms. The clinical history and examination can help determine the chronicity and, by extension, the etiology of the strabismus.
This patient has a right cranial nerve (CN) IV palsy, as evidenced by a right hypertropia that is slightly worse in left gaze, associated with right inferior oblique overaction, right superior oblique underaction, and right excyclotorsion. The fact that the deviation is fairly comitant suggests a spread of comitance, in which an incomitant deviation becomes comitant (ie, the measurements are very similar in all directions of gaze) with the passage of time. CN IV palsies are commonly associated with this phenomenon. Inferior oblique overaction is not specific to CN IV palsies and does not specifically indicate the chronicity of a CN IV palsy. Normal head position and small angle of deviation do not provide any indication of the chronicity of a CN IV palsy; in long-standing CN IV palsies, some patients adopt an anomalous head position to reduce or eliminate their diplopia.

Q966
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 52-year-old man noted blurred vision while gardening outdoors. Yesterday he developed a headache that he attributed to migraine. This morning he awoke with persistent symptoms. On examination, his visual acuity is 20/20 OU, with briskly reactive pupils; the slit-lamp examination of his anterior segment is unremarkable. What test is recommended to determine the cause of his visual field defects shown?
Correct answer: D. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain with diffusion-weighted imaging
Rationale
Automated perimetry shows incomplete bilateral quadrantic defects; hence the lesion must be posterior to the optic chiasm. MRI of the brain would be the best study to show the causative lesion, and diffusion-weighted imaging should be included because it is helpful in patients with acute stroke. MRI of the orbits with fat suppression is helpful in patients with optic neuropathy, and magnetic resonance venogram of the head is helpful to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis in patients with papilledema; however, the visual fields are suggestive of a cortical problem and not an optic neuropathy. Lumbar puncture would also be helpful in a patient with papilledema and may be helpful in some patients with stroke, but typically not as an initial study.

Q967
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient with an abnormal-appearing optic nerve undergoes fundus photography and B-scan ultrasonography, with the results shown in the figure. What is the most likely complication of this condition?
Correct answer: C. visual field defect
Rationale
The images demonstrate optic disc drusen, which appear as elevations of the optic disc with blurring of the optic nerve head (ONH) margin with scalloped edges, refractile bodies on the ONH surface without obscuration of retinal blood vessels. The B-scan ultrasonogram demonstrates focal, highly reflective elevation within the ONH due to calcium. These deposits are hyperautofluorescent. Visual field defects (following nerve bundles) occur in 75%-87% of cases, but most go unnoticed by the patient. Visual field defects either remain stable or worsen very slowly. Other symptoms may include transient visual obscurations associated with ONH swelling (8.6%). Rare complications include vascular complications such as flame hemorrhage, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or peripapillary subretinal neovascularization. Visual acuity rarely declines.

Q968
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What differentiates hemifacial spasm from benign essential blepharospasm?
Correct answer: A. Hemifacial spasms persist in sleep.
Rationale
It is important to differentiate between these 2 diagnoses. Hemifacial spasm (HFS) is characterized by intermittent synchronous contractures of the entire side of the face and is rarely bilateral. Unlike in benign essential blepharospasm, the spasms are present during sleep in hemifacial spasm. In most cases, the cause of HFS is a vascular compression of the facial nerve at the brain stem. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can document the ectatic vessel, and can also rule out other cerebellopontine angle lesions that may be the cause in less than 1% of cases. Botulinum toxin injection is commonly used in both conditions.

Q969
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What nerve fibers are affected in an Adie tonic pupil?
Correct answer: D. parasympathetic fibers
Rationale
Adie tonic pupil is caused by parasympathetic dysfunction that leads to diminished pupillary constriction. The etiology is idiopathic. Other causes of a tonic pupil include neurosyphilis, diabetes, chronic alcoholism, and dysautonomias. Tonic pupils are typically (80%) unilateral, and are more common in females (70%). These pupils are hypersensitive to parasympathomimetic agents (eg, diluted pilocarpine).

Q970
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 60-year-old diabetic, hypertensive man presents to the emergency department complaining that he awoke that morning and noticed he couldn’t see anything out of the inferior portion of his right eye. He is very distraught because this has been his "good eye" ever since a similar sudden loss of the inferior field of vision occurred in his other eye several months prior. Central vision in both eyes is 20/50. At the time of his first episode, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head and orbits was negative at an outside emergency department. Review of systems is negative. His fundus photos are shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. pseudo-Foster-Kennedy syndrome
Rationale
The correct answer is pseudo-Foster-Kennedy syndrome. Foster-Kennedy syndrome occurs when an intracranial mass on 1 side compresses the ipsilateral optic nerve, causing optic atrophy and thus optic nerve pallor, while also raising the intracranial pressure and causing the contralateral disc to swell. The normal MRI in the question rules this possibility out. Pseudo-Foster-Kennedy syndrome is caused by bilateral, sequential attacks of nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The first nerve affected becomes pale 4-8 weeks after the attack, and thus, when the second optic nerve becomes affected and acutely swollen, it yields the same appearance as Foster-Kennedy syndrome, with 1 optic nerve showing pallor and the other nerve showing edema. The 5-year risk for involvement of the fellow eye in NAION is approximately 15%.
Untreated giant cell arteritis (GCA) could indeed cause bilateral disc swelling and optic nerve pallor; however, GCA left untreated for several months would be expected to have caused much more profound vision loss. It was also noted that review of systems was negative, also making GCA less likely. This patient is diabetic, making diabetic papillopathy a consideration; however, the optic nerves are typically hyperemic in diabetic papillopathy, and approximately half of patients show prominent surface telangiectasias that are often mistaken for neovascularization of the disc. In addition, the majority (63%-80%) of patients with diabetic papillopathy have diabetic retinopathy, which this patient does not have.

Four days following a motor vehicle accident, a patient complains of headache and has mild ipsilateral ptosis and amaurosis fugax. What test is most likely to be useful?
Correct answer: C. computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the head and neck
Rationale
The patient's history and clinical findings are very concerning for an internal carotid artery dissection. Both MRI/MRA and CTA are used to detect a carotid dissection. CTA is often used in the acute setting because it is faster. CT of the brain and orbits would not be sensitive enough to detect a carotid dissection. Ultrasound is not adequate for detecting arterial dissection and can elicit a false-negative result in nearly one-third of cases.

Q972
Neuro-Ophthalmology
In patients with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), what is the most common type of visual defect?
Correct answer: D. altitudinal defect
Rationale
Altitudinal visual field defect is the most common visual field defect seen in NAION. Pathophysiology of this defect likely involves temporary failure of perfusion of one of the posterior ciliary arteries, which perfuses half of the optic disc and peripapillary choroid. Temporal wedges and nasal steps are suggestive of glaucoma. An enlarged blind spot often is found in papilledema, as the retina is pushed outward by the expanding optic nerve diameter. A cecocentral defect is often detected in a toxic, nutritional, or genetic (eg, LHON) optic neuropathy when bilateral.

Q973
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What neuroimaging finding is characteristic of tuberous sclerosis?
Correct answer: A. intracranial calcified hamartoma
Rationale
Tuberous sclerosis is associated with intracranial calcified astrocytic hamartomas. Acoustic neuroma is the classic neuroimaging finding for neurofibromatosis type 2. Cerebellar hemangioblastoma is associated with von Hippel–Lindau disease. Leptomeningeal vascular malformation is a feature of Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalofacial angiomatosis).

Q974
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 72-year-old man presents with complaints of intermittent double vision for the past few weeks. He has not had any headache, jaw claudication, or vision loss. When asked, he has noticed a slight weight loss and increased fatigue over the same time period. His visual acuity is 20/25 OU and motility is grossly normal. There is intermittent incomitant esotropia that does not correspond to any particular nerve palsy. What is the most prudent step to take in his workup?
Correct answer: B. order complete blood cell (CBC) count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein levels
Rationale
Giant cell arteritis (GCA) should be suspected in this scenario, and the next step is to order tests of complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. GCA can have varied clinical manifestations. Although many people present with the classic symptoms of headache, jaw claudication, and temporal tenderness, it is also possible for the symptoms to be more subtle. For any patient who is in the appropriate age range for GCA but whose new onset diplopia does not have an obvious, explained cause, tests are warranted to rule out GCA. The diplopia in GCA is due to extraocular muscle ischemia, as opposed to any specific nerve palsy.
If GCA laboratory test results are negative, then the other answer choices (order thyroid function studies, order acetylcholine receptor antibody levels, order magnetic resonance imaging [MRI] of the brain/orbits with gadolinium) would be useful to consider to find a cause for the patient's diplopia; however, in this scenario, GCA is the most urgent condition that has to be ruled out.

Q975
Neuro-Ophthalmology
In a patient with CN IV palsy, what finding would place the lesion at the nuclear or predecussation fascicular level?
Correct answer: C. afferent pupillary defect ipsilateral to the CN IV palsy
Rationale
A lesion of the brachium of the superior colliculus will produce a relative afferent pupillary defect in the absence of color vision loss or a visual field defect. The relative afferent pupillary defect will be ipsilateral to the CN IV palsy due to the decussation of nasal pupillary fibers at the chiasm and the decussation of CN IV after it exits the brainstem. A contralateral Horner syndrome can occur due to the proximity of the descending sympathetic fibers. A homonymous hemianopia would not occur with a pure brainstem injury. Ipsilateral facial weakness would not localize to the midbrain.

Q976
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An 80-year-old woman reports persistent flashes OU with worsening night vision over 2 months. She has constricted visual fields by confrontation and bilateral retinal pigment deposition anterior to the arcade vessels. Full-field electroretinogram (ERG) shows minimal signal from both eyes. What is the suggested management for this patient?
Correct answer: C. serum testing and evaluation of chest/abdomen/pelvis for mass lesions
Rationale
Paraneoplastic syndromes such as cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) present with constant photopsias, impaired color vision, nyctalopia, impaired dark adaptation, dimming, ring scotoma, and peripheral and/or central visual field loss. The fundus can initially appear normal, but the ERG response shows markedly reduced amplitudes. As the disease progresses, the retinal arterioles become attenuated, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) thinned and mottled, and the optic discs pale. This patient has the typical features of CAR and should undergo workup for anti-retinal antibodies and to identify an occult malignancy.
The differential diagnosis of this presentation includes other bilateral retinopathies with ERG abnormalities, including retinitis pigmentosa and its various syndromes, or mitochondrial myopathies such as Kearns-Sayre syndrome. Rod or rod-cone retinal dystrophies show similar abnormalities on ERG and can be associated with retinal pigmentation. Examination of family members is useful in determining the inheritance pattern. Pigmentary retinopathies such as Usher syndrome can be associated with hearing difficulties and require audiology consultation. Kearns-Sayre syndrome is associated with cardiac conduction blocks, a life-threatening complication, hence the need for cardiology consultation. These patients tend to present earlier in life than the patient in this case, and likely will have other retinal or ocular examination features to suggest the alternative diagnosis, for example, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia with motility dysfunction and progressive ptosis in Kearns-Sayre syndrome.

Q977
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For an optic nerve glioma, what is the most likely finding on orbital imaging?
Correct answer: D. fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve
Rationale
Most optic nerve gliomas (ONGs) exhibit a fusiform shape on computed tomography (CT) and MRI. Globular or multilobulated shapes may occur, but are less common. The optic nerve may also have a characteristic tortuosity or kinking. If mucinous degeneration has occurred, cystic spaces within the lesion may be evident. ONG is typically either isointense or hypointense to gray matter on precontrast T1-weighted MRI. Enhancement with gadolinium is the rule, although it is less intense than that seen in optic nerve sheath meningioma (ONSM).
"Tram-tracking" is a classic sign of ONSM, due to tumor growth along the nerve sheath. Of note, fusiform shapes are also quite common with ONSM; the optic nerve should appear as a lucency on imaging of ONSM, as opposed to ONG.
A dilated superior ophthalmic vein is usually a sign of orbital and cavernous sinus congestion and is classically seen in carotid-cavernous fistula.

Q978
Neuro-Ophthalmology
To what area of the brain does a lesion cause the combination of symptoms of formed hallucinations, insomnia, and excessive daytime somnolence?
Correct answer: A. midbrain
Rationale
In rare cases, lesions involving the mesencephalon (midbrain) cause formed, often constant hallucinations frequently associated with an inverted sleep-wake cycle (peduncular hallucinosis). Depending on the extent of the midbrain lesion, there can be accompanying neurologic symptoms. Disorders of the nondominant parieto-occipital area cause palinopsia, the illusion of persistent afterimages that can be associated with visual hallucinations. Temporal lobe lesions most often produce olfactory and gustatory hallucinations; visual phenomena from this area are usually complex, formed hallucinations in the ipsilateral or contralateral visual field. Occipital lobe lesions commonly cause unformed hallucinations, which are sometimes described as geometric colors or patterns.

Q979
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents with signs and symptoms consistent with a compressive lesion of CNIII. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is obtained and read as negative. What would be the best next step to take?
Correct answer: A. Call neuroradiologist for review of MRI.
Rationale
If a neuroimaging study does not reveal a structural lesion in the area that is suspected based on clinical examination, the physician should first review the study with a neuroradiologist to ensure that the appropriate imaging study was performed, and the area of concern was adequately imaged. Additional clinical history can be helpful to the neuroradiologist to ensure that a structural lesion was not overlooked on the original study. If the study is truly negative after review, additional workup or referral to a neuro-ophthalmologist would be appropriate.
Repeating neuroimaging would not necessarily yield the appropriate concerns. The answer choice "repeating neuroimaging" suggests that another MRI (not MRA) of the brain should be performed without first consulting the neuroradiologist and reviewing the images with them. This would not increase the likelihood of detection of an aneurysm, whereas consultation with a neuroradiologist may result in discovering a subtle lesion (as most larger aneurysms are detectable by MRI as well), and if this did not work, would lead to suggestion of cerebrovascular imaging. While in clinical practice, it is unlikely that a CN III palsy would undergo neuroimaging without cerebrovascular imaging, the most correct answer is still to ask for the neuroradiologist to review the MRI.

Q980
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 79-year-old woman presents with an acute onset of binocular horizontal diplopia and dizziness. Examination reveals a right head turn with an esotropia that is worse on right gaze. There is decreased corneal sensation and lagophthalmos on the right. What is the location of the lesion?
Correct answer: B. cerebellopontine angle (CPA)
Rationale
This scenario describes right V (decreased corneal sensation), VI (esotropia worse on right gaze), VII (lagophthalmos), and possibly VIII cranial nerve palsies (dizziness) in combination. CPA tumors, especially acoustic neuroma or meningioma, can cause V, VI, VII, and/or VIII nerve palsies with the above findings, as well as ipsilateral decreased hearing. Other common locations of multiple cranial nerve palsies are the orbital apex, cavernous sinus, and brainstem. However, isolated orbital apex lesions do not cause decreased V, VII, or VIII nerve palsy. Cavernous sinus lesions do not affect the VII or VIII nerve. Midbrain lesions develop more rostrally than the nuclei of the described cranial nerves, and thus affect III and/or IV cranial nerves instead.

Q981
Neuro-Ophthalmology
While hospitalized for a presumed exacerbation of asthma, a 50-year-old man is noted to have moderate right upper eyelid ptosis. The ptosis has been intermittently present for several months. The ophthalmologist discusses management of the patient with the gastroenterologist, who was called to evaluate dysphagia. What diagnostic test offers the advantages of safety, speed, and specificity?
Correct answer: B. ice-pack test
Rationale
Considering the constellation of ptosis, breathing difficulties, and trouble swallowing, myasthenia gravis is a reasonable and somewhat urgent concern. After 2 minutes of cooling with an ice pack, improvement of ptosis can be seen in most patients with MG. If further testing is needed, the patient could undergo edrophonium (Tensilon) testing to confirm the diagnosis. Edrophonium testing may be associated with rare but serious adverse effects such as bradycardia, bronchospasm, cholinergic crisis, respiratory arrest, or syncopal episodes. Although antibody testing is useful, it will take time to get the results. Pupillary abnormalities are not associated with myasthenia gravis.

Q982
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For 2 months, a 67-year-old Filipino man has had blurred vision. He is on treatment for a chronic pulmonary infection from mycobacterium avium-intracellulare. His visual acuity is 20/200 OU, his color vision is reduced on D15 testing, and his optic discs show mild pallor. What pattern of visual-field loss might be expected on perimetry?
Correct answer: D. cecocentral scotomas
Rationale
Ethambutol is a common medication used in the treatment of mycobacterium avium-intracellulare. This is one of the most common medications implicated in toxic optic neuropathy. Optic neuropathy resulting from toxic exposure is characterized by a gradual, progressive, and painless vision loss. Visual fields typically show either bilateral central or cecocentral scotomas. An arcuate scotoma is a nerve fiber bundle defect typical of glaucoma. Homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing can be seen with optic tract, optic radiation, and occipital lobe lesions. Enlarged blind spots are classically seen with papilledema.

Q983
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Computerized axial tomography (CT) is usually more helpful than magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in patients with what condition?
Correct answer: D. orbital fractures
Rationale
CT is superior to MRI in detecting bony deformities, especially in the orbits and sinuses. Therefore, orbital fractures are best seen on orbital CT rather than on MRI, as CT allows detailed views of fracture location in relation to soft tissue.
"Chiasmal lesion" is not correct, because axial CT often misses pituitary abnormalities. Coronal T1-weighted post-gadolinium imaging is particularly useful to evaluate proximity of the optic chiasm to a pituitary mass and to identify extension into the adjacent cavernous sinuses.
"Optic neuritis" is not correct, because demyelinating disease is poorly viewed on CT. Demyelinating lesions are well-characterized by MRI with T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images of the brain, and T1-weighted fat-suppressed images with gadolinium contrast of the orbit.
"Choroidal melanoma with orbital extension" is not correct, because it is a soft tissue lesion abutting the soft tissue globe, and MRI is superior to CT in defining soft tissue borders.

Q984
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 56-year-old man presents with acute onset right-sided neck pain and right upper lid ptosis following chiropractic manipulation. The pupils were 3 mm OD and 4 mm OS. He has a severe allergy to iodinated contrast. What imaging modality should be used for this patient to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. magnetic resonance imaging/magnetic resonance angiography (MRI/MRA)
Rationale
This patient is presenting with symptoms of an acute painful Horner syndrome following chiropractic manipulation, which is concerning for a right-sided carotid dissection. The imaging modality of choice to detect a carotid dissection is CTA and MRI/MRA of the head/neck. The patient has a severe contrast allergy to iodinated contrast; therefore, CT/CTA is contraindicated, which makes MRI/MRA the correct answer. Gadolinium is not an iodinated contrast dye, and patients with an allergy to iodinated dye are not likely to be allergic to gadolinium. Carotid ultrasonography can detect some cases of carotid dissection, but is not the imaging modality of choice, because of its inferior sensitivity. PET is helpful for detecting occult malignancy, but it is not used for diagnosing carotid dissection.

Q985
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For 3 days, a 33-year-old woman was noted to have bilaterally enlarged, poorly light-reactive pupils. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU. She is orthotropic at distance and her motility at near is shown. What disorder most likely accounts for her findings?
Correct answer: A. bilateral pharmacologic mydriasis
Rationale
This woman demonstrates symmetric, round pupils nonreactive to accommodation. In the absence of a third nerve palsy, the most likely explanation is bilateral pharmacologic mydriasis. Patients with severe bilateral visual loss from optic neuropathy may have dilated pupils that react poorly to light but should react well with accommodation and convergence. Tonic pupils also typically react better with convergence and also are frequently irregular due to sectoral denervation of the iris sphincter muscle. Isolated pupil involvement (no ptosis and no ductional deficits) in third nerve palsy is rare in an otherwise healthy patient, and in this patient who is orthotropic at distance, would be unexpected.

Q986
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What test is the most sensitive means of detecting abnormal visual function in a patient with papilledema?
Correct answer: B. visual field testing
Rationale
With acute papilledema, optic nerve function, including visual acuity and color vision, is usually normal. Pupillary responses are also normal; visual field tests may demonstrate only enlargement of the blind spot. Optic nerve function can deteriorate in patients with chronically elevated intracranial pressure and long-standing papilledema. With chronic papilledema, visual field defects can include nasal field loss, arcuate scotomata, and generalized peripheral depression. Central visual field involvement with decreased visual acuity typically does not occur until late.

Q987
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What complication following third cranial nerve (oculomotor) palsy is suggestive of a nonischemic cause?
Correct answer: A. aberrant regeneration
Rationale
Aberrant regeneration may develop after congenital or traumatic third cranial nerve palsy, but does not after ischemia. Aberrant regeneration most commonly produces eyelid retraction in downgaze, eyelid elevation or pupil constriction on attempted adduction, and globe retraction on attempted upgaze. Aberrant regeneration does not occur with ischemic causes, which include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, atherosclerosis, and migraine.

Q988
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 35-year-old man has vertical, binocular diplopia that seems worse when driving. He has a left hypertropia of 5 PD in primary gaze, absent on right gaze, increasing to 9 PD on left gaze with clockwise gaze-evoked nystagmus. There is no head tilt. What additional finding on examination would help to support the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. slow left-eye adducting saccade
Rationale
This patient has an incomitant left hypertropia (worse in left gaze) and gaze-evoked nystagmus. The hypertropia does not follow a cranial nerve pattern, and the presence of nystagmus suggests a supranuclear disorder such as skew deviation. Skew deviation may occur with internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young person who has demyelinating disease, and in an older person may result from ischemia. Given the left hypertropia, the lesion causing the skew deviation is most likely on the left side of the brainstem; the hallmark of a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) would therefore be slowed adduction saccadic velocity in the left eye.
Both thyroid eye disease (which can cause proptosis) and ocular myasthenia gravis (which can cause fluctuating ptosis) may cause the same ocular deviation (left hypertropia worse in left gaze), but would not produce the nystagmus. Increased vertical fusional amplitude is seen most commonly with longstanding cranial nerve (CN) IV palsy or other vertical strabismus and would not be expected in this patient, whose strabismus does not fit that pattern.

Q989
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Slit-lamp examination of a large pupil that is minimally reactive to light reveals vermiform movements. The pupil reaction is slow to near stimulus. The patient has no ptosis, and ocular motility is normal. Where is the responsible lesion located?
Correct answer: D. ipsilateral ciliary ganglion
Rationale
The findings are characteristic of damage either to the iris sphincter muscle or its innervation from the parasympathetic system, as in Adie tonic pupil. Herpes zoster can give this same picture.
Lesions at the dorsal midbrain also produce light near dissociation, but findings are bilateral and not vermiform in terms of constriction.
Fascicular CN III lesions should give either ptosis and/or a motility deficit along with the pupil dilation, and vermiform movements are again not present.
Sympathetic denervation at the second-order neuron (ciliospinal center) leads to Horner syndrome with a miotic pupil.

Q990
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An otherwise asymptomatic 52-year-old man notes that his left pupil is larger than the right pupil. A diagnostic drop was placed in each eye, and 30 minutes later he has the external appearance shown. What is the clinical condition?
Correct answer: A. right Horner syndrome
Rationale
The patient has right upper eyelid ptosis and right lower eyelid ptosis (elevation of the lower lid) that is present 30 minutes after instillation of a diagnostic drop. His left upper eyelid has elevated, the left pupil has dilated, and the left lower eyelid has depressed 30 minutes after installation of the same diagnostic drop. This is highly suggestive that the diagnostic drop was cocaine, and that this is a right Horner syndrome. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft and should dilate a normal pupil but fail to dilate a pupil with Horner syndrome.
Supersensitivity may occur with alpha adrenergic agonists such as apraclonidine, which may cause dilation of a pupil with Horner syndrome, and reversal of the anisocoria in addition to improvement in the ptosis.
Dilute pilocarpine testing for Adie pupil would not affect the eyelid position. Likewise, full-strength or higher concentrations of pilocarpine to test for pharmacologic mydriasis would also not affect the eyelid position.

Q991
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 39-year-old woman has had episodic diplopia for 2 years. Ductions are normal, and there is no ptosis. Alternate cover testing shows a 12 prism diopter, intermittent left hypertropia in primary position that increases to 25 prism diopters on right gaze and downgaze; it decreases to 3 prism diopters in upgaze and left gaze. She has a right head tilt and becomes diplopic on left head tilt. What additional finding is most likely to accompany this condition?
Correct answer: C. documentation of a right head tilt in a photograph taken at age 18
Rationale
This patient has a strabismus pattern consistent with left fourth nerve palsy (left hypertropia worse on right gaze and left head tilt). She is able to fuse a 12 prism diopter vertical deviation, which represents an abnormally high fusional amplitude. This can develop in adults but usually results from a longstanding vertical strabismus such as congenital or childhood trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy. Even minor head trauma can cause CN IV palsy, and the condition may not become symptomatic until later in adulthood, when the well-controlled strabismus starts to break down. Old photos frequently show a compensatory head tilt being present for many years before the diplopia started.
A patient with a newly acquired CN IV palsy in adulthood would not be able to fuse the deviation measured here. While myasthenia gravis can mimic a CN IV palsy, that is less likely here because of lack of ptosis and chronicity without any change. Thyroid eye disease causes restrictive strabismus, and ductions would not be normal. Multiple sclerosis (MS) rarely causes cranial nerve palsies.

Q992
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 70-year-old man reports intermittent diplopia for 3 weeks. His motility is shown. What is the most likely underlying etiology of his motility disturbance?
Correct answer: B. demyelination
Rationale
The patient has had a stroke on the left side of the brainstem. This motility pattern represents a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). The INO is caused by disruption to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which carries fibers from the sixth cranial nerve nucleus on one side to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus, and thus results in slow saccades and often limitation of motility on adduction. There is often an associated abducting nystagmus of the other eye. An INO is named for the side on which there is limited adduction. In this case, there is impaired adduction of the left eye, representing a problem with the MLF on the left side. The most common causes of INO are demyelination and stroke. As one may expect, demyelination is the most likely cause in young and middle-aged patients, while microvascular stroke is the most common cause in the elderly.
Myasthenia gravis can cause pseudo-INO; however, there are usually other signs of myasthenia present, such as ptosis. The pseudo-INO of myasthenia gravis would be expected to transiently resolve during a Tensilon test. Type II Duane syndrome does affect adduction; however, with Duane syndrome there is typically narrowing of the palpebral fissure and retraction of the globe on attempted adduction due to co-contraction of the horizontal rectus muscles. In addition, because Duane syndrome is congenital, it would not be expected to cause new onset diplopia in this 70-year-old patient.

Q993
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What imaging method is preferred to identify calcium in an orbital lesion?
Correct answer: A. computed tomography (CT) scan
Rationale
CT scan is optimal for analysis of calcium in lesions, such as meningiomas. MRI is a less effective and more expensive option for visualizing calcium. PET scanning would not be a cost-effective technique for visualizing intralesional calcium. Gamma ray-emitting radionuclides such as technetium-99 do not provide comparable anatomical details to contrast imaging, but they may be useful for evaluating obstructions of the tear ducts.

Q994
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents with oscillopsia worse in downgaze. Examination demonstrates downbeat nystagmus, which follows Alexander's law. If a causative structural lesion is present, what is the most likely location of the lesion?
Correct answer: A. cervicomedullary junction
Rationale
Downbeat nystagmus is the most common form of central vestibular nystagmus. It results from lesions that produce defective vertical gaze holding, characterized by an upward drift, then correction with a downward saccade. Lesions that cause downbeat nystagmus compromise the vestibulocerebellum (including the nodulus, uvula, flocculus, and paraflocculus) and decrease the tonic output from the posterior semicircular canals to the ocular motor neurons. According to Alexander's law, the downbeating movements are accentuated in downgaze. Patients usually report oscillopsia.
If there is a structural lesion causing the downbeat nystagmus, then it most commonly is located at the cervicomedullary junction. The most common causative lesion is a Arnold-Chiari I malformation, a developmental abnormality characterized by posterior fossa crowding and cerebellar tonsillar protrusion into the foramen magnum.
A lesion of the dorsal midbrain may produce a Parinaud syndrome, characterized by upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, mid-dilated pupils with light-near dissociation, eyelid retraction, skew deviation, disruption of convergence, and increase square-wave jerks.
A lesion of the sella may produce a bitemporal hemianopia secondary to chiasmal compression and, rarely, a see-saw nystagmus.
A lesion of the lateral medulla may produce a Wallenberg syndrome, characterized by ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature sensation, contralateral loss of body pain and temperature sensation, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, ipsilateral first-order Horner syndrome, and ipsilateral ocular tilt reaction.

Q995
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What structure lies adjacent to the fascicles of cranial nerve III?
Correct answer: B. substantia nigra
Rationale
The portion of cranial nerves that courses within the brainstem is called a fascicle. The fascicles of the cranial nerves will pass adjacent to other major structures. Lesions within these areas will result in specific clinical syndromes that help to localize the lesion to a specific area of the brainstem. Cranial nerve III (oculomotor nerve) passes adjacent to the superior cerebellar peduncle, cerebral peduncle, red nucleus, substantia nigra, and corticospinal tracts. Lesions in these areas may cause Nothnagel syndrome (superior cerebellar peduncle), Benedikt syndrome (red nucleus and substantia nigra), Weber syndrome (cerebral peduncle), and Claude syndrome (superior cerebellar peduncle and red nucleus). Cranial nerve IV (trochlear nerve) courses below the pineal gland; large pineal tumors may cause CN IV palsies. The nucleus of cranial nerve VI (abducens nerve) lies below the fourth ventricle and its fascicles pass medial to the superior olivary nucleus.

Q996
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Where is the lesion responsible for the visual field defect shown in the image below?
Correct answer: B. anterior right occipital lobe
Rationale
The Goldmann perimetry image depicts a largely monocular defect in the left eye that sits beyond 40° from fixation. It is evident subtly in the right eye, with some truncation of the I4e isopter in the same region. Thus, it is a homonymous hemianopia that is essentially monocular because of the much greater extent of the temporal field on the affected side ("temporal crescent"). 
A posterior chiasmal lesion gives a bitemporal defect near fixation. Left parietal lesions produce right inferior hemianopias, and lateral geniculate body defects cause a homonymous sectoranopia.

Q997

A patient with myasthenic strabismus and ptosis returns for examination 5 years after diagnosis via a single fiber electromyography (EMG). The patient currently has no systemic manifestations of generalized myasthenia. What is the likelihood of progression to generalized disease?
Correct answer: D. low risk
Rationale
Up to 20% of patients who present with isolated ocular myasthenia gravis (MG) (no systemic weakness) may progress to generalized MG, but this typically occurs in the first 2 years. This patient is at low risk for generalized MG because the manifestations have remained purely ocular for 5 years.

Q998
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 56-year-old woman presented with a long-standing 4th nerve palsy. Prior records show that initially she had a 15 prism diopter (PD) right hypertropia (RHT) in primary position, 10 PD RHT in right gaze and 25 PD RHT in left gaze. On your examination, the deviation measures 15 PD in all directions. What process occurred to explain this?
Correct answer: A. spread of comitance
Rationale
An incomitant deviation may become comitant with the passage of time, which is called spread of comitance. Suppression is an adaptation that occurs in early onset strabismus. It reduces the responsiveness of the visual neurons in the occipital cortex to the input from 1 eye to avoid symptoms of diplopia. Vergence is the simultaneous movement of both eyes in opposite directions to maintain single binocular vision. Convergence is a type of vergence where the eyes rotate toward each other to look at a near object.

Q999
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 62-year-old patient presents with a left facial droop, left abduction deficit, and numbness over the left side of the face. There was no weakness of the arms or legs noted on examination. What part of the brainstem is most likely affected?
Correct answer: C. left dorsal pons
Rationale
The clinical vignette describes a left cranial nerve (CN) V, left CN VI, and left CN VII palsy without body weakness. This is most consistent with Foville syndrome, in which intra-axial lesions of the CN VI fascicles also injure CN VII fascicles, the tractus solitarius, and the descending tract of CN V. This results in an ipsilateral abduction palsy, facial weakness, loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and facial hypoesthesia.
The CN VI nucleus lies within the dorsal caudal pons, and dorsal lesions to the pons can cause Foville syndrome, whereas lesions of the ventral pons can damage CN VI and CN VII, along with the corticospinal tract, which results in contralateral hemiplegia, ipsilateral facial weakness, and abduction deficit. This is called Millard-Gubler syndrome

Q1000
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the best initial treatment option for the condition shown? The woman pictured is trying to relax her face.
Correct answer: B. botulinum toxin injection
Rationale
Botulinum toxin injection into the facial muscles has proved very effective and is the treatment of choice for hemifacial spasm. Reinjection is required, at intervals of 3-4 months. Irritation of the facial nerve at its root exit zone (from the brainstem) by an aberrant blood vessel is thought to be the cause of hemifacial spasm in most patients. Chronic transmission of arterial pulsation leads to inappropriate facial nerve-firing and orbicularis contraction. Therefore, microvascular decompression of the nerve and placement of a spacer between it and the artery is curative in over 90% of patients, but this would not be the first treatment choice.
RF ablation of the trigeminal ganglion is a treatment for trigeminal neuralgia. Facial nerve section leads to paralysis and an unacceptable outcome. Orbicularis extirpation may be done bilaterally for essential blepharospasm but not hemifacial spasm.

Q1001
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 49-year-old patient presents with a central scotoma and optic disc pallor in the right eye and a superotemporal visual field defect with a normal-appearing optic disc in the left eye. What diagnostic test is the best next step in evaluation?
Correct answer: D. magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Rationale
The clinical scenario describes a patient with a junctional scotoma (optic neuropathy in 1 eye and a superotemporal visual field defect in the other eye) that localizes to the anterior chiasm.
Non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) is a diagnosis of exclusion that typically presents with unilateral vision loss in the setting of optic disc edema. The optic disc edema should resolve within 2 months, with subsequent development of optic disc pallor (either diffuse or sectoral). The visual field defect typically persists in NAION, although the density of the defect may improve. A temporal visual field defect in the contralateral eye would not be explained by NAION. Although giant cell arteritis should be considered in patients with suspected bilateral optic neuropathy, the patient's age makes giant cell arteritis much less likely. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and toxic-nutritional optic neuropathies typically present with central or cecocentral visual field defects. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy may be unilateral, sequential, or bilateral in presentation. Toxic-nutritional optic neuropathies are bilateral in presentation and typically symmetric, with a similar appearance to both optic nerves. Vitamin B12, folate, copper, and thiamine deficiencies have been implicated in nutritional optic neuropathy.

Q1002
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 28-year-old woman with new blurred vision at near has anisocoria with the left pupil being larger and reacting poorly to direct or consensual stimulus. With sustained reading, the left pupil constricts and then redilates slowly. What systemic finding may sometimes be associated?
Correct answer: A. absent deep tendon reflexes
Rationale
This patient has light-near dissociation and tonic constriction of the left pupil with sustained near stimulus. The most likely diagnosis is Adie pupil (idiopathic tonic pupil), which may occur in the context of Adie syndrome with decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes. Patients with Adie syndrome are much more likely to have bilateral simultaneous or sequential eye involvement. While Horner syndrome in the eye with the smaller pupil, in this case the right, must be considered, the presence of light-near dissociation on the left identifies it as the abnormal pupil.
Urinary incontinence may be seen with many neurological disorders, such as MS and normal pressure hydrocephalus, and these conditions are not associated with the pupil findings seen here. Palmar rash can occur with acquired syphilitic infection, especially in secondary syphilis. Decreased facial sweating (facial anhidrosis) is a characteristic of Horner syndrome.

Q1003
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For the past 2 months, a 58-year-old woman has noted binocular diplopia, which is worse in downgaze. The ophthalmologist obtains the orbital computed tomography (CT) scan shown. What condition might complicate this woman's disorder?
Correct answer: C. optic neuropathy
Rationale
The coronal orbital CT scan reveals thickening of multiple extraocular muscles, particularly the superior rectus/levator complex and the inferior rectus. This is most suggestive of thyroid eye disease. Orbital imaging in patients with diplopia from thyroid eye disease shows that extraocular muscle involvement is most commonly bilateral. In this patient, the diplopia is worse in downgaze because of restriction of the thickened superior rectus muscle. About 5% to 10% of patients with thyroid eye disease may develop optic neuropathy, most commonly from crowding at the orbital apex.
Upper-eyelid retraction is common in thyroid eye disease and ptosis is rare (unless coexistent myasthenia gravis is present). Elevated IOP, not hypotony, may be seen with increased episcleral venous pressure. The CT scan does not show any evidence of orbital cellulitis, and therefore a subperiosteal abscess in this condition would be very unlikely.

Q1004
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the initial surgical correction for heavy eye syndrome?
Correct answer: D. bilateral loop myopexy between the superior and lateral rectus muscles
Rationale
Heavy eye syndrome occurs in the setting of high myopia, causing superotemporal prolapse of the posterior globe. This displaces the superior rectus muscle medially and the lateral rectus muscle inferiorly, causing limited supraduction and abduction of the eye. Bilateral loop myopexy between the superior rectus muscle and lateral rectus muscle restores the normal anatomic configuration. All the other surgical options listed (bilateral medial rectus muscle recession, bilateral lateral rectus muscle resection, bilateral loop myopexy between the inferior and medial rectus muscles) would not restore the normal anatomic configuration, thus leading to a suboptimal surgical outcome.

What drug has been most commonly associated with the condition that could cause mental status changes and hemianopsia in a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS)?
Correct answer: C. natalizumab
Rationale
Altered mental status in the presence of a hemianopic visual field defect raises concern for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a condition associated with natalizumab in patients who are John Cunningham (JC)-virus positive. The other therapies have either not been associated or been associated with encephalopathy only in rare cases. Fingolimod can cause macular edema.

Q1006
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Twenty-four hours after uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a healthy 8-pound girl, a 24-year-old woman presented with bilateral visual loss and severe headaches. She had pregnancy-induced hypertension, which was under good medical control, and proteinuria. Dilated eye examination was unremarkable. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed bilateral occipital lobe white matter hyperintensity on T2 sequences. What is the most likely cause of her vision loss?
Correct answer: A. posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
Rationale
This patient is most likely suffering from posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). PRES is characterized by headache, altered mental status, seizures, and visual disturbances (transient visual loss, scotomata, photopsias, dimming of vision); MRI shows edema involving the white matter of the cerebral posterior regions, especially parieto-occipital lobes. PRES can be caused by acute hypertension, and preeclampsia/eclampsia, and can be seen in the postpartum period. The abnormalities visible on neuroimaging are reversible, and the visual prognosis is usually excellent.
Neither idiopathic intracranial hypertension nor anterior ischemic optic neuropathy would  explain the occipital lobe T2 hyperintensities, and in both cases, there would be findings of optic disc edema. Stroke is less likely here, given the classic presentation of PRES.

Q1007
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 56-year-old woman has slowly progressive diplopia. In primary gaze, she has partial ptosis, a mid-dilated pupil, exotropia, and hypotropia of the right eye. In attempted adduction, the right eyelid rises and the pupil constricts. What would be a likely cause for her examination findings?
Correct answer: C. compressive third nerve palsy
Rationale
This patient is showing signs of a right third nerve palsy, as indicated by the ptosis, mydriasis, and the down and out eye position. In addition, the elevation of the eyelid and constriction of the pupil in adduction indicates the presence of aberrant regeneration, which can occur after damage to the nerve and is due to misrouting of fibers that regrow to innervate muscles other than those they original innervated. Classic findings include eyelid retraction with adduction or pupillary miosis with elevation, adduction, or depression.
The other answer choices (demyelinating third nerve palsy, congenital third nerve palsy, ischemic third nerve palsy) can cause or mimic a third nerve palsy, but only a compressive etiology would be expected to result in aberrant regeneration. A cavernous sinus meningioma or carotid aneurysm in the cavernous sinus are common lesions responsible for compressive third nerve palsies. Aberrant regeneration is common after trauma or compression by an aneurysm or tumor, but it is rarely seen in a third nerve palsy caused by microvascular ischemia or ophthalmoplegic migraine. This is because the nerve sheath typically needs to be disrupted for aberrant regeneration to occur.

Q1008
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 70-year-old man with a history of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy in the right eye 5 years prior presents for his annual follow-up examination. His acuity remains 20/20 in the affected eye. Humphrey visual field shows a stable inferior altitudinal defect. What pattern would be expected on the optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan of the retinal nerve fiber layer?
Correct answer: D. superior thinning
Rationale
OCT is a powerful tool for the evaluation of patients with optic neuropathies, and a growing body of literature suggests that measurement of retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) or macular integrity can be a surrogate for overall disease severity. In a patient with a prior nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), the degree and site of RNFL (and ganglion cell complex) thinning often correlates with the threshold sensitivity of the corresponding area of the visual field. Since this patient has an inferior field defect, we would expect the corresponding superior retinal nerve fiber layer to be thinned.
Diffuse thickening of the RNFL may be present in an acute NAION but will not be present months or years later.
A normal RNFL would not be expected in a nerve that has experienced an ischemic insult, leaving the patient with a residual visual field defect.

Q1009
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents with the clinical appearance shown in the figure. Clinical history is notable for a motor vehicle accident 2 weeks earlier and increasing neck pain. What is the most appropriate testing for this patient?
Correct answer: A. urgent computed tomography (CT) and CT angiography (CTA) head and neck
Rationale
The clinical presentation provided in this question stem makes it apparent that the patient in question has an obvious Horner syndrome in the setting of a motor vehicle accident with increasing neck pain. This should strongly raise the clinical suspicion of a carotid dissection, which requires emergent imaging of the carotid vasculature (typically with CT/CTA or MRI/MRA of the head and neck). Pharmacologic testing, while helpful, is not necessary to the diagnosis of Horner syndrome and can be difficult to obtain (cocaine and hydroxyamphetamine are not readily available in the US), can produce false negatives (apraclonidine in early Horner syndrome), or delay diagnosis (hydroxyamphetamine cannot be used immediately after cocaine testing and would require several hours for the effects of apraclonidine to wear off). The question is not addressing localization, but at recognizing that the next appropriate test in the setting of an obvious Horner syndrome should be emergent neuroimaging. While it is true that distal carotid dissections can cause a third-order Horner syndrome, hydroxyamphetamine testing serves no practical purpose in this patient's case (regardless of whether it is a second-order or third-order problem, the answer is still to scan), and depending on availability and previous testing, could delay diagnosis and appropriate treatment, which could lead to a thromboembolic event.
In cases where the diagnosis of Horner syndrome is in doubt and there are no clinical findings concerning for emergent workup, pharmacologic testing can be helpful for diagnosis. However, as Dr. Jonathan Trobe, a well-regarded neuro-ophthalmologist, stated in an editorial on Horner syndrome, "The traditional use of pharmacologic agents such as topical hydroxyamphetamine to assist in localization is a waste of time. These agents are difficult to obtain and do not provide information reliable enough to allow targeted imaging." (Trobe, J Neuro-Ophthalmol 2010;30:1-2).

Q1010
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 75-year-old male presents with abnormal eye movements. He appears to be unable to glance at objects to the right but is able to track a finger in all directions of gaze. What part of the brain may be affected?
Correct answer: D. left frontal lobe
Rationale
Saccadic eye movements are generated by the frontal eye fields, located in the frontal lobe, one on each side. Each frontal eye field initiates saccades to the contralateral side. Smooth pursuit eye movements are generated by the medial temporal (MT) visual area (V5) in the parietal lobe, and each area generates smooth pursuit eye movements to the ipsilateral side. The inability to initiate saccades is called ocular motor apraxia and may be present in childhood in several conditions or may be acquired as a result of injury to the frontal lobe. Patients with ocular motor apraxia thrust their heads to establish fixation on their object of interest and use their vestibulo-ocular reflex to compensate for the inability to initiate saccadic movements. In this patient, the inability to look to the right suggests damage to the left frontal eye field, located in the left frontal lobe.

Q1011
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 55-year-old male with a history of diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obstructive sleep apnea awoke with painless vision loss in his left eye. He had no vision changes in the right eye. Examination showed hyperemic disc edema and peripapillary hemorrhages in the left eye. What nerve appearance would be expected in the right eye?
Correct answer: D. small, crowded nerve
Rationale
In a 55-year old man, the most common cause of acute painless vision loss upon awakening is nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), especially in the setting of vascular risk factors. NAION is associated with the following risk factors: structural crowding of the disc (disc-at-risk), systemic hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnea, and hyperlipidemia. NAION presumably relates to compromised optic disc microcirculation in eyes with structural “crowding” of the disc.
A cupped nerve would be suggestive of glaucoma, bilateral optic nerve swelling would be concerning for papilledema, and a pale nerve would indicate a prior optic neuropathy, none of which are consistent with this clinical scenario.

Q1012
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Approximately what percentage of patients with acute isolated demyelinating optic neuritis have eye pain?
Correct answer: C. 90%
Rationale
Acute isolated demyelinating optic neuritis is the most common form of optic neuritis. It typically presents in young white women and is characterized by subacute unilateral painful vision loss over 1 to 3 days. Examination findings include decreased visual acuity, visual field defects, dyschromatopsia (especially red-green) significantly worse than loss of visual acuity, and relative afferent pupillary defect (if unilateral). The optic nerve is edematous in 35% (papillitis) and appears normal in 65% (retrobulbar optic neuritis).
According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), 92% of cases have periorbital pain, especially with eye movement. This eye pain often precedes the visual loss by 1 to 2 days. The ONTT noted that the eye pain typically improves after 3 to 5 days; eye pain lasting more than 1 week is considered atypical for optic neuritis. It is theorized that the eye pain is worse with eye movements due to the proximity of the annulus of Zinn (especially with the superior and medial recti muscles) to the inflamed optic nerve sheath dura.

Q1013
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 57-year-old man has been experiencing intermittent diplopia as well as lid droopiness over the past 3 weeks. His symptoms are worse in the afternoon and evening and seem to improve after a good night’s rest. He does not report any trouble speaking, swallowing, or breathing. What laboratory testing is most useful to establish a diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. acetylcholine receptor binding antibody
Rationale
The correct answer is acetylcholine receptor binding antibody. Binding antibodies are most commonly requested, since they are detected in almost 90% of patients with generalized myasthenia gravis and 50% of patients with ocular myasthenia. The patient in this case needs serologic testing to evaluate for ocular myasthenia gravis.
Blocking antibodies are usually requested when the binding antibody is negative. Blocking antibodies are rarely present (1%) when the binding antibody is absent. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are most commonly associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis and are not commonly drawn in the initial workup for myasthenia gravis. Anti-muscle specific kinase (MuSK) antibodies can sometimes be detected in patients who do not have anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, but they are not detected more frequently than binding antibodies. Neuromyelitis optica antibodies can be found in Devic disease or neuromyelitis optica.

Q1014
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 32-year-old woman has bilateral elevated optic discs as shown. She complains of headaches, present for the past 3 years. Spontaneous venous pulsations were seen in both eyes. What test would best support the diagnosis of this condition?
Correct answer: C. B-scan ultrasonography
Rationale
This patient has visible optic disc drusen OU. These calcium and hyaline deposits are often seen as hyperechoic lesions at the optic nerve head on B-scan ultrasonography. They may also be visualized with fundus autofluorescence or on computed tomography (CT) scans. Nerve fiber bundle visual field defects, worse inferonasally, are the most common type of visual field defects seen with optic disc drusen but are not diagnostic. Although the calcium in optic disc drusen may be visible on CT scan, it is poorly imaged by MRI and might not be detected. Intracranial hypertension is associated with papilledema but is not an expected diagnosis in this patient.

Q1015
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 52-year-old woman has transient, painless vertical binocular diplopia lasting for seconds. It is accompanied by an odd sensation in her right eye when it occurs. What finding on slit-lamp examination of the right eye during an episode is most consistent with these symptoms?
Correct answer: B. rhythmic torsional oscillation
Rationale
The patient is reporting symptoms suspicious for superior oblique myokymia, which is characterized by monocular, paroxysmal, high-frequency bursts of superior oblique contraction. The resulting eye movements are of very small amplitude and usually require magnification (such as at the slit lamp or with a 20 D lens) for observation.
Many conditions, including ocular myasthenia gravis and decompensated phorias, may produce fleeting double vision. In these cases, patients do not experience the tremulous ocular sensation that is present with superior oblique myokymia. The diagnosis may be challenging unless an episode is observed, and high clinical suspicion is required once alternative diagnoses are excluded with motility and cover testing. Phacodonesis should not cause diplopia, nor would anterior chamber shallowing. Pulsatile proptosis is usually constant and thus rarely causes transient diplopia as noted here.

Q1016
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 28-year-old woman reported having a small left pupil for the past few weeks. She denied ptosis, diplopia, or pain. In light, her pupils were 6 mm OD and 3 mm OS. In a dim setting, her pupils were 6 mm OD and 4.5 mm OS. What investigation is most likely to yield useful information?
Correct answer: A. dilute pilocarpine in each eye
Rationale
Although she complains of the small left pupil, this patient presents with anisocoria worse in light than dark, indicating a problem with iris sphincter constriction in light and thus the parasympathetic nervous system in the larger pupil. (See Figure 1, Flowchart for evaluation of anisocoria.) A dilated, poorly reactive pupil, in the absence of ptosis or motility dysfunction, is consistent with idiopathic tonic (Adie) pupil. (Idiopathic tonic pupil is known as Adie pupil.) Additional characteristics of Adie pupil include light-near dissociation (poor reaction to light but strong pupillary response to near), sectoral palsy of the iris sphincter, and supersensitivity of the short ciliary nerves to parasympathomimetics such as pilocarpine. (See Figure 2, Sectoral palsy of iris sphincter in Adie pupil. The sphincter is paralyzed between the 7 o’clock and 9 o’clock sectors [arrows].) While normal pupils would be expected to constrict to 1% pilocarpine, only the Adie pupil will constrict to 0.1% dilute pilocarpine.
Cocaine 10% is a test for Horner syndrome, not Adie pupil.
MRI of the neck with fat suppression would be appropriate as part of the work up of Horner syndrome. Adie pupil is generally benign and does not raise concern for compressive mass, aneurysm, or dissection.

Q1017
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 24-year-old woman presents for evaluation of headache. She denies having any visual complaints or pulse-synchronous tinnitus. Her vision is 20/20 in each eye with normal visual fields and normal color vision. Her optic nerves are shown. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) is performed; the MRV is normal, but the MRI reports "findings suggestive of increased intracranial pressure." What is the most appropriate next step in management?
Correct answer: A. lumbar puncture
Rationale
The clinical scenario is most consistent with papilledema, which is optic nerve head edema resulting from increased intracranial pressure (ICP). On ophthalmoscopy, papilledema is indistinguishable from other causes of optic nerve head edema.
Suspicion of papilledema warrants urgent brain imaging, ideally MRI and magnetic resonance venography of the brain and orbits with contrast, to rule out an intracranial mass lesion and cerebral venous thrombosis. Normal brain imaging results should prompt evaluation of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure and composition by lumbar puncture.
Observation is not recommended when there is suspicion of papilledema, because chronic papilledema can result in permanent visual loss.
There are several radiographic features that might suggest increased intracranial pressure; however, after normal brain imaging, a lumbar puncture with opening pressure and CSF studies should be performed next.
Acetazolamide is the first-line medical treatment for idiopathic intracranial hypertension. However, treatment without confirmation of the diagnosis by neuroimaging and lumbar puncture is not recommended.

In a patient with an acute optic neuropathy, what symptom suggests the arteritic form?
Correct answer: C. prior transient monocular visual loss
Rationale
Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy causes isolated, sudden, permanent vision loss, often preceded by or associated with episodes of transient visual loss or episodes of transient diplopia.

For 1 month, a 56-year-old man has noticed binocular double vision. His visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye at distance and near. Both pupils are 8 mm in diameter in the light and are sluggishly reactive, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. With a near fixation target, both pupils constrict briskly. His fundi are normal. Given his brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shown, what is the most likely cause of his double vision?
Correct answer: B. skew deviation
Rationale
The T1-weighted MRI with contrast shows an enhancing lesion involving the tectum of the midbrain, which confirms the diagnosis of dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome. This syndrome encompasses convergence-retraction nystagmus, upgaze deficit, skew deviation, eyelid retraction, convergence abnormalities, and poorly reactive pupils with light-near dissociation. Skew deviation is the most likely cause of diplopia in this syndrome. Divergence insufficiency is not associated with dorsal midbrain syndrome. Although third and fourth nerve palsies may occur because of midbrain lesions, the clinical presentation is most consistent with dorsal midbrain syndrome.

A young man presents with recurrent episodes of transient monocular visual loss in the right eye following a car accident. He also reports experiencing ipsilateral headache. What clinical finding is highly suggestive of a right internal carotid artery dissection?
Correct answer: C. right Horner syndrome
Rationale
An acute painful Horner syndrome is highly suggestive of an ipsilateral internal carotid artery dissection, especially in a patient with recurrent episodes of transient monocular visual loss. Hemiparesis contralateral to the eye involved or retinal emboli in the affected eye both suggest a possible internal carotid artery stenosis, but these findings are not specifically suggestive of dissection. Diplopia should be expected with vascular events in the posterior circulation.

In a patient with Adie tonic pupil, what pupillary reaction is typically observed in the affected eye after sustained near viewing?
Correct answer: C. gradual sectoral redilation over seconds
Rationale
Adie pupils have poor light reaction but develop a tonic constriction to near stimulus. This effect may last several seconds after viewing the near target; then the pupil will slowly return to its baseline size over several seconds. The dilation may not occur evenly; however, the vermiform movement that accompanies the initial constriction is not part of redilation. The Adie pupil does not exhibit hippus (alternating constriction and dilation).

Q1022

What tool can be used to quantify relative afferent pupillary defects (RAPDs)?
Correct answer: D. neutral-density filters
Rationale
Neutral density filters can be used to quantify a RAPD. The filters come in 0.3 log unit strengths.  The amount of RAPD can be quantified by placing increasingly stronger filters in front of the normal eye to decrease the intensity of the light stimulus until there is no RAPD on the swinging light test.
The Pelli-Robson chart is a contrast sensitivity visual acuity chart.  Bagolini lenses are used to test for strabismus and anomalous retinal correspondence. The red-green duochrome test is used to refine a manifest refraction.

Q1023

An obese and asymptomatic 15-year-old girl is found to have optic disc abnormalities. B-scan echography shows normal retrobulbar optic nerve size and refractile bodies beneath the disc surface. What management is recommended for this patient?
Correct answer: B. optic disc photos and visual field monitoring
Rationale
This case describes a young patient with optic disc drusen (ODD), which represent refractile, often calcified nodules located within the optic nerve head.
When buried beneath the retinal nerve fiber layer (NFL), they crowd the optic disc and elevate the retinal NFL, mimicking true optic nerve edema (ie, pseudopapilledema). They demonstrate hyperechoic signal on B-scan or CT.
ODD can cause visual field defects similar to those of glaucoma, and they tend to be nonprogressive. There is no proven treatment to prevent visual loss, and the prognosis is usually very good.
Acetazolamide is a first-line agent in treating idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), which causes true papilledema (optic nerve head edema from increased intracranial pressure).
Intravenous steroid is the initial treatment of choice for acute optic neuritis.

Q1024

A 70-year-old diabetic man presents with an acute left head turn and a left mouth droop, but no diplopia. What is the most likely etiology?
Correct answer: D. abducens nuclear lesion
Rationale
This case describes a patient with a left gaze palsy, as indicated by the compensatory left head turn. Many of these patients do not have diplopia because the sixth nerve nucleus contains 2 populations of motoneurons: (1) those that innervate the ipsilateral lateral rectus, and (2) those that travel via the medial longitudinal fasciculus to innervate the contralateral medial rectus. In addition, the mouth droop indicates facial palsy from 7th nerve fascicle fibers that wrap around the 6th nerve nucleus prior to exiting the pons.
Other diagnoses such as myasthenia gravis and the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome can present with a variety of motility complaints and facial weakness, but an ischemic lesion of the pons in this 70-year-old vasculopathic man is most likely.
A cavernous sinus lesion would be expected to produce a peripheral abducens nerve palsy, not lateral gaze palsy, and would not affect the facial nerve.

T pallidum, B henselae, and B burgdorferi

This patient has a constellation of findings typical for neuroretinitis, including mild vision loss, disc swelling, and a star pattern of lipid in the fovea. Common causes include Bartonella henselae/cat scratch disease, syphilis, and Lyme disease, and patients should be screened for infections and possible treatment. Papilledema severe enough to cause vision loss and foveal exudate within 10 days should be much greater than seen here, so lumbar puncture would not be the desired first step. MRI is not indicated for neuroretinitis. FAF and EDI rarely provide additional diagnostically useful information in patients with neuroretinitis.

What type of eye movements are primarily affected in ocular motor apraxia?

As described by Cogan, congenital ocular motor apraxia is idiopathic and is characterized by increased latency and intermittent failure of horizontal saccadic initiation. Vertical eye movements are normal.

Q1027
