Gaze-evoked transient monocular visual loss is indicative of what condition?
Correct answer: D. orbital tumor
Rationale
Gaze-evoked transient monocular visual loss (TMVL) is classically associated with an orbital tumor that is either large or located in the orbital apex, such as a hemangioma or meningioma. The TMVL likely results from a combination of direct compression of the optic nerve and ischemia from positional vascular obstruction. Careful examination usually reveals other orbital findings, such as proptosis or limited ocular motility.
The visual loss of optic neuritis is not gaze dependent. However, pain with eye movement is a common feature.
Visual loss from papilledema can be exacerbated by body position. Patients often complain of transient visual obscurations when standing up from a sitting position.
Visual loss from optic disc drusen (ODD) can be progressive, but is not gaze-induced; up to 75% of patients with ODD can develop visual field defects, usually peripheral. A 41-year-old female presents for evaluation of double vision. She reports that her double vision persists with occlusion of the left eye but resolves with occlusion of the right eye and is present in all directions of gaze. Her ductions and versions are full, and she does not have any deviation noted on cover testing. Her corrected visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. What diagnostic test is the most appropriate next step for this patient?
Correct answer: B. pinhole vision testing
Rationale
The clinical vignette is describing monocular diplopia (diplopia present in one eye), which typically results from abnormalities of the refractive media. The use of a pinhole to resolve the diplopia proves an optical etiology and obviates the need to pursue neurological workup. Corneal topography is appropriate in the workup of some cases of monocular diplopia (eg, keratoconus), but is not necessary in all cases of monocular diplopia. OCT of the macula may help uncover retinal pathology, but retinal pathology does not commonly cause monocular diplopia. Edrophonium is used in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis and would not be indicated in the workup for monocular diplopia.

Q1029

A 40-year-old woman had sudden onset of severe headache, diplopia, and decreased vision in both eyes. Examination shows bilateral ptosis, poorly reactive pupils, and ophthalmoparesis. What abnormality is most likely to be present on neuroimaging of the head and orbits?
Correct answer: A. hemorrhagic sellar/suprasellar mass
Rationale
The constellation of bilateral vision loss, ophthalmoparesis, and ptosis shows involvement of multiple cranial nerves as well as the optic nerves in the pathological process. Tumors or other skull base disorders can give all of these findings, either unilaterally or bilaterally. The sudden onset with headache should create suspicion for pituitary apoplexy, where rapid tumor expansion with hemorrhage causes compression of the chiasm and/or optic nerves as well as cranial nerves in the cavernous sinuses.
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm should give unilateral findings without vision loss, since the optic nerve is not compressed. Internal carotid artery dissection in the cavernous sinus can give cranial nerve paresis, again without vision loss and almost always unilaterally. Demyelinating disease presents in a less acute, and rarely painful, manner.

Q1030
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Aberrant regeneration of the third nerve without a history of third nerve palsy indicates a lesion in what location?
Correct answer: C. parasellar
Rationale
Aberrant regeneration, also known as oculomotor synkinesis, is a well-described phenomenon frequently resulting from trauma, tumors, or aneurysms. It is rare in microvascular disorders. Aberrant regeneration without a history of CN 3 palsy, which is called primary aberrant regeneration, is presumptive evidence of a slowly expanding parasellar lesion, most commonly a meningioma or carotid aneurysm within the cavernous sinus, which requires appropriate neuro-imaging.
The 6th nerve is vulnerable in the prepontine space. Fistulas can develop between the carotid and the cavernous sinus. A posterior communicating artery aneurysm can also cause a 3rd nerve palsy but not with primary aberrant regeneration.

Q1031
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequence would be best for detecting the demyelinating lesions associated with multiple sclerosis (MS)?
Correct answer: B. fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR)
Rationale
Both active and inactive demyelinating lesions are best detected with FLAIR images. FLAIR provides T2-weighted images without the high (bright) CSF signals, making this imaging modality ideal for detecting periventricular white matter lesions in a demyelinating process such as MS. Only active lesions may be seen with T1/contrast images, and DWI is insensitive for MS. T2, though similar to FLAIR in some respects, is still less sensitive for detecting white matter lesions as seen in MS because a bright signal from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) may mask some lesions.

Q1032
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What horizontal movement is preserved in one-and-a-half syndrome?
Correct answer: C. abduction of the eye opposite the lesion
Rationale
One-and-a-half syndrome is a condition in which a pontine abnormality is of sufficient size to involve both the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) and the cranial nerve (CN) VI nucleus (or the adjacent paramedian pontine reticular formation [PPRF]) on the same side. This results in a combination of a unilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) and a horizontal gaze palsy. If the lesion is on the right side, the PPRF/nuclear lesion would impair gaze to the right side for both eyes. Because the MLF on the right side carries fibers from the left CN VI nucleus that ultimately will stimulate the right medial rectus, adduction of the right eye is also impaired. As a result, the right eye has no horizontal movement at all (the "one") and the left eye has impaired adduction (the "half"). The only preserved horizontal movement in one-and-a-half syndrome is abduction on the side opposite the lesion.

Q1033
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A man with HIV infection that was untreated for several years developed rapid peripheral vision loss over 3 weeks. He is otherwise well, without fever or chills, although he is slightly confused. Visual acuity is 20/400 OU, pupils react briskly, and the fundus appears normal. What abnormality can be expected to be found in his cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)?
Correct answer: D. John Cunningham (JC) virus positivity
Rationale
Many immunocompromised states, including HIV infection, can lead to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) and neurological dysfunction. PML can cause confusion, memory problems, focal weakness, and/or vision loss, depending upon the part of the brain that is involved. In this case, the occipital cortex was affected bilaterally, and this led to central and peripheral vision loss. Characteristic findings on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) include T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) white matter hyperintensity in multiple locations. PML is associated with JC virus activity; this virus can be latent in many immunocompetent persons and become active only with immunosuppression.
The MRI findings are not consistent with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, in which the 14-3-3 protein is usually positive in the CSF. Cryptococcal meningitis (diagnosed by staining the organisms with India ink) also does not cause the type of neurological deficits seen here. The patient's findings are not typical of multiple sclerosis, so oligoclonal band testing is not useful.

Q1034
Neuro-Ophthalmology
During automated static perimetry, a false positive represents what response?
Correct answer: D. the patient responds but no light stimulus is displayed
Rationale
During automated static perimetry testing, reliability is assessed using several indices. A false-positive error is recorded when the patient responds but the perimeter presents no light stimulus: a rate of less than 25% on threshold testing and less than 15% on the Swedish interactive threshold algorithm (SITA) testing is considered acceptable.
A false-negative error occurs when the patient fails to respond to a light of greater intensity than the determined threshold for that spot, with an acceptability rate of less than 25% (keeping in mind that the incidence will increase in areas of true visual field loss).
When the patient responds to a stimulus presented in the blind spot, it is a fixation loss because the patient's blind spot is presumed to have moved from the previously plotted area into the seeing eye field.
A patient blinking during presentation of a light stimulus will cause the gaze-tracking strip to deflect off of the midline and may result in a false-negative error.

Q1035

With regard to the pupil exam, what is light-near dissociation?
Correct answer: D. when the near response exceeds the bright light response
Rationale
Light–near dissociation is demonstrated when the near response exceeds the best constriction that bright light can produce. Care should be taken to provide appropriate accommodative targets, and a lack of near response usually indicates that the patient isdissociation not trying hard enough. The other scenarios are not consistent with light-near dissociation.

Q1036
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the appropriate length for a temporal artery biopsy in the evaluation of giant cell arteritis?
Correct answer: A. at least 2-3 centimeters
Rationale
Due to the possibility of skip lesions, it is possible to miss the diagnosis with small specimens of temporal artery. Thus, a negative biopsy does not rule out giant cell arteritis (GCA). In fact, false negative biopsy rates are believed to be anywhere from 3% to 9%. To avoid a false negative result, it is recommended to obtain a specimen at least 2-3 cm in length. In cases where the degree of suspicion for GCA is high but the initial temporal artery biopsy is negative, biopsy of the contralateral temporal artery may be undertaken. Once GCA is suspected, temporal artery biopsy should be done expeditiously, but it is generally accepted that performing the biopsy within 1 week of starting steroid therapy will not compromise the histopathological diagnosis.

Q1037
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 54-year-old woman presents with a progressive painless decline in vision in her right eye over a year. Examination shows mild, chronic-appearing disc edema and dilated veins in the right eye. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) T1-weighted images with contrast are shown in the figure. Based on the history, examination, and imaging, what is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. optic nerve sheath meningioma
Rationale
The findings of progressive, painless vision loss; mild, chronic-appearing disc edema; and optic nerve sheath enhancement on MRI (red arrows) are consistent with an optic nerve sheath meningioma. These meningiomas are usually detected in adults aged 40-50 years and affect women 3 times as often as men. Disc edema may be present, especially if the tumor extends anteriorly. Neuroimaging shows enhancement of the optic nerve sheath, displaying a “tram track” appearance on axial images and a “bull’s eye” appearance on coronal images.
Optic nerve gliomas are the most common primary tumors of the optic nerve, but typically occur in younger people, and neuroimaging shows fusiform or globular enlargement of the optic nerve. Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common intraorbital tumor in adults, but will cause an intraconal mass that is distinct from the optic nerve. Optic perineuritis will cause enhancement of the optic nerve sheaths on MRI that looks similar to an optic nerve sheath meningioma, but presents with acute or subacute painful vision loss.

Q1038
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents with convergence retraction nystagmus after a stroke. What is the most likely associated finding?
Correct answer: D. limitation of conjugate upgaze
Rationale
Convergence-retraction nystagmus is a feature of the dorsal midbrain syndrome. Also known as the pretectal or Parinaud syndrome, dorsal midbrain syndrome includes some or all of the following findings: conjugate limitation of vertical gaze (usually upgaze), co-contraction of extraocular muscles with attempted upgaze (convergence-retraction nystagmus), mid-dilated pupils with light–near dissociation, retraction of the lids in primary position (Collier sign), skew deviation, disruption of convergence (convergence spasm or convergence palsy), and increased square-wave jerks.
Limitation of conjugate upgaze is the most common feature and occurs with damage to the pretectum, an isthmus between the superior colliculi and the thalamus. Supranuclear fibers decussate through the pretectum as they pass to the rostral interstitial nucleus of medial longitudinal fasciculus (riMLF), the midbrain structure that functions as the saccadic generator for vertical eye movements.
Comitant esotropia, monocular elevation deficit, and apraxia of eyelid opening are not the correct answers because they are not part of the dorsal midbrain syndrome.

Q1039
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 78-year-old man presents with acute difficulty doing simple math, difficulty writing, inability to recognize his fingers, and left-right confusion. These symptoms are typical of a stroke involving what part of the brain?
Correct answer: B. dominant parietal lobe
Rationale
The correct answer is the dominant parietal lobe. Gerstmann syndrome is defined by acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, and left-right confusion, and it occurs with damage to the dominant parietal lobe. Other signs of parietal lobe damage include contralateral homonymous hemianopias or contralateral inferior quadrantanopias or optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) abnormalities due to damage to the pursuit pathways in targets moving toward the lesion. Disorders of attention, including hemispatial neglect, also occur with nondominant parietal lobe involvement.

Q1040
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 63-year-old diabetic man developed a worsening of vision, proptosis, diplopia, and eye pain over the past week. His computed tomography (CT) scan showed a lesion in the sinus extending to the orbital apex. Surgical debridement was performed, and the resulting histopathological specimen is shown in the figure. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. mucormycosis
Rationale
The figure shows a biopsy specimen demonstrating the typical nonseptate hyphae seen with rhinocerebral mucormycosis.
Rhinocerebral zygomycosis (Mucor or Rhizopus) usually occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus, patients taking corticosteroids, or neutropenic patients receiving antibiotics. The initial infection spreads from the facial skin, nasal mucosa, paranasal sinuses, or hard palate. The fungus spreads to the nearby blood vessels, affecting the orbital vessels, carotid arteries, cavernous sinuses, or jugular veins. Orbital and neurologic signs are produced by infarction, thrombosis, or hemorrhage. If untreated, rhinocerebral zygomycosis may bring about rapid deterioration, leading to death within days. A few patients may have a chronic course with little indication of systemic illness. The most common signs and symptoms include fever, nasal necrosis, periorbital swelling, decreased vision, ophthalmoplegia, sinusitis, and headache. Retinal infarction, ophthalmic artery occlusion, and optic nerve infiltration are mechanisms of blindness. Neurologic signs include hemiparesis, aphasia, seizures, and altered mental status.
Aspergillus can present with 3 main types of infection: allergic aspergillosis, aspergillomas, and invasive aspergillosis. Aspergillomas, or fungus balls, may arise in the orbit, paranasal sinuses, or brain. They can occur in either immunocompromised or immunocompetent patients. Aspergillomas are often slow growing and can produce gradually worsening proptosis, vision loss, diplopia, and pain as they invade the orbital apex. In contrast to zygomycetes, Aspergillus has septate hyphae on histological examination.
Cryptococcosis is a fungal disease caused mainly by Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii. Inhalation of these fungi and subsequent pulmonary infection may spread to the central nervous system (CNS), causing meningitis or meningoencephalitis. The most common neuro-ophthalmic abnormality is papilledema from cryptococcal meningitis.
Zoster does not typically cause invasive rhino-orbital disease.

Q1041
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What pharmacologic agent is used to confirm the diagnosis of Horner syndrome?
Correct answer: A. cocaine
Rationale
Horner syndrome (figure) can be confirmed with cocaine drops. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine released at neuromuscular junctions of the iris dilator muscle. Following instillation of cocaine in the normal eye, the pupil will dilate. In Horner syndrome, whether pre- or postsynaptic, the pupil dilates poorly because there is little or no norepinephrine being released into the synaptic cleft. Hydroxyamphetamine can be used to localize the lesion producing Horner syndrome to preganglionic or postganglionic. Hydroxyamphetamine will dilate the pupil in a normal eye or in a preganglionic Horner syndrome (because the postganglionic neuron is intact). In a postganglionic Horner syndrome the nerve terminal has degenerated and the pupil will dilate poorly. Norepinephrine and epinephrine are not used pharmacologically in the diagnosis or evaluation of Horner syndrome.

Q1042
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 30-year-old man has bilateral ptosis and an adduction deficit of the left eye from myasthenia gravis (MG). What would an examination of his pupils most likely reveal?
Correct answer: C. normal pupillary function with normal constriction and normal redilation
Rationale
Although MG can cause eyelid ptosis and ocular motility disorders of almost any pattern, pupillary abnormalities and sensory disturbances are not associated with MG, and their presence should provoke a search for another diagnosis. Thus, a patient with known ocular MG should demonstrate normal pupillary function on examination.
The other options, which describe dilated or constricted pupils with poor function, would suggest an efferent pupillary disorder, such as unilateral or bilateral Adie tonic pupil if noted in isolation, or third cranial nerve palsy or Horner syndrome with eyelid findings.

Q1043
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What test is indicated after examining a 15-year-old female who has bilateral ptosis, limited ductions, and pigmentary retinopathy?
Correct answer: A. electrocardiogram (EKG) and cardiology consult
Rationale
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) is an inherited mitochondrial myopathy that causes slowly progressive, symmetric limitation in extraocular muscles (EOM) and ptosis with weakness of the orbicularis oculi muscles. CPEO and pigmentary retinopathy in a young patient should raise concern of Kearns-Sayre syndrome, a triad of CPEO, pigmentary retinopathy with visual field loss, and heart block. It is therefore important to order an EKG and consider involving cardiology.
Audiogram and otolaryngology consultation would be indicated in the management of Usher syndrome (retinitis pigmentosa and congenital neurosensory hearing loss).
Lumbar puncture and neurology consultation would be indicated in the management of suspected multiple sclerosis, which can cause optic neuritis and/or ocular motility disorders.
Renal imaging and urology consultation would be indicated in a patient with foveal hypoplasia from aniridia due to WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformation, and mental retardation).

Q1044
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What cranial nerve passes below the petroclinoid ligament to enter the cavernous sinus?
Correct answer: D. cranial nerve VI
Rationale
Cranial nerve VI starts at its nucleus in the dorsal base of the pons, exits the pons anteriorly, ascends along the clivus, crosses the petrous apex, and passes below the petroclinoid ligament to enter the cavernous sinus, where it runs between the lateral wall and the carotid artery. Because of this 90 degree turn over the tip of the clivus and under the petroclinoid ligament, it is poised for brain compression from abnormally high or low intracranial pressure, causing bilateral VI nerve palsies. CN III, CN IV, and CN V (V1) have a separate course through the subarachnoid space and into the cavernous sinus.

Q1045
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most common pattern of color confusion associated with acquired color vision defects?
Correct answer: A. blue-yellow
Rationale
Acquired color vision defects are most frequently blue-yellow or tritan abnormalities; they affect females and males equally. Blue-yellow color defects often accompany an optic neuropathy but also can occur in a maculopathy.
Hereditary color vision defects are most frequently red-green abnormalities. They are most often X-linked recessive and affect 5%-8% of males and 0.5% of females.

Q1046
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most common primary tumor of the optic nerve?
Correct answer: B. glioma
Rationale
Optic pathway gliomas are uncommon, accounting for only about 1% of intracranial tumors. However, they are the most common primary tumor of the optic nerve. Optic pathway gliomas are more common in children, with 90% of tumors detected by the second decade of life.

Q1047
Neuro-Ophthalmology
If a patient has a left Horner syndrome with anhidrosis limited to the left forehead, what structure must the lesion be at or distal to?
Correct answer: C. left superior cervical ganglion
Rationale
A lesion of the oculosympathetic pathway occurring anywhere from the hypothalmus to the pupillary dilator muscle will result in Horner syndrome. Anhidrosis of the ipsilateral head, face, and neck  occurs with first or second order Horner syndrome, whereas anhidrosis limited to the ipsilateral forehead occurs with a lesion at or distal to the superior cervical ganglion (third order Horner syndrome).

Q1048
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What optic nerve finding is most characteristic of dominant optic atrophy?
Correct answer: A. wedge-shaped optic nerve pallor
Rationale
Dominant optic atrophy typically presents before age 10, with visual acuity ranging from 20/40 to 20/100. Visual fields show a central or cecocentral scotoma with normal peripheral isopters. Color vision reveals a blue dyschromatopsia (tritanopia). Clinically, the optic disc shows temporal pallor with an area of triangular excavation. Superotemporal or inferotemporal notching is characteristic of glaucoma. Peripapillary telangiectasia is a characteristic of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON). A yellow peripapillary halo with a ring of pigmentation is characteristic of optic nerve hypoplasia.

Q1049
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Resting pupil size is influenced by several factors, including ambient light, level of arousal, patient age, and neurologic disease. What typically causes small pupils?
Correct answer: A. pontine hemorrhage
Rationale
Extremely small pupils suggest pontine hemorrhage, narcotic intoxication, or pilocarpine use.  Pupils typically become smaller as a result of age. Elevated intraocular pressures and anxiety can lead to larger pupils.

Q1050
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is a clinical feature of Adie tonic pupil?
Correct answer: D. sectoral iris constriction
Rationale
Adie tonic pupil is a parasympathetic denervation of the pupillary sphincter resulting in a fixed (tonic) and dilated pupil. Because the denervation is segmental, there can be sectors of the iris that still constrict, but not to the same degree as a normal contralateral pupil. This results in anisocoria that is more pronounced in bright light. Because the parasympathetic innervation of the ciliary muscle may also be affected, accommodative insufficiency, not spasm, may occur, resulting in blurred vision. Because the afferent visual pathway is uninvolved, there is no relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus-Gunn pupil) despite the unequal parasympathetic tone to the pupillary sphincter muscles. The parasympathetic fibers associated with the light reflex are affected more than those for the near response; this results in light-near dissociation. Adie tonic pupil, when associated with decreased deep tendon reflexes, is called Holmes-Adie syndrome.

Q1051
Neuro-Ophthalmology
The conjunctival vessel appearance is characteristic of what disorder?
Correct answer: B. arteriovenous fistula
Rationale
In reference to conjunctival vessels, the term "corkscrew" describes the abnormal appearance of arterialized episcleral and conjunctival vessels, which occurs when there is a fistulous connection between the arterial and venous blood supplies. Graves orbitopathy can cause congestion and inflammation of the conjunctival vessels, but it does not cause abnormal arterialization that results in a corkscrew appearance. Meningioma and lymphangioma are not associated with this appearance.

Q1052
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 65-year-old pseudophakic woman presents with loss of central vision over 3 weeks in her right eye. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) is 20/200 OD, 20/30 OS, a trace right relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is present, color vision is impaired OU, and visual fields show central scotoma OD only. She complains of flashes in her central vision bilaterally, with worsening night vision. Fundus exam appears normal OU. What clinical test is most likely to be abnormal in this setting?
Correct answer: C. electroretinogram (ERG)
Rationale
This clinical scenario is most consistent with an autoimmune or paraneoplastic retinopathy, not optic neuropathy, due to the photopsias and nyctalopia described. While MRI orbit may be considered with a clinical optic neuropathy, the electroretinogram (ERG) would be most likely to reveal photoreceptor dysfunction in this case. Optical coherence tomography of the macula (OCT) may show disruption of the ellipsoid zone in the outer retina. While serum testing for antibody to recoverin (23kD protein) is the most common anti-retinal antibody associated with cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR), it is not present in the majority of cases. Thus, patients with occult retinopathies revealed on multifocal and/or full-field ERG should undergo evaluation for underlying malignancy to exclude paraneoplastic retinopathies such as CAR and MAR, which may mimic optic neuropathies.
Aquaporin-4 IgG antibody disease, or neuromyelitis optica (NMO), usually presents as a severe unilateral or bilateral optic neuritis and may have a similar presentation, but would be less likely to create photopsia and nyctalopia and should have a larger right RAPD, possibly with pain on eye movement. In addition, other areas of the optic pathway, brainstem, and cervical spine may be concurrently affected in NMO.

What is the smallest diameter of cerebral aneurysm detectable by high-quality magnetic resonance angiography?
Correct answer: B. 3 mm
Rationale
Current computed tomographic angiography or magnetic resonance angiography techniques reliably detect cerebral aneurysms of at least 3 mm diameter.

Q1054
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What feature characterizes the mydriasis caused by Adie pupil?
Correct answer: D. light-near dissociation
Rationale
Mydriasis caused by neurologic disease such as Adie pupil (idiopathic tonic pupil) is easily overcome with instillation of full-strength or even dilute pilocarpine.
Damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves produces an Adie pupil, which is characterized by a large pupil with poor reaction to light but a strong and tonic pupillary response to near vision (light-near dissociation). The pupil experiences a slow tonic redilation on looking from near to far distances. Stromal thinning is observed in areas of sphincter paralysis.

Q1055
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 31-year-old woman had subacute painful vision loss to counting fingers in the right eye that recovered over the subsequent 3 months. One year later, visual acuity is 20/30 OD, 20/20 OS with a trace right relative afferent pupillary defect and minimal right optic disc pallor. Visual evoked potential test results show markedly delayed P100 latency in both eyes. What abnormality is most likely present on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain?
Correct answer: C. periventricular white-matter lesions on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences
Rationale
This patient initially presented with a right optic neuritis and later was shown to have an abnormal visual evoked potential (VEP) in both eyes.
Abnormalities on VEP testing may indicate optic nerve dysfunction and can suggest an etiology. The most common wave measured in VEP testing is the P100 wave. Reduced amplitudes are less specific than is delayed P100 latency, which typically is seen with demyelinating optic neuropathies.
Based on the history of optic neuritis and the evidence of bilateral optic nerve demyelination based on VEP, there is concern for multiple sclerosis. Therefore, central nervous system (CNS) white-matter lesions may be present as well. Asymptomatic demyelination, as may be present in this patient, can be diagnosed when the P100 latency is severely delayed.
Compressive and ischemic lesions do not usually cause such marked change to the P100 latency, although they may affect P100 amplitude. Optic nerve enhancement should not be seen with disease that was active 1 year prior.

Q1056
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 45-year-old man presents with several episodes per day of severe left-sided orbital and temporal pain that lasts 5–10 minutes, occasionally associated with left ptosis and miosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. paroxysmal hemicrania
Rationale
Paroxysmal hemicrania is a form of trigeminal autonomic cephalgia associated with short bouts of pain highly responsive to indomethacin. Although cluster headache is also unilateral and frequently associated with autonomic features, the bouts of excruciating pain are of longer duration (15–180 minutes). Hemicrania continua is characterized by a continuous unilateral headache. Idiopathic stabbing headache manifests as episodic, very brief, sharp, jabbing pains, unassociated with autonomic features.

Q1057

A 50-year-old female patient presents with an intermittent electric shock-like pain in her right forehead and cheek. She has noticed her symptoms seem to be precipitated by wind on her face. Her examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. trigeminal neuralgia
Rationale
Trigeminal neuralgia usually occurs in middle-aged patients and is described as a paroxysmal burning or electric-shock type pain in the face, lasting seconds to minutes. It can be primary or secondary, with the majority of cases caused by vascular compression of cranial nerve V (CN V). In primary trigeminal neuralgia, the pain usually involves CN V2 or V3 distribution unilaterally. Involvement of CN V1 distribution only is suggestive of a secondary cause. The facial pain may be precipitated by chewing, tooth brushing, or cold wind on the face. Examination is normal in primary trigeminal neuralgia. Occipital neuralgia by contrast causes a paroxysmal stabbing pain in the distribution of the greater or lesser occipital nerves. There is usually tenderness to palpation over the affected nerve. Temporomandibular disease pain may be referred to the ear, preauricular region, or neck. There may be a click or pop upon jaw opening. Internal carotid artery dissection usually produces unilateral facial pain and is often associated with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome.

Q1058
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Optociliary shunt vessels are a feature of what entity?
Correct answer: D. optic nerve meningioma
Rationale
Orbital meningiomas originate in the arachnoid of the optic nerve sheath. They most commonly occur in women in their third and fourth decades of life. Symptoms include gradual, painless, unilateral loss of vision. Examination findings may include decreased visual acuity; relative afferent pupillary defect; proptosis; ophthalmoplegia; normal, atrophic, or swollen optic nerve head; and visible optociliary shunt vessels (also identified as "tortuous vessels").
Orbital cavernous hemangiomas also occur more commonly in women. They are the most common benign neoplasm of the orbit. Findings include progressive proptosis, retinal striae, hyperopia, optic nerve compression, increased intraocular pressure, and strabismus. Orbital fibrous dysplasia is a benign developmental disorder of bone. Computed tomography (CT) shows hyperostotic bone. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows lack of dural enhancement, which distinguishes fibrous dysplasia from meningioma.

Q1059

A 10-year-old boy with a recent history of otitis media presents with fever, lethargy, and headache. Ocular examination reveals bilateral disc edema. What diagnostic procedure would be most helpful?
Correct answer: A. lumbar puncture
Rationale
This child presents with signs and symptoms of meningitis, which is diagnosed clinically and supported by the presence of increased white blood cell count in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), as well as changes in CSF protein, glucose, and cultures. Lumbar puncture (done after neuroimaging) to collect CSF is the most helpful diagnostic procedure. Neuroimaging is usually obtained prior to lumbar puncture to rule out large mass lesions, and blood testing with cultures also helps in associated sepsis management, but orbital MRI, CT angiography, and chest radiography are unlikely to be initially helpful.

Q1060

A 49-year-old woman complains of blurred vision in her left eye. On examination, her right eye is normal. Her left eye has visual acuity of 20/40 and an afferent pupillary defect. The left eye also has a deficit of adduction, elevation, and abduction, and levator function of 10 mm. What management should be initiated?
Correct answer: C. Obtain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits with contrast.
Rationale
This patient has signs of orbital apex syndrome with a left optic neuropathy, ptosis, and limited ductions. Temporal arteritis does not give insidious symptom onset; therefore, it is unlike the case here and is very unlikely in a 49-year-old person. Because there is also an optic neuropathy, diseases like Guillain-Barré syndrome (and its Miller Fisher variant) and myasthenia gravis (MG) are also unlikely, as they do not cause optic nerve dysfunction. An MRI of the brain and orbit is needed to look for orbital apex pathology and possible intracranial spread.

Q1061
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What nerve courses along the surface of the clivus?
Correct answer: C. abducens nerve
Rationale
The abducens nerve (CN VI) exits the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle and courses anteriorly over the clivus and underneath the petroclinoid (Gruber) ligament to enter the Dorello canal. Lesions within the clivus and certain skull base fractures may damage the abducens nerve in this location. The oculomotor nerve and trochlear nerve course above the clivus for most of their subarachnoid course to enter their dural canals near the clivus as they pass into the cavernous sinus. The trigeminal nerve courses extra-axially before entering the dura near the petrous pyramid.

Q1062

A 48-year-old woman suddenly develops painful vision loss in her right eye. Two weeks later, she develops similar symptoms in her left eye. She is counting fingers with the right eye and hand motion with the left eye, without a relative afferent pupillary defect, but with sluggishly reactive pupils. Her dilated exam in the right eye is normal, but she has mild optic nerve head (ONH) edema in the left eye. MRI shows bilateral enhancement of the optic nerves. After treatment with IV methylprednisolone, she experiences only minimal vision recovery. What underlying condition is the most likely cause of her bilateral vision loss?
Correct answer: A. neuromyelitis optica
Rationale
This vision loss is most consistent with bilateral optic neuritis. The bilateral nature of the vision loss, along with the severity of visual impairment and minimal recovery after treatment, raise a concern for neuromyelitis optica. It is uncommon for MS to present with bilateral optic neuritis with minimal recovery. Giant cell arteritis can cause bilateral severe vision loss associated with headache, but it does not affect young patients. Fingolimod has been associated with macular edema, which would cause blurred vision, but not this degree of vision loss.

Q1063
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Two weeks ago, a 29-year-old woman noted a "spot" in the vision of her left eye that has progressed over the last 3 days. Visual acuity is 20/20 OD and 20/60 OS. The pupils react briskly, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. There is a left central scotoma. Funduscopy is normal in the right eye and shown for the left eye. Vitreous cells are noted in the left eye. The most likely diagnosis is from what pathologic category?
Correct answer: B. infection
Rationale
The fundus photograph of the left eye shows optic disc edema with exudate in the macula in a star pattern. Inflammation is the most common explanation for this feature constellation and includes both sterile (sarcoidosis and vasculitis) and infectious etiologies. However, noninfectious inflammation is not offered as an option for this constellation of features. The most common infectious agent responsible for optic disc edema with macular exudate in this pattern is that from cat scratch disease (Bartonella henselae), but less commonly, other infections such as syphilis and toxoplasmosis may cause a similar presentation. Demyelination associated with optic neuritis rarely has this appearance, but the presence of vitreous cells would make this alternative much less likely compared to an infectious agent. Ischemic optic neuropathy and compressive optic neuropathy would not be associated with vitreous cells.

Q1064
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An 18-year-old woman reports tunnel vision in both eyes. Visual acuity is 20/400 OU, pupils react briskly, and anterior and posterior segments are normal. She is able to ambulate without difficulty. What finding on Goldmann perimetry confirms a nonorganic component to her vision loss?
Correct answer: C. overlapping and spiraling isopters
Rationale
The disparity between visual acuity and examination result raises suspicion for nonorganic vision loss. In Goldmann kinetic perimetry, the visual field is tested continuously in a clockwise or counterclockwise direction, starting with the (smallest) I4e stimulus. A common nonorganic response shows a spiraling isopter getting closer and closer to fixation as testing continues. As larger stimuli are employed, there is often further constriction, resulting in overlapping isopters.
A step across the vertical or horizontal midline (eg, nasal step) may indicate at least some physiologic component to the field abnormality.
Central scotomata may occur in many disease processes, such as toxic or nutritional optic neuropathy or Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, and are not suggestive of nonphysiologic disease.
While generalized field constriction can occur in the setting of nonphysiologic visual loss, it also can occur in disease processes such as retinitis pigmentosa. Generalized constriction does not confirm nonorganic vision loss.

Q1065
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For 3 days, a 67-year-old man has had difficulty reading with his right eye. Visual acuity is normal, but he has an inferior altitudinal visual field defect, superior optic disc swelling, and a small peripapillary hemorrhage. In taking the patient's recent history, what question could reveal a risk factor for the most likely ocular disorder?
Correct answer: A. Do you snore and wake frequently while sleeping?
Rationale
The most common cause of acute acquired optic neuropathy in adults is nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). Patients with NAION classically have inferior altitudinal visual field defects with superior optic disc edema and peripapillary hemorrhages. Sleep apnea is a risk factor for NAION. NAION is also associated with structural crowding of the disc (strongest risk factor), diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.
Thrombophilia, not hemophilia, is a proposed risk factor for NAION. Episodic right-sided headache with tearing and eye redness is suggestive of a cluster headache, which is associated with Horner syndrome, not NAION. Evening drooping of the upper lid could suggest myasthenia, which would be unrelated to NAION.

Q1066
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most frequent cause of a complete, pupil-sparing cranial nerve III palsy?
Correct answer: B. ischemia
Rationale
Microvascular disease is the most common cause of a complete, pupil-sparing cranial nerve III palsy. The parasympathetic pupillary fibers are located in the periphery of the nerve at its superonasal aspect and are thought to be spared the deeper ischemic insult seen in microvascular disease (hypertension, diabetes, etc.) in many cases. In contrast, an expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm compresses the third nerve preferentially at its periphery, resulting in pupillary involvement.
Blunt head trauma and demyelinating disease can result in oculomotor nerve palsy, but they are far less frequent etiologies than ischemia. Of note, traumatic third nerve palsy typically requires significant intracranial trauma with associated neurologic injury,
Two other issues regarding third nerve palsy are worth mentioning. First, the "rule of the pupil" applies only to complete third nerve palsy. A partial (evolving) third nerve palsy—regardless of pupillary involvement—should be treated with the same urgency as a pupil-involving complete third nerve palsy: An expanding aneurysm may cause only partial involvement of the oculomotor nerve early in the process.
The second issue is work-up of third nerve palsy. All partial or pupil-involving complete third nerve palsies are considered emergencies and require urgent neuroimaging including noninvasive angiography. While urgent neuroimaging may not be required in a complete, pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in an older patient with vascular risk factors, many ophthalmologists and neuro-ophthalmologists choose to image all third nerve palsies to avoid missing dangerous pathology.

Q1067
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 76-year-old man has worsening constant diplopia over 6 months. He has a history of excised left-sided facial squamous cell carcinoma and diabetes mellitus. Examination reveals 3 mm left ptosis and reduced left eye motility. His right eye moves normally. Numbness of his left cheek is found on examination. What is the most likely cause of his diplopia?
Correct answer: D. cavernous sinus tumor
Rationale
Constant left-sided ptosis and ophthalmoplegia suggests cranial nerve (CN) III palsy. Ipsilateral facial numbness indicates CN V2 lesion. The most common location for multiple CN palsies is the cavernous sinus, and differential diagnosis is broad. Given a history of facial malignancy, anesthesia of CN V2 suggests recurrence of squamous cell carcinoma with perineural spread into the cavernous sinus. Perineural spread usually indicates malignant tumor such as adenoid cystic carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma, as in this case.
Sympathetic chain denervation would not lead to dysmotility.
Uncontrolled type II diabetes mellitus causes an ischemic, not slowly progressive, CN palsy. An opportunistic cavernous sinus infection secondary to uncontrolled diabetes, such as mucormycosis, would be expected to progress rapidly, have other findings such as necrotic nasal debris, and render the patient acutely ill.
ICA aneurysm would not account for the presence of CN V and CN VI palsy.

Q1068

A 65-year-old man with polymyalgia rheumatica presents for evaluation of transient vision loss. He has recently experienced pain when chewing and tenderness when combing his hair. An urgent workup for what disease is indicated?
Correct answer: A. giant cell arteritis
Rationale
Approximately 10% of patients with polymyalgia rheumatica eventually develop the vasculitis underlying GCA. Symptoms include jaw claudication and scalp tenderness. Optic nerve insult may result from GCA; it is an ischemic event rather than an inflammatory etiology, as in some other causes of optic neuritis. GCA can be associated with retinal arterial occlusions, but an embolic workup is not usually indicated. Cavernous sinus syndrome would present with orbital apex impairment symptoms including ophthalmoplegia and proptosis.

Q1069
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient who has multiple sclerosis and a past history of a single severe episode of optic neuritis in her right eye that resulted in a relative afferent pupillary defect after resolution presents with equally round and reactive pupils with no afferent pupillary defect. What is the most common cause of the above finding in this patient?
Correct answer: C. optic neuritis in the left eye
Rationale
A patient who has had an episode of severe right optic neuritis in the past would be expected to have a relative afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the right eye. However, if the patient developed damage of a similar magnitude to the other optic nerve, then the patient would be expected to have "loss" of the APD. In this patient, optic neuritis in the left eye would result in "loss" of the right afferent pupillary defect if the degree of optic nerve involvement matched that in the right eye. It is important to remember the term "relative" when thinking about afferent pupillary defects, which detect the amount of light perceived by the optic nerve. If both optic nerves are equally damaged, then the amount of light perceived by each is similarly decreased and there is no relative difference between them to produce an APD. An APD is most commonly seen with processes affecting the optic nerve and is very sensitive at detecting asymmetries in optic nerve conduction.
Although an APD can be caused by pathology other than that affecting the optic nerve (large retinal detachments, for example), the most common cause of an APD is optic nerve pathology. Recurrent optic neuritis in the right eye would worsen the relative afferent pupillary defect. A cataract will not cause loss of the right RAPD. Transient visual changes brought on by exercise (Uhthoff sign) occur despite recovery from the initial optic neuritis episode and do not affect the appearance of the APD. Therefore, this is not helpful in regard to possible optic neuritis in the left eye. In this scenario, loss of the APD is most suggestive of an optic neuritis or optic nerve damage in the left eye.

What is the preferred order of surgical procedures for a patient with severe thyroid eye disease that requires multiple surgeries?
Correct answer: C. orbital decompression, strabismus surgery, eyelid surgery
Rationale
Orbital decompression will often alter or augment pre-existing strabismus, so it should always precede strabismus surgery. Similarly, the strabismus surgery often alters the position of the eyelids, particularly the inferior eyelids. Eyelid surgery should be the last step.

Q1071
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What component of the ocular exam is more suggestive of an optic neuropathy than of a maculopathy?
Correct answer: C. large relative afferent pupillary defect
Rationale
A large relative afferent pupillary defect is highly suggestive of unilateral or asymmetric optic neuropathy (although CRAO and CRVO an also cause large APDs). A small relative afferent pupillary defect can be seen with significant asymmetric retinal damage involving the macula. Color vision can be altered in patients with maculopathies or optic neuropathies. A central scotoma might be seen in both maculopathies and optic neuropathies. Mild optic nerve head pallor is common in numerous chronic retinopathies such as cone dystrophies.

Q1072

A 24-year-old obese white woman with a body mass index (BMI) of 41 presents with a few seconds of vision blurring with spontaneous recovery, headache, and a "swooshing" sound in her ears. She is found to have mild papilledema and a normal magnetic resonance imaging/magnetic resonance venography (MRI/MRV) result. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 45 cm of water. What features of her presentation are associated with poor prognosis?
Correct answer: C. morbid obesity
Rationale
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is a disease in which 90% of patients are women who are obese, and it peaks in the third decade of life. It presents with signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure. Common symptoms include headaches that are worse when lying down, transient visual obscurations, and pulsatile tinnitus. Visual field testing, along with acuity and color testing, are mandatory to evaluate visual status and determine further treatment. MRI/MRV and lumbar puncture are used to rule out other causes of increased intracranial pressure such as a mass, dural sinus thrombosis, or meningitis. Poor visual prognosis is associated with male gender, African American race, morbid obesity (a BMI of 40 or more), anemia, and severe papilledema.

Q1073
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What clinical sign is expected in patients with bilateral fourth cranial nerve (CN IV) palsies?
Correct answer: D. V-pattern esotropia
Rationale
The superior oblique muscle intorts, depresses, and abducts the eye. A patient with a bilateral CN IV palsy presents with crossed hypertropia (right hypertropia on left gaze and left hypertropia on right gaze), extorsion of at least 10°, a large V-pattern esotropia (esotropia greatest on downgaze), and chin-down positioning (as hypertropia decreases in upgaze). Intorsion of the hypertropic eye accompanies a skew deviation in the ocular tilt reaction.

Q1074
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 7-year-old child with a past medical history of sinus surgery presents for routine examination. There was no lid edema or proptosis, and there were no motility deficits after surgery. Her best-corrected visual acuity is no light perception in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. There is a dense relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye and her optic nerve has the appearance shown in the figure. What segment of the optic nerve is most likely to be affected?
Correct answer: C. intracanalicular optic nerve
Rationale
The intracanalicular optic nerve is most sensitive to trauma and sinus surgery. The optic canal is contained within the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, and the optic nerve sheath fuses to the periorbita as it exits the orbit and enters the optic canal. The ophthalmic artery and sympathetic nerves also travel within the optic canal. Because there is only a thin shell of bone between the optic nerve and the instrument, surgery within the sphenoid sinus has potential to damage the optic nerve directly; shear forces associated with closed head injury can indirectly damage the optic nerve at the level of the optic canal.
Hypoperfusion at the level of the prelaminar optic nerve can result in ischemic optic neuropathy. Intraorbital masses or extreme proptosis can result in injury to the intraorbital optic nerve. Sellar masses or internal carotid artery aneurysms may compress the intracranial optic nerve.

Q1075
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What percentage of patients with idiopathic isolated peripheral CN VII palsy (Bell palsy) spontaneously improve?
Correct answer: A. 85%
Rationale
Bell palsy refers to an isolated, unilateral, peripheral dysfunction of cranial nerve (CN) VII that causes an acute hemifacial paresis. Approximately 85% of patients with Bell palsy experience a satisfactory spontaneous recovery. Subtle signs of aberrant regeneration can be detected on examination. Recovery typically begins within 3 weeks of onset of the deficit and is complete by 2-3 months. In the remaining patients, recovery is incomplete, and significant synkinesis with co-contraction of a variety of facial muscles is common. Complete facial palsy at the time of presentation, impairment of lacrimation, dysacusis, pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, and advanced age are all poor prognostic factors.
Although facial numbness has been reported, a true decrease in cutaneous facial sensation would suggest concurrent CN V involvement. CN V involvement, bilateral facial weakness at onset, and elevated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) white count, should prompt a workup for secondary causes of facial palsy, such as infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic etiology.

Q1076
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 47-year-old man noted difficulty reading with his left eye. His visual acuity was 20/40 in the left eye, 20/20 in the right. Humphrey visual field testing showed a central scotoma in the left eye and superotemporal loss in the right eye. Neuroimaging showed a lesion affecting the afferent visual system. Where would the lesion be located?
Correct answer: A. anterior chiasm
Rationale
This patient has a junctional scotoma with central loss in the ipsilateral eye and a temporal hemianopia in the opposite eye. This is caused by a lesion compressing the optic nerve at its junction with the anterior optic chiasm. Posterior chiasmal compression typically causes a bitemporal hemianopia. Optic tract lesions and lateral geniculate nucleus lesions cause homonymous hemianopia.

Q1077

A 21-year-old woman presents with a 1-week history of pain with eye movements to the left and blurred vision worse in left gaze. Her pupils react briskly, with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Her automated perimetry is normal in each eye. Her computed tomography (CT) scan is shown. She reports having several previous episodes with similar symptoms over the past 3 years. What tests are most appropriate in the workup of this condition?
Correct answer: B. cytoplasmic staining pattern (c-ANCA), antinuclear antibody (ANA), angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), lysozyme, IgG4
Rationale
Pain with eye movement is commonly seen in optic neuritis but may also be found with orbital inflammation, particularly myositis. Her axial CT scan shows thickening of the left medial rectus muscle and tendon, supporting the diagnosis of myositis. The tendon is not involved in thyroid disease, so testing for thyroid function would not be appropriate. An MRI is not necessary for further evaluation of orbital myositis if the CT findings are as shown. A lumbar puncture with opening pressure is important in the diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension but not orbital myositis. Recurrent orbital myositis is sometimes associated with systemic disease, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, IgG4 disease, and lymphoma.

What is the most important reason that magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should not be performed on a patient with a metallic foreign body in the eye?
Correct answer: A. potential for dislodging the metallic foreign body
Rationale
The magnetic field can dislodge a metallic foreign body. In patients with intraocular metallic foreign bodies, this can result in severe damage to the eye. Exposure to ionizing radiation and lack of sagittal imaging are problems associated with computed tomography (CT) scans. Overestimation of vascular stenosis can occur with magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) scans.

Q1079

Three days ago, a 62-year-old woman experienced transient visual loss in the right eye that lasted 10 minutes. She denies prior similar episodes and has had no headaches, weight loss, or jaw pain with chewing. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU. Color vision, pupillary reactions, and ocular motility are normal OU. Given the right fundus appearance shown, what test would be most likely to confirm the cause of her findings?
Correct answer: B. carotid ultrasonography
Rationale
Fundus photography shows an arteriolar embolus in the distribution of the superotemporal artery of the right eye. The carotid arteries, heart valves, and aorta would be the most likely source of the embolus, unless the patient has a patent foramen ovale or other shunt.
A fasting serum lipid profile may be helpful to evaluate underlying risk for atherosclerosis but will not reveal the source of the embolus. Giant cell arteritis can cause central retinal artery occlusion, but since none of the vessels in the retina have an elastic layer, they typically cannot cause branch retinal artery occlusions or emboli. Therefore, testing for erythrocyte sedimentation rate is not indicated. The yield of blood testing for a hypercoagulable state is exceedingly low and would not be a first-line test in this setting.

Q1080
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Facial nerve palsy combined with hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction should prompt consideration of what diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. cerebellopontine (CPA) angle mass
Rationale
CPA lesions can result in a constellation of findings, including ipsilateral facial nerve palsy (upper and lower face), decreased tearing, dysgeusia, loss of salivary secretion, loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, hearing impairment, nystagmus, vertigo, ataxia, and/or adjacent cranial nerve findings (CN V, CN VI).
Bell palsy is an isolated facial nerve palsy with no clear etiology. It is usually unilateral and is thought to be from inflammation or to be a sequela to herpes zoster infection.
The seventh cranial nerve is the cranial nerve most commonly involved in sarcoidosis. This sarcoidosis involves the parotid gland, which affects the facial nerve branches passing through this gland.
Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is associated with recurrent unilateral or bilateral facial paralysis, accompanied by chronic facial swelling and lingua plicata (furrowing of the tongue). The etiology of this disorder, which usually begins in childhood or adolescence, is unknown. Of the listed answer choices, only a CPA mass would produce hearing and vestibular dysfunction in addition to a CN VII dysfunction.

Q1081
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What clinical finding is consistent with aberrant regeneration of CN III?
Correct answer: B. eyelid retraction with adduction
Rationale
Aberrant regeneration of CN III occurs after damage results in regrowth and misrouting of fibers with innervation of muscles not normally activated together. This causes abnormal synkinetic phenomenon such as eyelid retraction with adduction or pupillary miosis with supraduction, adduction, or infraduction. Eyelid retraction with supraduction is a normal response to CN III activation. Aberrant regeneration of CN III is common after traumatic injury, but can also occur with compressive lesions such as aneurysms and tumors. Microvascular ischemic CN III does not cause aberrant regeneration.

Q1082
Neuro-Ophthalmology
If the pupil affected by Horner syndrome fails to dilate with hydroxyamphetamine, where is the defect?
Correct answer: D. postganglionic neuron
Rationale
Hydroxyamphetamine acts to release norepinephrine from the presynaptic terminal. In the case of a normal eye or in a preganglionic Horner syndrome, the postganglionic neuron is usually intact, and one would expect normal dilation of the pupil. In a postganglionic lesion, the nerve terminal has degenerated, and the pupil will dilate poorly. Hydroxyamphetamine has no effect on pupillary muscles or their motor endplates

Q1083

A 48-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome developed severe headache and diplopia over the past 2 weeks. On examination, she is 20/20 OU and has enlarged blind spots on automated visual fields. She has bilateral abduction deficits. Fundus examination reveals severe bilateral optic-disc swelling with hemorrhages. What diagnostic test should be performed next?
Correct answer: C. brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV)
Rationale
The patient is presenting with classic signs and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure. Although the most common cause of raised intracranial pressure is idiopathic intracranial hypertension that affects young obese women, this is a diagnosis of exclusion only after neuroimaging and lumbar puncture have been performed to rule out an underlying cause.
Imaging is always performed prior to a lumbar puncture to ensure that no large mass is present that could possibly lead to brainstem herniation.
This patient has a history of anitiphospholipid antibody syndrome and has developed subacute onset of severe bilateral disc edema and bilateral abduction deficits, indicative of a fairly rapid increase in intracranial pressure. This is concerning for a possible cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, especially within the transverse or superior sagittal sinus, which often presents with signs and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure. Therefore, an MRV of the head is recommended to evaluate for a cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, in addition to an MRI brain scan to evaluate for other structural causes of raised intracranial pressure.
If the patient had a sudden onset of symptoms within the past day, a CT scan of the head would be appropriate to evaluate for intracranial hemorrhage. However, her symptoms have been present for the past 2 weeks, and therefore more detailed imaging with magnetic resonance is recommended to better evaluate for the cause. An aneurysm can present with headache, but it would be expected to cause other neurologic deficits if the patient had raised intracranial pressure from a ruptured aneurysm, and therefore an MRA is not warranted here.

Q1084

According to the results of the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), what is the likely benefit of intravenous (IV) corticosteroid treatment in a patient with typical retrobulbar optic neuritis that started 5 days ago?
Correct answer: A. Visual function may recover more rapidly with treatment.
Rationale
The ONTT enrolled patients with a first episode of optic neuritis who presented for evaluation within 8 days of symptom onset. Patients were randomized to intravenous corticosteroid treatment for 3 days, followed by oral prednisone for 11 days, oral prednisone for 14 days, or oral placebo. IV treatment was associated with more rapid visual improvement at 6 weeks after onset of symptoms, but final visual outcomes at 6 months were not statistically different amongst the 3 treatment groups. Analysis at the 2-year timepoint indicated that patients treated with IV steroids were less likely to progress to developing MS, but this effect did not persist even into the third year and was not observed after 5 years. The major predictor for risk of progression to MS was found to be the presence of one or more white matter lesions on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain.

A 25-year-old individual has noticed episodes of intermittent vertical diplopia for several months. He has no history of recent injury or illness. Strabismus evaluation reveals a right hyperphoria in the primary position that increases on left gaze and on right head tilt. Fusional vertical amplitudes are 15 diopters. What next step would be helpful in arriving at the correct diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. viewing old family photographs
Rationale
The history and findings are consistent with a congenital superior oblique weakness. Old family photographs may reveal a longstanding compensatory head tilt. The large vertical fusional amplitudes help differentiate a congenital superior oblique weakness from a recently acquired onset. This distinction is important. If this were a recent onset of paresis and there was no history of trauma, a neurological evaluation and an MRI would be indicated. There are no associated signs that would indicate the individual has endocrine myopathy. There is no variability in the strabismus and no ptosis, which makes myasthenia gravis unlikely.

Q1086

A 79-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of difficulty chewing food, and of weight loss and headache. Her dentist recently diagnosed her with temperomandibular joint (TMJ) inflammation and prescribed ibuprofen. Over the past week, she has experienced transient visual loss in the left eye. The ophthalmologic examination is normal except for 1 cotton-wool spot in the left fundus. What is the best next step?
Correct answer: D. Obtain a Westergren sedimentation rate and begin systemic corticosteroids while awaiting the result.
Rationale
The patient's clinical picture is highly suggestive of giant cell arteritis (GCA). GCA is an ophthalmologic emergency because of the potential for bilateral, irreversible visual loss. This patient is already visually symptomatic and has evidence of possible posterior segment ischemia (cotton-wool spot). The most important next step is the immediate initiation of appropriately dosed systemic corticosteroids, either orally or intravenously, along with initial serologic testing; in cases with a high suspicion for GCA, the results of serologic testing should not delay corticosteroid therapy. Serology usually includes the triad of Westergren sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and platelet count.
The gold standard for the diagnosis of GCA remains temporal artery biopsy (TAB), which can be safely performed in most patients even while anticoagulated. TAB should be performed as soon as possible, ideally within 2 weeks, but in some cases remains positive for months after the initiation of treatment.
While carotid stenosis may certainly present with amaurosis fugax, and carotid ultrasonography may in fact be necessary should the work-up for GCA prove negative, the leading diagnosis in this case remains GCA.
Jaw claudication can be misdiagnosed by clinicians as TMJ disease, but jaw or tongue claudication is the symptom most specific for GCA. This symptom should always be sought by the clinician in any patient over the age of 50 years with complaints of transient visual loss.

The most common cause of nasal visual field loss is glaucoma, but the disc pictured here has no cupping and is elevated without any obscuration of the retinal nerve fiber layer or blood vessels. This appearance is suggestive of optic nerve head drusen, which may be sporadic or inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. When drusen are suspected, appropriate imaging will help to confirm the diagnosis. Disc drusen appear hyperechoic on B-scan ultrasonography.
A decrease in the diameter of the optic nerve sheath when patient looks 30 degrees away from primary gaze describes a positive 30-degree test, which is characteristic of papilledema.

Q1089
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An 83-year-old man presents with 1-day history of sudden onset of visual loss in both eyes. His visual acuity is no light perception (NLP) OU. His brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is shown. What pupil finding is expected in this condition?
Correct answer: B. normal pupil reaction
Rationale
This patient's axial MRI shows hyperintense lesions within both occipital lobes, highly suggestive of cortical visual loss. In severe cases, bilateral occipital lobe lesions may cause visual loss to the level of no light perception. The pupils are unaffected because the afferent pupillary fibers travel to the midbrain, remote from the occipital lobe. Therefore, the pupils are brisk in patients with cortical visual loss. Light-near dissociation is present in lesions in the midbrain or may be seen in patients with partial damage to the ciliary nerves (such as Adie tonic pupil or after extensive panretinal photocoagulation). A relative afferent pupillary defect would only be present if the afferent pupillary fibers on one side were preferentially damaged. Patients with bilateral NLP vision secondary to lesions anterior to the point along the optic tracts where the afferent pupillary fibers diverge will have bilateral fixed and dilated pupils.

Q1090
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 65-year-old woman presents with new-onset complaints of intermittent double vision for the last 6 months. On examination, double vision persists when covering the left eye, but disappears when covering the right eye and improves when the patient blinks. What diagnostic test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. corneal topography
Rationale
Monocular diplopia is caused by aberrations in the optical system. It usually results from abnormalities of the refractive media. This can include uncorrected or irregular astigmatism, basement membrane dystrophy, tear film abnormalities, or cataract. Less commonly, monocular diplopia can result from macular pathology such as fluid, epiretinal membrane, or fibrosis.
Wavefront analysis will describe lower-order and higher-order optical aberrations but will not establish the etiology of the aberrations. Motility testing would be helpful in binocular diplopia. Macular pathology can cause double vision but would not be affected by blinking.

Q1091
Neuro-Ophthalmology
After a first episode of optic neuritis in a patient, what is the best predictor for the future risk of multiple sclerosis (MS)?
Correct answer: C. periventricular white-matter lesions on brain MRI
Rationale
An abnormal brain MRI scan showing at least one white-matter lesion consistent with demyelinating disease is the best predictor of MS in patients after a first episode of optic neuritis. The risk for developing MS is estimated at 72% after 15 years in patients with presence of abnormalities on MRI compared with about 25% in patients with normal brain MRI at presentation.

Q1092
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Automated static perimetry has several indices to gauge the reliability of a visual field test. What reliability index measures how often the patient identifies the stimulus in the previously placed physiologic blind spot?
Correct answer: D. fixation losses
Rationale
The reliability of perimetry results is assessed by identifying the following patient response characteristics:
  • Fixation losses: how often the patient identifies the stimulus in the previously plotted physiologic blind spot location (ie, a response not expected), indicating that the eye is not aligned with the fixation target.
  • False-positive response rate: how frequently the patient signals when no target is displayed.
  • False-negative response rate: how often the patient fails to signal when a target brighter than the previously determined threshold for that spot is displayed.
  • Gaze tracker: tracks the pupil and checks for eye movements, which are signaled as upward deflections, and blinks, which are signaled as downward deflections.

Q1093
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 75-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents to clinic after an episode of transient monocular vision loss, characterized by acute, painless vision loss in the right eye only, preceded by a descending curtain over the vision, which then resolved over 10 minutes. The episode occurred earlier that morning. Ocular examination is unremarkable. What is the best next step in management?
Correct answer: C. Evaluate immediately in the emergency department, preferably one associated with a stroke center.
Rationale
In a patient of this age with transient monocular visual loss, 2 potentially devastating vascular causes must be evaluated immediately: (1) giant cell arteritis and (2) embolic phenomena. If an embolic cause is suspected, then a complete vascular and cardiac work up must proceed urgently, due to the increased risk of morbidity and mortality from stroke in this setting. Giant cell arteritis must also be ruled out in patients over age 50. Embolic evaluation must include (1) imaging of the carotid arteries (with Doppler, MRA, or CTA), (2) MRI with diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) to evaluate for associated cerebral ischemia, and (3) echocardiography to evaluate for valvular and cardiac wall defects, intracardiac tumors, and large thrombi. If a cardiac or carotid source for embolism is not found, then other systemic processes that could contribute to stroke must also be considered, including advanced age, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, smoking, and sleep apnea.

Q1094
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Decreased levator function, lid lag on downgaze, and absent or poorly formed upper eyelid crease are characteristics of what condition?
Correct answer: B. congenital ptosis
Rationale
Decreased levator function, lid lag on downgaze, and absent or poorly formed upper eyelid crease are characteristics of congenital ptosis. CN III palsy causes ptosis with decreased levator function and there may be the appearance of lid lag on downgaze if there is aberrant regeneration causing lid retraction on downgaze, but there is no absent or poorly formed upper eyelid crease. Levator aponeurosis dehiscence is usually characterized by normal levator function and high upper eyelid crease. There is no lid lag on downgaze. Horner syndrome is characterized by normal levator function. The mild ptosis is due to denervation of the sympathetically innervated Müller muscle in the upper eyelid. The upper eyelid crease is normal and there is no lid lag on downgaze.

Q1095
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What examination and/or ancillary test finding is most likely in a 40-year-old man with history of alcohol abuse and gastric bypass surgery who reports gradually progressive bilateral visual loss over a 4-month period?
Correct answer: B. cecocentral scotoma on perimetry
Rationale
Gastric bypass surgery may lead to malabsorption of vitamin B12, and poor food intake with alcoholism may exacerbate this problem and lead to depletion of the body's vitamin B12 stores. This vitamin deficiency may cause optic neuropathy that primarily affects the papillomacular bundle and results in central vision loss with a cecocentral scotoma on visual field testing. Small pupils with light-near dissociation are seen with syphilitic infection or midbrain disorders, and are not associated with central vision loss. Optic disc swelling is not seen with nutritional deficiency. Macular edema, also, is not a consequence of poor nutritional intake, as seen in this case.

Q1096
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What branch of the ophthalmic division of cranial nerve V  (V1) both supplies the tip of the nose and carries sensory fibers from the cornea?
Correct answer: D. nasociliary
Rationale
Sensory innervation to the area surrounding the orbit is provided by the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve. The ophthalmic division (V1) further divides into 3 branches: the frontal, lacrimal, and nasociliary. These branches enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. In addition to supplying the sensory input to the nasal septum, turbinates, and tip of the nose, the nasociliary nerve branches into the long ciliary nerves that carry the sensory input from the cornea, ciliary body, and iris. The supraorbital nerve is a branch derived from the frontal nerve.

Q1097
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 65-year-old man has the gradual onset of diplopia. He has an esodeviation greater at distance than near. The deviation is equal in right and left gaze. Ocular motility is normal. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
Correct answer: D. inferior displacement of lateral rectus muscles
Rationale
This patient has divergence insufficiency. Divergence insufficiency is an esodeviation that is greater at distance than near. Primary divergence insufficiency, also known as age-related distance esotropia, is a benign condition that usually occurs in patients older than 50 years. The etiology is involution of the connective tissue band between the superior and lateral rectus, leading to inferior displacement of the lateral rectus muscles (sagging eye syndrome). Treatment consists of base-out prisms, botulinum toxin injection of the medial rectus muscle, or strabismus surgery.
There is a secondary form of divergence insufficiency that is rare and associated with neurologic abnormalities, such as pontine tumors, severe head trauma, or increased intracranial pressure. When present as an isolated finding, divergence insufficiency does not require further workup.
A sixth nerve palsy causes an esodeviation greater at distance than near, but the deviation is worse when looking to the side of the affected nerve. There is an abduction deficit. Elevated intracranial pressure and ischemia can cause sixth nerve palsies.

Q1098
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient with a left face turn has absent left eye abduction with left globe retraction upon adduction. She denies diplopia. What brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) finding would be consistent with this clinical condition?
Correct answer: B. absent left sixth cranial nerve
Rationale
Absent unilateral or bilateral abduction with globe retraction upon attempted adduction occurs in Duane syndrome. The left eye is more frequently affected, and the condition is more common in females. Duane syndrome is caused by a congenital maldevelopment or absence of the sixth nerve nucleus and/or nerve. A cavernous carotid aneurysm can cause sixth nerve palsy, but it will not produce globe retraction on adduction. A sixth nerve nucleus infarction results in a gaze palsy on the affected side. Lateral rectus aplasia will produce esotropia but not globe retraction on adduction.

Q1099
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What visual field defect is most commonly found in cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR)?
Correct answer: B. ring scotoma
Rationale
Cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) is a paraneoplastic disease of the eye, associated with the presence of extraocular malignancy and circulating autoantibodies against retinal proteins. CAR is a subacute, progressive autoimmune retinopathy that induces visual loss and visual symptoms that often manifest before the diagnosis of cancer. The most common malignancies related to CAR are carcinomas including small cell carcinoma of the lung, non-small cell carcinoma, and endometrial, ovarian, cervical, breast, prostate, and colon carcinomas.
The most common visual field defect associated with CAR is the ring scotoma. The diagnostic evaluation should include electroretinography (ERG) in patients with unexplained visual glare and subacute visual loss, screening for anti-retinal antibodies associated with anti-recoverin (23-kDa protein) and anti-alpha-enolase (46-kDa) antibodies, and screening for systemic cancer.

Q1100
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What condition is visual evoked potential (VEP) testing most helpful in confirming?
Correct answer: D. demyelinating optic neuropathy
Rationale
Visual evoked potential (VEP) testing measures electrical signals over the occipital cortex produced in response to a visual stimulus. It shows an increased latency in demyelination. Other optic neuropathies generally have a normal latency, but might show a decrease in the VEP's amplitude.
