Q1101
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 64-year-old woman presents following an episode of transient vision loss in her right eye. Associated clinical history includes recent headaches, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness. Her vision and intraocular pressure are normal, and the clinical examination shows mild refractive error, but the anterior segment and fundoscopic examination results are otherwise normal. What clinical laboratory test is considered to be most specific in confirming the etiology?
Correct answer: A. C-reactive protein (CRP)
Rationale
This patient's clinical symptoms are highly suspicious for giant cell arteritis (GCA) or temporal arteritis. When evaluating patients whose clinical symptoms are suspicious for GCA, diagnostic testing should begin with laboratory tests of ESR, CRP, and CBC.
CRP is a sensitive indicator of inflammation and is typically obtained in conjunction with the ESR; however, the ESR may be normal in up to 16% of cases of GCA. CRP may increase diagnostic accuracy of GCA because it may be more specific and less affected by increasing age and anemia when compared to ESR.
CBC is obtained in order to evaluate for thrombocytosis (increased platelet count), which may suggest active disease, but is not specific to GCA.
Fasting blood glucose testing is useful to determine the etiology of clinical findings suggestive of diabetic retinopathy changes but has limited value in temporal arteritis.

Q1102
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Following his final round of chemotherapy for leukemia, a 53-year-old man reports new diplopia and vision loss. His visual acuity is 20/200 OD, 20/20 OS with a right relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). He has ptosis and reduced motility OD. His fundus appearance is normal. What would be the most worrisome result from his sinus biopsy?
Correct answer: B. nonseptate fungal hyphae
Rationale
A biopsy demonstrating nonseptate fungal hyphae would indicate rhinocerebral mucormycosis, which typically occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus or in immunocompromised patients. The initial infection spreads from the facial skin, nasal mucosa, paranasal sinuses, or hard palate. The fungus spreads to the nearby blood vessels, affecting the orbital vessels, carotid arteries, cavernous sinuses, or jugular veins. Orbital and neurologic signs are produced by infarction, thrombosis, or hemorrhage. Untreated, rhinocerebral mucorrmycosis can lead to rapid deterioration, resulting in death within days.
This patient has vision loss and ophthalmoplegia, indicating an orbital apex syndrome. Patients with orbital apex syndrome from mucorrmycosis have nearly a 100% chance of permanent vision loss and > 60% mortality rate, despite aggressive surgical debridement and administration of antifungal agents.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters, resistant to methicillin, indicating methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), atypical mycobacterial infection, and granulomatous lesions with noncaseating centers, such as sarcoidosis, carry some risk of mortality and morbidity, but not to the extent of rhinocerebral mucormycosis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1103
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 37-year-old man complains of new onset anisocoria. His right pupil is 4.0 mm, and his left is 3.0 mm. His right palpebral fissure is 11 mm, while his left is 9.5 mm. What test would confirm an oculosympathetic paresis on the left side?
Correct answer: D. anisocoria of 1 mm or more (left smaller than right) after instillation of cocaine drops OU
Rationale
The patient has ptosis and a smaller pupil on the left indicative of a lesion to the oculosympathetic pathway, resulting in a left Horner syndrome. Other findings in a Horner syndrome are the presence of anisocoria that is greater in dim light than in bright light, dilation lag of the affected pupil, lower lid ptosis (rising of the lower lid), and anhidrosis of the ipsilateral face.
Horner syndrome can be confirmed with pharmacologic testing. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine released at sympathetic nerve terminals in the eye, causing pupillary dilation, eyelid retraction, and conjunctival blanching in the unaffected eye. With Horner syndrome, little or no norepinephrine is released into the synaptic cleft. Therefore, cocaine has no effect, and the miotic pupil remains unchanged. A postcocaine anisocoria of 1 mm or more is diagnostic of Horner syndrome on the side of the smaller pupil.
Topical apraclonidine can also be used to confirm Horner syndrome. A pupil with Horner syndrome will dilate in response to topical apraclonidine (weak alpha1-adrenergic agonist) because of iris dilator supersensitivity that develops several days after injury to the sympathetic pathway.
Hydroxyamphetamine testing can be used to localize a lesion after Horner syndrome is confirmed, but it is not helpful in diagnosing a Horner syndrome. Dilute pilocarpine is used to diagnose an Adie tonic pupil.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1104
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 41-year-old man has small, irregular, poorly reactive pupils on routine examination. The fundus has mild pigmentary changes. What additional testing should be performed?
Correct answer: B. Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay (TP-EIA)
Rationale
Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay (TP-EIA)

The Argyll Robertson pupil occurs in patients with tertiary syphilis involving the central nervous system. Affected patients have small pupils (< 2 mm) that are often irregular. The pupils do not react to light, but the near response and subsequent redilation are normal and brisk. This feature distinguishes Argyll Robertson pupils from bilateral chronic tonic pupils, which may also result from neurosyphilis. In addition, iris atrophy frequently occurs, portions of the iris transilluminate, and dilation is poor after instillation of mydriatic eyedrops.
Argyll Robertson–like pupils are observed in widespread autonomic neuropathies, such as bilateral tonic pupils (chronic), diabetes mellitus, and chronic alcoholism, as well as in encephalitis and after panretinal photocoagulation. Serologic tests for syphilis, such as the serum Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay (TP-EIA), fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test, rapid plasmin reagin (RPR), and Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test (VDRL), should be considered in the evaluation of patients with bilateral pupillary light-near dissociation with miosis, especially with retinal pigmentary changes.
Herpes zoster PCR evaluation tests for the varicella zoster virus, which does not cause Argyll Robertson pupils.
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for Borrelia burgdorferi tests for Lyme disease, which does not cause the Argyll Robertson pupillary response.
Quantiferon gold assay tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which does not cause the Argyll Robertson pupillary response.

Q1105
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For 3 months, a 50-year-old woman has noticed decreased vision OS, which she discovered when covering the right eye while looking in a mirror. Visual acuity is 20/20 OD and 20/100 OS. Further evaluation of the left eye shows a central and inferior field defect, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and the fundus image as shown. Funduscopy was normal OD. What is her most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. optic nerve sheath meningioma
Rationale
The fundus photograph shows a pale optic disc with a retinochoroidal shunt vessel. Optic disc shunt vessels develop in patients with compressive lesions involving the optic nerve, central retinal vein occlusion, and post-papilledema neuropathy. As venous return is obstructed, these shunt vessels develop from dilation of pre-existing venous shunts between the retina and choroid. They are not seen in uncomplicated retinal artery occlusion, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or optic neuritis.

Q1106
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For the past week, an 82-year-old woman with hypertension and hypercholesterolemia has noted painless transient visual loss in the left eye that culminates in sudden profound vision loss in the left eye on the day of presentation. She denies any headaches, jaw claudication, or scalp tenderness. Visual acuity is 20/25 OD and hand motions OS. She has a large (1.2 log unit) left relative afferent pupillary defect. As expected, her color vision and perimetry are normal OD. The optic discs are shown. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 32 mm/hr, and C‑reactive protein (CRP) is 0.9 mg/dL (normal <0.5 mg/dL). What is the best next step in management?
Correct answer: C. corticosteroids and temporal artery biopsy
Rationale
The left optic disc is pallid and swollen from giant cell arteritis (GCA). Fundoscopy shows a normal right optic disc with a cup-to-disc ratio of about 0.3 and massive infarction (with a pallid white or "chalky" white appearance) of the left optic disc, with extension into the surrounding retina. Although this patient has no systemic symptoms, the optic disc appearance on the left is suggestive of infarction that occurs in the setting of vasculitis, and in this patient, the most common type of vasculitis would be giant cell arteritis.
A temporal artery biopsy should be performed, but treatment with corticosteroids should not be delayed to obtain the biopsy. The ESR is not considered elevated in this patient for her age ([age+10]/2 is the upper limit of normal for ESR in women), but up to 16% of cases of GCA may have normal ESR levels.
When arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AAION) due to GCA is suspected, immediate initiation of high-dose corticosteroid therapy is crucial. It is estimated that with observation, 50% or more of patients will lose vision in the initially unaffected eye within 1 week. Additional tests with carotid ultrasonography and neuroimaging would not be necessary if the biopsy was positive and should not be done in advance of treatment with corticosteroids. When patients present with GCA and vision loss in 1 eye, it is often recommended to use high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for the first 3-5 days). Tapering of steroid treatment should be slow; there can be a risk of recurrence (7%) in either the same or the other eye during withdrawal.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1107
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is considered the gold standard for the evaluation of aneurysms or carotid stenosis?
Correct answer: B. catheter angiography
Rationale
The gold standard for intracerebral vascular imaging remains catheter angiography. With this technique, a catheter is placed intra-arterially, and iodinated radiodense contrast dye is injected. The contrast dye outlines the column of flowing blood within the injected vessel and demonstrates stenosis, aneurysms, vascular malformations, flow dynamics, and vessel wall irregularities such as dissections or vasculitis.
MRA and CTA have the advantage of being less invasive than catheter angiography. CTA requires injection of contrast material and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation, whereas MRA can be performed without any contrast material and does not involve any radiation exposure. While not considered the "gold standard," both CTA and MRA are technically adequate for detecting aneurysms that cause third nerve palsies.
Color doppler ultrasonography is primarily used in ophthalmology to evaluate for cervical carotid stenosis in patients presenting with transient monocular visual loss. Notably, it is not accurate at detecting carotid artery dissection.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1108
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 32-year-old woman complains of "drooping" of both eyelids that has worsened over the past 4 years. She denies any visual symptoms. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU. She has limited ductions OU in all fields of gaze. Given her left fundus (shown) and the symmetry of the peripheral retinal changes, what additional features of her condition might an ophthalmologist expect to find?
Correct answer: A. cardiac conduction deficits
Rationale
This patient has retinal pigment epithelial clumping and depigmentation, termed "salt and pepper" retinopathy. This finding, combined with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, led the ophthalmologist to her diagnosis of Kearns-Sayre syndrome, a variant of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia. The BCSC notes that Kearns-Sayre syndrome is an inherited mitochondrial myopathy. The literature suggests though while the condition is associated with mitochondrial mutation, most cases are sporadic. Optic neuropathy and vertigo are not manifestations of this syndrome, although cerebellar ataxia and hearing loss are. Cardiac conduction deficits may be life-threatening if untreated.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1109
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 23-year-old man presents with a gradual loss of eye movements, pigmentary changes in the retina, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. What additional finding is expected on examination?
Correct answer: D. ptosis
Rationale
Kearns-Sayre syndrome is an inherited mitochondrial myopathy that includes chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO), pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. CPEO is characterized by slowly progressive, symmetric ophthalmoplegia often associated with bilateral ptosis.
Blepharospasm is typically seen in older patients and is not part of Kearns-Sayre syndrome. Variability is expected in myasthenia gravis. Improved eye movements with doll’s head maneuver indicate a supranuclear gaze palsy. Ophthalmoplegia associated with CPEO cannot be overcome with doll’s head maneuver.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1110
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents with gaze-evoked nystagmus that dampens on prolonged right gaze. When returning to primary gaze, a left beat nystagmus ensues. Where is the lesion?
Correct answer: B. cerebellum
Rationale
Gaze-evoked nystagmus occurs due to inability to maintain fixation in eccentric gaze. There is an ocular drift back to primary gaze as a result of the elastic properties of the orbit, and a corrective saccade to view the eccentric target. The amplitude of the nystagmus increases with eye movement in the direction of the fast phase. Gaze-evoked nystagmus is most commonly caused by the loss of neural integration.

Neural integration for horizontal gaze is mediated by the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi and the medial vestibular nuclei, whereas neural integration for vertical gaze is mediated by the interstitial nucleus of Cajal. The cerebellum is also involved in neural integration of horizontal and vertical gazes.

Rebound nystagmus is described in the above clinical scenario. Prolonged eccentric viewing causes compensatory brainstem/cerebellar induced-tonic innervation toward eccentric gaze, decreasing the amplitude of gaze-evoked nystagmus. However, when the patient returns to primary gaze, the tonic innervation continues to drive the eyes rightward, inducing a corrective leftward saccade. Gaze-evoked nystagmus with rebound nystagmus in primary gaze is frequently due to cerebellar disease.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1111
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 10-year-old boy was noted to have an enlarged blind spot and the fundus finding below. His vision is 20/20 in each eye with normal pupil reaction and a normal contralateral optic nerve. What feature is most helpful in distinguishing this condition from optic disc drusen?
Correct answer: D. retinal vessel obscuration
Rationale
The boy has myelinated retinal nerve fibers at the optic nerve margin, a congenital condition. They can cause an appearance of optic disc edema, and like optic disc drusen may be mistaken for papilledema (pseudopapilledema). Both conditions may be associated with blurred margins, spontaneous venous pulsations, and visual field defects. However, optic disc drusen is not associated with retinal vessel obscuration; both myelinated nerve fibers and true optic nerve edema may have retinal vessel obscuration.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1112
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 32-year-old woman has chronic headache that suddenly worsened 2 days ago. She cannot elevate either eye, and they move nasalward on attempted upgaze. She has bilateral disc edema and mild blind-spot enlargement by perimetry. What radiologically detectable finding would be expected in this clinical disorder?
Correct answer: A. cerebral aqueductal stenosis
Rationale
This prompt describes convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, a finding in dorsal midbrain syndrome (also termed pretectal syndrome or Parinaud syndrome). Dorsal midbrain syndrome is caused by compression of the posterior commissure, which controls horizontal conjugate eye movements. It includes any of the following findings: conjugate limitation of vertical gaze (usually upgaze), convergence-retraction nystagmus, mid-dilated pupils with light-near dissociation, lid retraction in primary position, skew deviation, convergence spasm or palsy, and increased square-wave jerks. Given the papilledema with enlarged blind spots bilaterally, there is likely increased intracranial pressure from a mass or hydrocephalus compressing the dorsal midbrain at the level of the pineal gland, associated with cerebral aqueductal stenosis.
Periventricular white-matter lesions are often seen in multiple sclerosis. Demyelination from multiple sclerosis can produce dorsal midbrain syndrome but would not cause papilledema and signs of increased intracranial pressure demonstrated in this case.
Transverse sinus thrombosis could cause increased intracranial pressure and papilledema but would not cause dorsal midbrain syndrome.
Occlusion of the vertebrobasilar artery that supplies the pretectum could cause dorsal midbrain syndrome, but it is not associated with increased intracranial pressure.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1113
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An ophthalmologist sees a patient whose examination results show an infiltrative optic neuropathy in association with leptomeningeal enhancement on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and an abnormal computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest. Bronchoscopic biopsy demonstrates noncaseating granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
Correct answer: B. sarcoidosis
Rationale
Sarcoid optic neuropathy is a granulomatous inflammatory condition and can present as an infiltrative optic neuropathy. Hilar adenopathy on chest CT would raise suspicion of sarcoidosis, and biopsy demonstrating noncaseating granulomata is consistent with sarcoidosis. In cases of neurosarcoidosis, MRI scan commonly shows pachymeningeal and leptomeningeal enhancement. Corticosteroids and other immunomodulators like methotrexate and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blockers are the mainstays of treatment.
While the imaging characteristics described in this case could be consistent with tuberculosis, characteristic pathologic findings include caseating granulomata (rather than the noncaseating ones of sarcoidosis). Lyme disease can present as an optic neuropathy without chest CT findings. It usually causes neuroretinitis with macular exudates in addition to optic disc edema. A CT chest would not be initially helpful in detecting syphilis infection.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1114
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What ocular motility abnormality is classically included in dorsal midbrain syndrome?
Correct answer: B. convergence-retraction nystagmus
Rationale
The presence of convergence-retraction nystagmus localizes the disease process to the dorsal midbrain; it is part of dorsal midbrain syndrome (also known as pretectal or Parinaud syndrome). Convergence-retraction nystagmus results from co-contraction of the extraocular muscles on attempted upgaze; the co-contraction of all extraocular muscles causes the globe to retract into the orbit. Dorsal midbrain syndrome also includes lid retraction, upgaze deficit, pupillary light–near dissociation, and increased square-wave jerks. Ptosis, opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, and ocular flutter are not components of dorsal midbrain syndrome.

Q1115
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What disease-modifying medication used for treating multiple sclerosis is most likely to cause flulike symptoms?
Correct answer: C. interferon
Rationale
Interferon therapy is a common treatment for multiple sclerosis. Interferon treatment, such as interferon-beta1b, can often cause flulike symptoms, liver enzyme changes, bone marrow suppression, and thyroid dysfunction. Cystoid macular edema is a side effect of fingolimod, which is a different class of disease-modifying medication for multiple sclerosis. Natalizumab, which is a humanized monoclonal antibody against the cell adhesion molecule α4-integrin, has been associated with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, especially in patients who have previously been exposed to John Cunningham (JC) virus, as well as nausea, infection, and liver dysfunction. Glatiramer acetate causes skin irritation, skin lipoatrophy, and panic attack–like events.

Q1116
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 42-year-old woman had sudden onset of severe right eye redness, mild pain, limited motility, and diplopia. She has normal visual acuity, 7 mm proptosis OD, and intraocular pressure (IOP) 33 mm Hg OD, 12 mm Hg OS. She reports a noise in her right ear. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
Correct answer: D. blunt head trauma
Rationale
Abnormal connections between the cavernous sinus and the carotid artery or its branches introduce high arterial pressure into the normally low-pressure venous circulation of the cavernous sinus. These connections can be either high flow or low flow.
The question stem describes signs and symptoms consistent with a direct, high-flow, carotid cavernous fistula, which most commonly occurs after severe head trauma. With acceleration/deceleration injuries, such as head trauma in motor vehicle accidents, the cavernous carotid artery is susceptible to shear forces that may produce a rent in the arterial wall. Pulsatile tinnitus results from arterial flow out of the cavernous sinus and into the inferior petrosal sinus.
Skull base tumors may encase the cavernous carotid but do not cause fistulae to form.
Hypertension, especially in older women, is associated with development of indirect (dural) arteriovenous fistulae with low flow and milder symptoms with insidious onset.
Demyelinating disease does not cause fistula formation.

Q1117
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most appropriate next step in managing a new diagnosis of pupil-involving, isolated, complete third cranial nerve palsy?
Correct answer: D. contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)
Rationale
Third cranial nerve palsies with pupillary involvement must be assumed to be secondary to an aneurysm until proved otherwise. Emergent cerebrovascular imaging (eg, catheter angiography, MRA, or computed tomography angiography [CTA]), depending on clinical scenario and neuroradiologic consultation, should be undertaken.
Careful observation, rather than neuroimaging, may be appropriate when there is an acute, isolated, pupil-sparing, but otherwise complete third nerve palsy in a patient over 50 years of age with appropriate vascular risk factors but without a history of cancer. Complete pupil-sparing third nerve palsies in this setting are almost always due to microvascular ischemia and improve over 3 months. In contrast, some proportion of partial third nerve palsies with normal pupillary function are related to compressive lesions and may later progress to involve the pupil, warranting imaging.
CT with contrast of the orbits is the appropriate next step when a patient presents with an orbital fracture or for compressive orbital lesion detection when MRI is contraindicated, but it can miss an intracranial aneurysm unless paired with CTA.
Carotid doppler ultrasonography is an appropriate next step in the workup of transient unilateral vision loss in order to detect the source of intra-arterial emboli, unrelated to the third nerve palsy in the question.

Q1118
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An 85-year-old woman presents with binocular horizontal diplopia at distance. She does not have diplopia with reading. She says that she started wearing glasses in her 40s. Examination demonstrates deep superior sulci, high lid creases, and bilateral ptosis. She has a 10-prism-diopter esotropia at distance, which is comitant. She has mild upgaze limitation with both eyes. What is the most likely cause for her symptoms?
Correct answer: C. sagging eye syndrome
Rationale
Sagging eye syndrome presents in older patients with a mild- to moderate-angle esotropia at distance (ie, divergence insufficiency). Lateral gaze is full, but there can be limitation of supraduction. In sagging eye syndrome, the lateral rectus-superior rectus band degenerates, with inferior displacement of the lateral rectus muscle, along with prolapse of connective tissue superotemporally. In addition, patients often experience degenerative changes causing deep superior sulci, high lid creases, and ptosis resulting from levator aponeurosis dehiscence. 
Myasthenia is less likely because her misalignment is comitant. Heavy eye syndrome can present with progressive esotropia and hypotropia; however, this condition occurs in patients with high myopia. Bilateral sixth-nerve palsies would produce bilateral abduction deficits, and the esotropia would be worse in both right and left gazes.

Q1119
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient with new onset diplopia has generalized limitation of left eye movement, 3 mm left ptosis, and inferior orbital pain. Visual acuity is normal with no relative afferent pupillary defect, no proptosis, and a normal fundus exam OU. What is the most likely location for the causative lesion?
Correct answer: A. cavernous sinus
Rationale
Unilateral painful ophthalmoparesis without a change in visual function or orbital signs such as proptosis is most likely to occur from a cavernous sinus process. Malignancy, inflammation, and thrombosis all can cause multiple cranial neuropathies and pain.
An orbital apex lesion should affect the optic nerve as well and cause vision loss and/or a relative afferent pupillary defect. Dorsal midbrain lesions cause a Parinaud syndrome with upgaze paresis and eyelid retraction bilaterally; this is not a painful condition. Thalamic disease can cause pain and esotropia but not ophthalmoparesis.

Q1120
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For what condition is optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) indicated?
Correct answer: C. sinus thrombosis with increased intracranial pressure, optic disc edema, and visual loss
Rationale
In the presence of substantial loss of vision without prominent headache, ONSF may represent the preferred surgical option because it directly protects the optic nerve. However, ONSF carries a 10% to 15% complication rate, including a 1% to 2% risk of vision loss from optic nerve injury, central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), or central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). It does not lower intracranial pressure (ICP) and thus often does not treat headache. A reduction of papilledema in the contralateral eye can occur, but bilateral ONSF may be required. The long-term success rate of ONSF remains unclear. Repeat ONSF may be performed but is technically more difficult because of scarring.
Central retinal vein occlusion with panretinal hemorrhage and macular edema would not be treated with ONSF. Terson syndrome is associated with intraocular hemorrhage associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage. There is no role for ONSF in this setting. Similarly, optic neuropathy from trauma does not improve with ONSF; however, it may improve with orbital decompression of the optic canal in certain cases.

Q1121
Neuro-Ophthalmology
The stellate pattern of exudation present in neuroretinitis is a result of fluid deposition and subsequent resorption in what retinal layer?
Correct answer: C. outer plexiform
Rationale
The characteristic feature of neuroretinitis is a stellate or "star" pattern of exudates in the macula. This pattern is a result of diffuse optic nerve head edema that spreads through the outer plexiform layer into the macula along the papillomacular bundle around the fovea. Fluid resorption leaves behind lipid precipitates in the characteristic star pattern.

Q1122
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 75-year-old man reports that the vision in his right eye dims out whenever he goes outside into bright light and that his vision slowly improves once he goes back indoors. On examination, the ophthalmologist notices that the central retinal artery "flashes" when gentle pressure is applied to the globe. What diagnostic test should be ordered?
Correct answer: B. carotid angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) to look for carotid occlusion on the right
Rationale
Ocular ischemic syndrome is characterized by a hypotensive, ischemic retinopathy with low retinal artery pressure, poor perfusion, and midperipheral retinopathy. Ocular ischemic syndrome can cause transient or persistent blurred vision or transient visual loss upon exposure to bright light. Gentle pressure collapsing the central retinal artery indicates that the perfusion to the central retinal artery is compromised. A CTA or MRA is indicated to look for carotid occlusion ipsilateral to the symptoms.
Compression of the optic nerve typically causes a gradual painless decrease in vision. Enlarged extraocular muscles could cause diplopia or compressive optic neuropathy. Automated perimetry and diurnal intraocular pressure measurements would be indicated if one suspected glaucoma.

Q1123
Neuro-Ophthalmology
In a school screening examination, a 9-year-old girl was found to have reduced visual acuity. School records from the prior year revealed her visual acuity was 20/40 OU. On examination her visual acuity is 20/60 OU. Her pupils react briskly without a relative afferent pupillary defect. She sees 3 of 10 color plates correctly OU. Her fundi are shown. She has normal multifocal electroretinography OU. What diagnostic test would help confirm this patient's condition?
Correct answer: A. genetic testing
Rationale
This patient demonstrates bilateral temporal optic disc pallor from dominant optic atrophy, which has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Hereditary optic neuropathy, toxic optic neuropathy, and degenerative retinopathy would be included among entities that can cause bilateral optic atrophy. The clinical history is suggestive of a slowly progressive optic neuropathy. In addition, a retinopathy is not likely, because the multifocal electroretinogram was normal. Dominant optic atrophy, the most common hereditary optic neuropathy, would be the most likely diagnosis. The most common mutation in dominant optic atrophy is in the OPA1 gene, most commonly on chromosome 3. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy may be associated with cardiac conduction deficits (pre-excitation syndrome), but dominant optic atrophy is typically thought to be an isolated ocular condition. A muscle biopsy would not be warranted in the evaluation of hereditary optic atrophy.

Q1124
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Following a brainstem stroke, a 68-year-old woman developed diplopia. On examination, the right pupil is larger than the left and is poorly reactive to both direct and consensual stimulus. Both eyes cannot elevate above the horizontal midline. The left eye otherwise moves normally, whereas the right eye can only abduct. Given this clinical presentation, what additional eyelid findings might be expected?
Correct answer: B. bilateral upper-eyelid ptosis and poor levator function
Rationale
This patient is showing signs of a complete right 3rd nerve palsy and elevation deficit on the left. The symptoms occurred after a brainstem stroke. The bilateral elevation deficit indicates that the stroke involved the right third nerve nucleus within the midbrain.
The third nerve nucleus is a nuclear complex that contains subnuclei for 4 extraocular muscles (superior, inferior, and medial recti, and inferior oblique), a single subnucleus for the levator palpebrae muscles (central caudal nucleus), and paired subnuclei for the pupillary constrictor muscles (Edinger-Westphal nuclei). Because the single central caudal nucleus controls both levator palpebrae muscles, and the superior rectus fascicles decussate just after emerging from their subnuclei, lesions of the third nerve nuclear complex can cause bilateral ptosis and bilaterally affect the superior rectus muscles.
Left upper-eyelid ptosis and lower-eyelid elevation with a smaller pupil is suggestive of Horner syndrome; however, this overall clinical presentation is not consistent with oculosympathetic paresis. Right upper-eyelid ptosis with fatigability suggests myasthenia. However, myasthenia would not cause anisocoria. Bilateral rhythmic eyelid movements with attempted convergence are seen with dorsal midbrain syndrome. Dorsal midbrain syndrome can cause elevation deficits but would also not cause anisocoria.

Q1125
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 19-year-old woman has new headaches and transient visual obscurations. She has severe acne and uses a topical medication prescribed by her dermatologist. She weighs 110 pounds and is 5 feet, 2 inches tall. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Static perimetry shows blind spot enlargement bilaterally, and ductions are full. Her anterior segments are normal. What optic disc finding might you expect to see on fundoscopy?
Correct answer: D. bilateral optic disc swelling
Rationale
Bilateral optic disc swelling is observed in papilledema from increased intracranial pressure. Use of topical anti-acne medication (including tetracyclines like minocycline, as well as retinoic acid) is associated with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), as in this case.
Normal disc appearance is incorrect because the patient's history and visual field findings are consistent with papilledema.
Optic nerve pallor is incorrect because there is no indication of optic neuropathy, suggested by visual field with only blind spot enlargement, normal color vision, and normal visual acuity.
Mild hyperemia with telangiectatic vasculature is characteristic of pseudopapilledema from Leber hereditary optic neuropathy in the acute stage, or possibly consistent with diabetic papillitis. Neither diagnosis is indicated in this prompt, which describes a young female with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure.

Q1126
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the cause of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in patients with hemianopic vision loss from an optic tract lesion?
Correct answer: C. asymmetric decussation of the pupillary fibers at the chiasm
Rationale
Anterior optic tract lesions from tumor compression or stroke create a homonymous hemianopia and may be accompanied by a RAPD contralateral to the lesion (ie, on the same side as the hemianopia). The RAPD occurs because the lesion affects more fibers from the contralateral optic nerve. About 53% of fibers from each optic nerve cross at the chiasm, and this asymmetry is enough to cause a mild RAPD with a tract lesion.
Although improper technique can lead the examiner to a false conclusion regarding the presence or absence of an RAPD, that is not the cause here.
Optic nerve involvement can actually negate the RAPD, because the contralateral RAPD would be balanced out by an ipsilateral optic neuropathy. CN III compression gives an efferent, not an afferent, pupillary defect.

Q1127
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What would be expected with a left cranial III nerve nucleus lesion?
Correct answer: A. bilateral ptosis, left adduction and depression deficit, right elevation deficit
Rationale
The CN III is a nuclear complex that contains subnuclei for 4 extraocular muscles (superior, inferior, medial recti, and inferior oblique), a single subnucleus (central caudal nucleus) for the levator palpebrae muscles, and paired subnuclei (Edinger-Westphal nuclei) for the pupillary constrictor muscles. Because the single central caudal nucleus controls both levator palpebrae superioris muscles, and the superior rectus fascicles decussate just after emerging from their subnuclei, lesions of the CN III nuclear complex either affect or spare both upper eyelids and may affect the contralateral superior rectus muscle (not ipsilateral rectus muscle). Therefore, a left CN III nuclear lesion would be expected to cause bilateral ptosis, right elevation deficit, and left adduction and depression deficits. Because the superior rectus fibers pass adjacent to the contralateral superior rectus subnuclei, bilateral elevation deficits can also be seen with CN III nuclear lesions.

Q1128
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 21-year-old woman develops asymptomatic, hyperemic disc edema in the right eye with telangiectatic changes. Her visual acuity is 20/20, and she has a trace relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). What is most likely responsible for this examination finding?
Correct answer: B. type 1 diabetes
Rationale
Of the answer choices provided, diabetic papillopathy is most likely in this younger woman with asymptomatic, unilateral, painless, hyperemic optic disc edema. Diabetic papillopathy can occur in type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Patients may have no symptoms or have nonspecific symptoms of “blurred vision” or “distortion” without pain. The optic nerve reveals hyperemic edema, but 50% of patients show marked dilation of the disc surface microvasculature that appears similar to neovascularization of the disc. Often, but not always, diabetic retinopathy findings such as retinal microaneurysms or dot-blot hemorrhages are present. Treatment is directed at correcting the underlying hyperglycemia.
Nocturnal hypotension in a patient with a crowded optic disc is associated with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). NAION occurs most frequently in middle-aged hypertensive patients on beta-blockers. It causes acute vision loss, especially upon waking and in the lower half of the visual field. It is rare in patients younger than 40 years old.
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is a mitochondrial myopathy, inherited through the female bloodline and phenotypically present primarily in male family members. It causes acute or subacute central vision loss in one, then both eyes. It is usually found in symptomatic males in their second and third decades.
Optic nerve glioma is a disease primarily of children, presenting as chronic, progressive optic nerve pallor and proptosis, not optic disc edema.

Q1129
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 51-year-old French-Canadian woman presents with constant ptosis, poor levator function, and difficulty swallowing. What inheritance pattern is most likely to be found for her condition?
Correct answer: C. autosomal dominant
Rationale
The constellation of findings in this woman supports the diagnosis of oculopharyngeal dystrophy. Oculopharyngeal dystrophy (also termed "oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy") is characterized by late-onset (usually after the age of 45 years) ptosis, swallowing difficulty, and a positive family history, with involvement of 2 or more generations. Oculopharyngeal dystrophy is inherited in either an autosomal dominant or an autosomal recessive manner. Sporadic inheritance is not characteristic of oculopharyngeal dystrophy, and X-linked mitochondrial patterns of transmission do not occur.

Q1130
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 60-year-old woman presents with lid retraction of both upper lids, bilateral proptosis, and limited abduction of both eyes. What finding on physical examination would confirm medial rectus muscle restriction?
Correct answer: D. positive forced ductions
Rationale
The patient presents with classic signs of thyroid eye disease, which has a predilection toward causing inferior rectus and medial rectus enlargement and restrictive strabismus. Restrictive strabismus can be confirmed with the forced duction test. A restrictive process produces a mechanical limitation of the range of eye movements that can often be felt by an examiner when forceps or a cotton swab is used to advance the limited eye movement.
Paretic conditions reduce the saccadic velocity, whereas restrictive conditions do not. Esotropia would be expected for a limitation of abduction of both eyes, but would not differentiate between a paralytic or restrictive process. A comitant misalignment is typically seen in patients with congenital or early-onset strabismus.

Q1131
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What supranuclear ocular motor system is responsible for maintaining an image on the fovea during brief head movements?
Correct answer: D. vestibular-ocular system
Rationale
The vestibular-ocular system holds the image of an object on the fovea during brief head movement. The optokinetic system holds the image of an object on the fovea during sustained head movement. The ocular fixation system holds the image of a stationary object on the fovea when there is no head movement. The vergence system enables the eyes to move in opposite directions so that the image of an object remains on the fovea of both the right and left eyes for near and distance viewing with normal ocular alignment.

Q1132
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What pharmacologic test result would confirm a third-order Horner syndrome?
Correct answer: C. lack of pupillary dilation with hydroxyamphetamine drop in the affected eye
Rationale
Horner syndrome is an ocular sympathetic paresis caused by a disruption of the superior cervical sympathetic chain. The interruption can be classified as first-, second-, or third- order neuron injury depending on the level of the injury.
Horner syndrome can be diagnosed pharmacologically with topical cocaine or apraclonidine. Topical cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine released in the synaptic clefts leading to pupillary dilation in an unaffected eye. However, in Horner syndrome, because there is no norepinephrine in the synaptic clefts, cocaine has no effect, and the miotic pupil does not dilate. Of note, apraclonidine can also confirm a Horner syndrome by reversal of anisocoria.
Similarly, a hydroxyamphetamine eyedrop dilates normal pupils by releasing catecholamines from the motor end plate. Dilation occurs if the third-order neuron is intact; no dilation occurs if the third-order neuron is involved. Therefore, no pupillary dilation with a hydroxyamphetamine drop confirms a third-order Horner syndrome. 
First-order neuron lesions arise from the hypothalamus to the spinal cord (often caused by vascular lesions or tumors); second-order neuron lesions arise from the spinal cord to superior cervical ganglion (often caused by trauma or tumors affecting the cervicothoracic spinal cord); and third-order neuron lesions arise from the superior cervical ganglion along the internal carotid artery to tarsal muscles and the pupillary dilator muscle (often caused by tumors, inflammatory lesions, trauma, or ischemia).
In summary, topical cocaine and apraclonidine can confirm a Horner syndrome, whereas hydroxyamphetamine can distinguish a 3rd order from a first- or second-order Horner syndrome.

Q1133
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What disease is characterized by an impaired ability to repair sunlight-induced damage to DNA and may manifest signs of keratoconjunctivitis sicca and blepharospasm?
Correct answer: D. xeroderma pigmentosum
Rationale
Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by an impaired ability to repair sunlight-induced damage to DNA. On exposed skin, patients develop hyperpigmentation, atrophy, actinic keratosis, and telangiectasia. Cutaneous neoplasms are common later in life. Ocular changes include keratoconjunctivitis sicca, blepharospasm, conjunctival telangiectasia and hyperpigmentation, symblepharon, eyelid atrophy and scarring, trichiasis, and ocular neoplasms (11% of patients, more common at the limbus).
Ichthyosis (AD) is a desquamating skin condition that is not responsive to corticosteroid treatment. It is known to have primary corneal opacities, band keratopathy, and cornea vascularization. The eyelids are frequently involved with scaling and cicatricial ectropion. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca may be present in these patients but it is not due to abnormal DNA repair.
Meige syndrome is a combination of essential blepharospasm with facial grimacing. This condition is not caused by abnormal DNA repair. The etiology of Meige syndrome is unknown. For these patients, consider checking a computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan to rule out posterior fossa lesions. Patients with Meige syndrome can be treated with botulinum toxin injections to the affected area or with systemic medications (tetrabenazine, lithium, carbidopa, clonazepam). Dry eye syndrome (DES) has been known to cause blepharospasm.
Sjögren syndrome is defined as keratoconjunctivitis sicca, xerostomia (decreased parotid flow rate), lymphocytic infiltration in the salivary glands on biopsy, and laboratory evidence of systemic autoimmune disease (positive ANA, RF, SS-A, or SS-B). Sjögren syndrome is not associated with abnormal DNA repair.

Q1134
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 45-year-old immunocompromised patient developed a left retrobulbar optic neuropathy, diplopia, and headache. He was found to have a lesion in the sphenoid sinus extending to the left orbital apex. Biopsy showed organisms with septate hyphae. What organism is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?
Correct answer: B. Aspergillus
Rationale
Aspergillus

Biopsy showed septate hyphae, which is consistent with Aspergillus. Aspergillomas, or fungus balls, can involve the sinuses and can extend to the optic canal or cavernous sinus, leading to optic neuropathy and diplopia. Mucormycosis, Candida, and Streptococcus pneumoniae would not show septate hyphae on culture.

Q1135
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 45-year-old man presents with suspected nonorganic vision loss after a motor vehicle accident. His attorney has asked for a visual evoked potential (VEP) test to assess optic nerve function. How will the VEP results be helpful in this case?
Correct answer: B. A normal VEP confirms intact afferent visual pathways, but an abnormal VEP is nonspecific and does not prove pathology.
Rationale
Visual-evoked potential (VEP) testing is an objective method to determine the integrity of the afferent visual pathway from the retina to the occipital cortex. Normal responses confirm intact visual pathways. Nevertheless, numerous factors may produce abnormal VEP waveforms in the absence of visual pathway damage, including uncorrected refractive error, media opacity, amblyopia, fatigue, and inattention (intended or unintended). VEP accuracy depends on patient cooperation and several other factors.
P100 latency is likely to be markedly delayed in demyelination of the optic nerve. Reduction in P100 amplitude may occur secondary to ischemic, compressive, or toxic optic nerve damage and is, therefore, not specific to a particular cause.

Q1136
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 55-year-old man has diplopia at distance with esotropia worse on left gaze. What office test is most helpful in differentiating a restrictive from a paralytic strabismus as the cause of the double vision?
Correct answer: A. forced duction test
Rationale
A restrictive process produces a mechanical limitation of the range of eye movements that can often be felt by the examiner when forceps or a cotton swab is used to advance the limited eye movements. To perform a forced duction test, topical proparacaine drops are applied to the eye and held over the limbal region with a cotton tip for 1 to 2 minutes. Then the conjunctiva at the limbus is grasped with toothed forceps, and the globe is passively rotated in the direction of limited abduction to assess for restriction of eye movement. A positive forced duction test results when there is restriction to passive eye movement.
Alternate cover testing, rather than cover/uncover, will unmask any phoria but will not inform the examiner about muscle function. Monocular occlusion is useful when the examiner suspects strabismus in a patient with no manifest deviation, as it breaks fusion and can unmask a latent strabismus. Orbital cooling has been suggested in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis but cannot distinguish other paretic causes (such as 6th nerve palsy) from a restrictive process.

Q1137
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What brainstem structure is responsible for generating horizontal saccades?
Correct answer: A. paramedian pontine reticular formation
Rationale
The excitatory burst neurons for generating horizontal saccades are located in the paramedian pontine reticular formation. The medial longitudinal fasciculus contains neurons that project from the CN VI nucleus to the contralateral CN III nucleus and mediates horizontal yoke muscle movement. The rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal are located in the midbrain and are involved in the generation of torsional and vertical saccades.

Q1138
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient has transient monocular vision loss that is associated with eye pain. The pain improves when the patient lies down. What is the most likely cause?
Correct answer: A. ocular ischemic syndrome
Rationale
Ocular hypoperfusion due to carotid occlusive disease (ocular ischemic syndrome) can cause transient monocular vision loss, typically in setting of bright light exposure. Recurrent eye pain that improves when the patient is lying down is highly suggestive of ocular ischemic syndrome. The examination may demonstrate midperipheral dot-blot hemorrhages and dilated veins due to low central retinal artery pressure. Patients may also develop episcleral injection and aqueous flare due to ischemic uveitis. Neovascularization of the angle or of the iris is common, although intraocular pressure (IOP) can be high, normal, or low. Low or normal intraocular pressure can result from ciliary body hypoperfusion.

Q1139
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 63-year-old man undergoes a prolonged spine surgery in the prone position and awakens with light perception vision in both eyes. What is the most likely appearance of the optic nerves?
Correct answer: B. normal
Rationale
Vision loss upon awakening from spine surgery is classically posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) affecting the optic nerve. Vision loss in perioperative PION is more commonly bilateral and profound. The appearance of the optic nerve initially is normal. Over time, pallor develops. Patients can have anterior ischemic optic neuropathy following surgery and present initially with optic disc edema, but PION is the classic presentation of vision loss following spine surgery and prolonged prone position. Cupping is seen in glaucoma and would not present this acutely.

Q1140
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most helpful neuroimaging modality in managing a 35-year-old female patient's first episode of acute, unilateral optic neuritis?
Correct answer: D. brain MRI with FLAIR imaging
Rationale
Optic neuritis is a clinical diagnosis based on historical and examination findings. Orbital MRI with T1 post-contrast fat-saturation, especially coronal and axial views, can confirm the optic nerve enhancement consistent with the diagnosis. However, of the choices provided, the correct answer is brain MRI with FLAIR imaging, because in managing this patient, the most important factor is determining her multiple sclerosis (MS) risk. Risk of MS is directly related to the presence of concomitant brain MRI demyelinating lesions, best seen on FLAIR and often periventricular.
Orbital MRI with FLAIR may show optic nerve diameter asymmetry and subtle enhancement but is of less prognostic value and is less helpful without fat saturation. Orbital CT with contrast is excellent in screening for large mass lesions of the orbit but has limited value with assessing inflammatory soft tissue disease and would not be prognostically helpful in this scenario.

Q1141
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient has slowly progressive left eye vision and visual field loss from an optic nerve sheath meningioma (ONSM). What treatment is most effective in preventing further visual loss?
Correct answer: D. radiation therapy
Rationale
Patients with vision loss from ONSM should be offered fractionated stereotactic radiation therapy, as this therapy has been shown to preserve or even improve visual function in up to 95% of patients.
Surgical excision carries a high risk of disrupting the blood supply to the nerve and should not be perfomed. Although steroids may temporarily improve optic nerve swelling (if present), they have no long-term effect. No effective chemotherapy for meningioma exists.

Q1142
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What cancer is most commonly associated with cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR)?
Correct answer: A. small-cell carcinoma of the lung
Rationale
CAR is also known as a paraneoplastic autoimmune retinopathy (pAIR). Although pAIRs have been described with numerous cancers, small-cell lung carcinoma is the most frequent cause of these disorders. Autoimmune retinopathy can be suspected when symptoms of nyctalopia and photopsias are elicited. Signs include visual field constriction, outer retinal disruption on optical coherence tomography, abnormalities on fundus autofluorescence, and abnormalities on electrophysiologic testing. A neoplastic etiology should be sought out; this typically includes a physical examination, laboratory testing, and radiographic imaging (computed tomography [CT], magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], or positron emission tomography [PET] scan).
Melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR), another type of pAIR, shares some features with CAR, but is given its own name (MAR) and is not referred to as CAR. One feature that seems to differentiate MAR from CAR is that color vision and central vision are typically preserved in MAR.
Metastatic adenocarcinoma (if it metastasized to the eye) would be expected to present as a choroidal mass. Colon cancer can produce pAIR, but small-cell lung cancer is more common. The ocular manifestation of central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma is as primary intraocular lymphoma (now increasingly referred to as primary vitreoretinal lymphoma). Paraneoplastic AIR has not been described in primary CNS or intraocular lymphomas.

Q1143
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 30-year-old woman presents with multiple subcutaneous nodules and the finding shown on slit-lamp examination (Fig. 1) An abnormality of what chromosome is most likely to be associated with this presentation?
Correct answer: B. chromosome 17
Rationale
The slit-lamp photo shows Lisch nodules, pigmented iris hamartomas present in 94%-97% of patients over 6 years old with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), also known as von Recklinghausen disease. NF1 is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and has been linked to chromosome 17. The disease is characterized by the presence of multiple cutaneous pigmented macules (café-au-lait spots), neurofibromas, iris (Lisch) nodules, optic pathway glioma, and osseous defects, including sphenoid wing dysplasia.
Chromosome 22 is linked to neurofibromatosis type 2, and Lisch nodules are not a common feature of this disease. NF2 classically involves bilateral acoustic neuromas, multiple meningiomas, and posterior subcapsular cataracts.
Chromosome 5 is linked to cri-du-chat syndrome, with a variety of ocular features such as strabismus and optic atrophy.
Chromosome 11 is linked to aniridia and the WAGR syndrome: Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary, and renal disorders.

Q1144
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 29-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of right eye pain and blurred vision. Her best-corrected visual acuity is 20/50 in the right eye and 20/15 in the left eye. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). Her color vision is 1/14 in the right eye and 14/14 in the left eye. Her right optic nerve and right visual field are shown below. The left eye is normal. What would be the most appropriate next step in management?
Correct answer: B. magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Rationale
This patient has a classic presentation of typical demyelinating optic neuritis, which is characterized by a subacute or acute unilateral visual loss associated with pain with eye movements, moderately decreased visual acuity with severe dyschromatopsia, and visual field loss (central scotoma in this case). The fundus is normal in approximately two-thirds of cases, with one-third of cases having optic nerve edema (anterior optic neuritis or papillitis).
While lumbar puncture and serologic testing may be helpful for atypical optic neuritis presentations and for helping to diagnose multiple sclerosis (MS), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain should be performed in every case of typical optic neuritis to assess the long-term risk for developing MS over the next 15 years (25% if no lesions, 72% with ≥ 1 lesion).
Treatment with Intravenous steroids may be useful for decreasing the risk of conversion to MS in isolated optic neuritis as well as improving recovery time, but it is not a necessary next step in management of optic neuritis.

What condition commonly leads to congenital Horner syndrome?
Correct answer: B. brachial plexus injury
Rationale
Congenital Horner syndrome is most commonly caused by birth trauma to the brachial plexus. If there is no history of trauma, then the patient should have a workup for congenital tumors such as neuroblastoma.

When does radiation optic neuropathy typically occur after radiation therapy?
Correct answer: C. after 1 to 2 years
Rationale
Radiation optic neuropathy is a complication that occurs after radiation that involves the optic nerves. This typically occurs months (average 18 months) after radiation treatment and produces subacute optic neuropathy. Radiation optic neuropathy is in part dose-related; it is more likely to occur with higher doses (typically > 5000 cGy). MRI typically shows enhancement of the optic nerves.

Q1147
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 60-year-old woman presents with the sudden onset of left-sided eye pain accompanied by ipsilateral ptosis, impaired ocular motility–sparing abduction, and a fixed and dilated (8 mm) pupil. What are head imaging studies most likely to show?
Correct answer: C. saccular aneurysm
Rationale
The possibility of an aneurysm at the origin of the posterior communicating artery from the internal carotid artery must be urgently evaluated in a patient presenting with a new-onset painful pupil-involving third cranial nerve palsy. Saccular (“berry”) aneurysms are the most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and the origin of the posterior communicating artery is a frequently involved site. Intracerebral hemorrhage, which is most commonly due to hypertension, can present with focal neurologic symptoms but a pupil-sparing third cranial nerve palsy would be atypical.
Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) can cause intracerebral hemorrhage as well as SAH. When associated with SAH, AVMs may manifest with focal seizures, progressive worsening of focal neurologic signs, and recurrent unilateral migraine-like headache. Intraventricular hemorrhage usually occurs as a secondary phenomenon in patients with an intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage. It typically manifests with sudden-onset headache, nausea, vomiting, and varying degrees of impaired consciousness. Microvascular ischemia to the third cranial nerve can also cause sudden-onset pain, ptosis, and partial ophthalmoplegia, but pupil involvement is generally mild (less than 1 mm of anisocoria).

Q1148

Following a motor vehicle accident 2 days ago, a 25-year-old woman reports painful sudden vision loss in her right eye. She has not lost consciousness and had no head or facial trauma. Visual acuity is light perception OD, 20/20 OS with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Anterior and posterior segment examination is normal. She reports diplopia viewing the 20/40 line with 4 PD base down OS. What is the most appropriate action in managing this patient?
Correct answer: C. re-examination in 1 week with reassurance
Rationale
This scenario describes nonphysiologic vision loss occurring after a motor vehicle accident. The key findings supporting this diagnosis are mechanism of injury not suggestive of severity of vision loss, as well as examination inconsistencies such as light perception (LP) vision OD without relative afferent pupillary defect. In addition, diplopia while testing the 20/40 line with mild induced prism over 1 eye demonstrates that her vision is much better than LP. In this setting, reassurance with close follow-up is appropriate.
Serologic testing for syphilis and Lyme disease, intravenous methylprednisolone, and/or urgent CT are not indicated in this case, because there was a normal eye examination with no demonstrable optic neuropathy.

Examination showed a pupil-involving third nerve palsy. Levator function is partially spared. What would be the preferred acute management?
Correct answer: B. monocular occlusion
Rationale
This patient developed a third nerve palsy from the clipping of the left posterior communicating aneurysm, which is a common complication of this surgery. Monocular occlusion is the preferred treatment in the acute setting for patients with symptomatic diplopia. Some patients get some spontaneous recovery and therefore immediate strabismus surgery is not recommended. Because of the incomitant nature and expected improvement in some cases, ground-in-prisms are not recommended. Pencil pushups are a treatment option for convergence insufficiency.

Q1151

A 13-year-old girl has headache and trouble reading. Visual acuity is normal; voluntary eye movements, oculocephalic maneuver, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain are shown. What additional eye movement abnormality is likely to be present on examination?
Correct answer: D. rhythmic movement of both eyes toward the nose on attempted elevation
Rationale
The patient has an inability to voluntarily elevate her eyes, which is overcome with doll’s head maneuver. MRI shows enlargement and enhancement of the pineal gland consistent with a pinealoma with compression of the dorsal midbrain. This is consistent with dorsal midbrain syndrome, which also often has convergence retraction nystagmus, characterized by rhythmic movement of both eyes toward the nose on attempted elevation. A pinealoma is a common cause of dorsal midbrain syndrome in young patients, while stroke is the most common cause in the elderly. In addition to limitation of vertical gaze and convergence retraction nystagmus, patients with dorsal midbrain syndrome often have light-near dissociation, retraction of the lids (Collier sign), and skew deviation.
Cerebellar disease would cause unsteady fixation with square wave jerks, rare saccadic intrusions, and also hypometric horizontal saccades. Incyclotorsion/elevation of one eye with excyclotorsion/depression of the other is see-saw nystagmus, which is caused by a lesion of the diencephalon.

In benign essential blepharospasm, where in the central nervous system is the seventh nerve hyperactivity thought to originate?
Correct answer: D. basal ganglia
Rationale
Functional neuroimaging suggests that benign essential blepharospasm occurs due to dysfunction of the basal ganglia. Hemifacial spasm occurs due to compression of the facial root in the cerebellopontine angle. Facial myokymia occurs due to intramedullary disease of the pons at the facial nucleus or fascicle.

A 38-year-old man has periodic right-sided headache with right eye redness and tearing. The pain occasionally wakes him from sleep. What additional right eye/orbital sign is most likely to be associated with his headache events?
Correct answer: B. 2 mm upper eyelid ptosis
Rationale
Unilateral headache with eye redness and tearing characterizes trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, which include cluster headache, sudden unilateral neuralgiform headache with conjunctival redness and tearing (SUNCT), hemicrania continua, and others. Autonomic dysfunction and Horner syndrome-like findings may accompany the headache pain, and 1 mm to 2 mm eyelid ptosis may be seen. The pupil may be miotic, not dilated (as may occur with migraine headache), and intraocular inflammation and/or disc swelling are not caused by these headaches.

Q1154
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 10-year-old boy with a history of neurofibromatosis type 1 presented with no light perception (NLP) vision, prominent and disfiguring proptosis, and corneal scarring OD. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve approaching the chiasm. What is the most likely preferred management of this lesion?
Correct answer: B. surgical resection
Rationale
Optic pathway gliomas (OPG) in children, including optic gliomas confined to the optic nerve body itself, are almost always benign astrocytomas whose natural history is stable without significant progression over time. Some may even show spontaneous regression. Thus, there is no universally accepted management of OPG, but indications for treatment depend on clinical progression by vision loss, loss of visual quality of life, or extension of the lesion into the optic chiasm (rare). Radiation or chemotherapy treatment depends on age and association with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Surgical treatment may be entertained in cases of severe vision loss, with the purpose of reducing disfiguring proptosis and extension into the chiasm.
In this case, careful observation is not preferred, because the tumor is approaching the chiasm, there is no visual potential in the affected eye, and the patient has disfiguring proptosis. Radiation is not preferred in this case, due to significant long-term side effects with NF1, although it can be an option in patients over 5 years old with progressive optic nerve glioma. Chemotherapy with carboplatin and vincristine is an emerging first-line treatment, but surgical resection is probably preferred in this case due to the need to better address the disfiguring proptosis and corneal scarring.

Q1155
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the biggest risk factor for the formation of a direct carotid-cavernous fistula?
Correct answer: B. trauma
Rationale
Abnormal connections between the cavernous sinus and the carotid artery or its branches introduce the high pressure of the arterial system into the normally low-pressure venous system, which may reverse flow in the superior ophthalmic vein and cause orbital congestion. Direct connections between the internal carotid artery and the cavernous sinus typically produce a high-flow fistula and usually occur after head trauma.
Low flow, indirect or "dural' cavernous fistulas occur when small meningeal arterial branches communicate with venous drainage. Indirect fistulas form most often as a degenerative process in older women with systemic hypertension and atherosclerosis.
Diabetes and neurofibromatosis are not risk factors for carotid-cavernous fistula formation.

Q1157
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. He is unconscious. The left pupil is larger than the right. What finding on his limited eye examination suggests trauma to the left optic nerve?
Correct answer: B. tonic left pupil after swinging a flashlight over the left pupil
Rationale
Eye examination is challenging in the unconscious patient due to inability to obtain subjective information such as vision, color, and visual field testing. Dilated fundus examination may initially be normal. However, the assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), heralded by an abnormal swinging-flashlight test, raises suspicion of traumatic optic neuropathy.
In this patient with anisocoria, RAPD can be detected only by reverse testing, as the dilated left pupil is more suggestive of traumatic mydriasis than optic neuropathy. Initial constriction of the healthy right eye to light over the right pupil, followed by dilation or poor constriction of the right eye to light over the left pupil, confirms an RAPD by reverse testing and suggests traumatic optic neuropathy in this context.
Tonic left pupil after swinging a flashlight over the left pupil is not the correct answer, because this observation cannot confirm an RAPD in the setting of baseline mydriasis.
Tonic right pupil after swinging a flashlight over the right pupil is not the correct answer, because this observation does not give information about the left eye.
Constriction of the left pupil after swinging a flashlight over the left pupil is not the correct answer, because this observation would suggest intact optic nerve function of the left eye.

Q1158
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 73-year-old woman reports several episodes of transient monocular vision loss over the past 2 weeks. Visual acuity is normal. The fundus examination is unremarkable. Fluorescein angiography shows delayed early perfusion and patchy choroidal filling in both eyes. Perimetry is normal. What is the next step in evaluating or managing this patient's condition?
Correct answer: C. oral prednisone 1 mg/kg immediately
Rationale
The fluorescein angiogram in this case confirms poor choroidal circulation. The choroid is supplied primarily from branches of the ophthalmic artery, which in this age group is a main target of giant cell arteritis (GCA). Since the concern for GCA is raised, even in the absence of arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient is to initiate immediate treatment with a high-dose steroid and obtain laboratory results regarding inflammation, then do a temporal artery biopsy to determine the pathologic diagnosis.
Catheter angiography with left carotid stenting is incorrect, because this patient's examination did not include the mid-peripheral dot-blot hemorrhages or anterior segment findings of ocular ischemic syndrome due to atherosclerotic occlusion of the carotid and ophthalmic artery, but this is within the differential diagnosis and carotid vascular evaluation may be necessary in the setting of negative temporal artery biopsy. Intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF therapy is not correct, because there are no signs of neovascularization mentioned on examination. Finally, multifocal electroretinography is unnecessary, because the choroidal circulation has already been defined as the source of her symptoms and would not contribute to the initial diagnostic workup.

A thin 57-year-old man complains of horizontal diplopia for the past week and a frontal headache for the past month that are worse upon awakening. On examination, he has bilateral optic disc edema. Visual fields are full, except for a blind spot enlargement. Magnetic resonance images (MRIs) of the brain with and without gadolinium reveal slightly small ventricles and posterior globe flattening. Lumbar puncture reveals an opening pressure of 425 mm of water with normal composition. What is the most appropriate patient management?
Correct answer: A. magnetic resonance venogram (MRV) of the cerebral venous drainage system
Rationale
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) can present with signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), similar to that of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), because of decreased venous outflow. It is important to rule out CVST with MRV, especially in patients who do not fit the classic demographic profile of IIH (obese woman of childbearing age). Treatment for CVST includes anticoagulation and systemic workup.
The other answer choices are incorrect because further diagnostic workup is indicated. IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion. Initial treatment of IIH begins with weight loss intervention and/or acetazolamide, an oral agent that decreases cerebrospinal fluid production. A low-sodium weight loss program would not be indicated for CVST. Although acetazolamide may be used in conjunction with anticoagulation for CVST, this answer is incorrect because the patient requires further diagnostic workup. ONSF is an option in patients with severe vision loss from papilledema, but this patient has only mild visual field defects.

Q1160

A 33-year-old man had sudden, complete, painless vision loss in his left eye that lasted 10 to 15 minutes, before remitting completely. On examination, his visual acuity, perimetry, and fundus appearance are normal. The right pupil is 1 mm larger than the left and dilates more quickly in darkness. There is no relative afferent pupillary defect. The left eyelid has 2 mm ptosis. What environmental insult might be elicited on further questioning?
Correct answer: A. recent high-speed roller coaster ride
Rationale
The patient’s examination result is concerning for a left Horner syndrome, which is characterized clinically by ipsilateral miosis, facial anhidrosis, and ptosis. A Horner syndrome can be caused an internal carotid dissection, which can lead to stroke or amaurotic episodes. Among the options provided, a roller coaster ride could increase the risk of a carotid dissection. The other options would not predispose a patient to a Horner syndrome or carotid dissection.
A long commercial flight could predispose to development of deep venous thrombosis. However, in the absence of a patent foramen ovale, this would not be expected to cause transient monocular vision loss, and it should not lead to a Horner syndrome.
It is possible that dehydration due to prolonged exertion could predispose to hypoperfusion and related ischemia, such as a nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Dehydration would not cause a Horner syndrome.
Restrictive diets can lead to vitamin deficiencies and nutritional optic neuropathy but would not be expected to cause transient monocular vision loss or Horner syndrome.

Q1161
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What condition is the most common cause of divergence insufficiency (DI) in an otherwise healthy adult patient?
Correct answer: D. connective tissue involution between the superior and lateral rectus muscles
Rationale
DI is an acquired ocular misalignment defined by an esodeviation that is greater at distance than near fixation, without lateral incomitance, and without abduction deficits. This disorder is usually benign and not related to neurologic dysfunction. In older patients, DI often results from involution of the connective tissue band between the superior and lateral rectus muscles, causing inferior displacement of the lateral rectus muscles (ie, sagging eye syndrome). The malpositioned lateral rectus muscles have reduced abduction force, resulting in DI pattern esotropia. Rarely, DI can be caused by neurological disorders such as increased intracranial pressure, midbrain tumors, Miller Fisher syndrome, head trauma, intracranial hypotension, Arnold-Chiari malformation, and cerebellar degeneration (often with other signs of these disorders).
A lesion in the CN VI nucleus results in a gaze palsy.
A lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus results in an internuclear ophthalmoplegia characterized by impaired adduction and an abducting nystagmus during horizontal gaze opposite the side of the lesion.
Enlarged medial rectus muscles that impair abduction are characteristic of thyroid-related orbitopathy.muscles

Q1162
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the preferred imaging test to evaluate a slowly progressive facial nerve palsy with myokymia?
Correct answer: A. MRI brain
Rationale
Slowly progressive facial palsies strongly suggest the diagnosis of a brainstem mass. Facial myokymia derives from continuous or undulating contraction of facial muscle fascicles, usually originating from the intramedullary pons. These rippling movements usually begin within a portion of the orbicularis oculi and may spread to involve other facial muscles. In children, a disorder of the pons is most likely a pontine glioma, and in an adult, the condition is most likely to be multiple sclerosis. Although myokymia may rarely be due to Guillain-Barré syndrome, imaging of the brainstem is most important. Neither a PET scan of the periventricular region nor a CT scan of the orbits would be likely to demonstrate pathology related to the facial nerve.

Q1163

A 78-year-old man developed a stroke with mild arm and leg weakness and a right facial nerve palsy. His right eyelids do not close completely. What other aspect of his examination is most important for his risk of corneal ulceration?
Correct answer: C. corneal sensation
Rationale
In patients with facial nerve palsy, the most crucial question is the status of the trigeminal nerve. Patients developing facial nerve palsy from stroke or intracranial surgery are also at risk of developing a trigeminal neuropathy that may eliminate their corneal sensitivity. The combination of an anesthetic cornea and lagophthalmos places these patients at a very high risk of developing corneal exposure and ulceration. Intact corneal sensation is protective for maintaining blink reflex and lacrimation, especially in patients who may lack concomitant upgaze with lid closure (Bell phenomenon). The risk of combined neurotrophic and neuroparalytic keratitis demands an aggressive approach that possibly includes early tarsorrhaphy or gold weight implant.
Although an intact Bell phenomenon may help protect the cornea from exposure in some cases of lagophthalmos, corneal sensation is the most important exam finding to help determine risk of corneal ulceration. Lissamine green stain may highlight devitalized conjunctival epithelial cells, but this is not predictive for ulceration. Conjunctival culture to assess the ocular surface flora is also not predictive of risk of corneal complications.

Q1164

A 67-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presents with progressively worsening diplopia and decreased vision in the left eye. On examination, the left eye shows a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), ptosis on the left, and limited ductions of the left eye in all directions. Also, corneal sensation is diminished in the left eye. Based on this constellation of symptoms, where is the lesion expected?
Correct answer: D. orbital apex
Rationale
This patient has signs of a left optic neuropathy (left RAPD), affecting at least the left cranial nerves (CNs III, V1, and VI), based on the findings of ptosis, limited ductions in all directions, and decreased corneal sensation. The combination of CN II and ophthalmoplegia localizes to the orbital apex. If CN II is unaffected, the location of the lesion would be expected in the ipsilateral cavernous sinus.
The hallmark of ophthalmoplegia secondary to a lesion of the cavernous sinus is ipsilateral ocular motor nerve dysfunction involving any combination of third, fourth, fifth, and sixth CNs and sympathetic fibers. The offending lesion may extend toward the optic foramen or into the orbital apex, in which case optic nerve function can be compromised. The designation orbital apex syndrome is then applied.
A brain stem lesion can cause various craniopathies, but would not be expected to cause an optic neuropathy.
A cortical lesion would not be expected to cause an optic neuropathy or unilateral ophthalmoplegia.

The lacrimal pump system is driven by what nerve?
Correct answer: B. cranial nerve VII
