The lacrimal pump is driven by the action of the pretarsal orbicular oculi muscle, which is innervated by the facial nerve, or CN VII. CN III is the oculomotor nerve that supplies the medial, superior, and inferior rectus and oblique muscles, as well as the levator muscle. CN V is the trigeminal nerve; it supplies sensory innervation to the face as well as motor innervation to some muscles of mastication. CN VI innervates the abducens nerve.

A 32-year-old woman slipped on ice and sustained blunt head trauma. Her workup including a computed tomography (CT) scan, which was negative. Since then, she has experienced horizontal uncrossed diplopia, which is greater in left gaze. It does not vary with the time of day. The vision is 20/20 in each eye. When the right eye fixes, the deviation in the primary position is 20 prism diopters of left esotropia, 10 prism diopters on right gaze, and 30 prism diopters on left gaze. When the left eye fixes, the right esotropia in the primary position is 30 prism diopters, 20 prism diopters in right gaze, and 40 prism diopters in left gaze. What best explains the difference in the measurements dependent on which eye is fixing?
Correct answer: B. A secondary deviation is greater than a primary deviation.
Rationale
The findings are consistent with a weakness of the left lateral rectus. The amount of innervation to synergist muscles is determined by the fixating eye. The primary deviation is the amount of strabismus present with the normal eye fixating. The secondary deviation is the amount of strabismus with the paretic eye fixating. Since the deviation was greater with the left eye fixating, it was the result of secondary deviation. Increased innervation to the weak left lateral rectus is necessary to allow the paretic eye to move to the point of fixation, which creates the same extra innervation to the yoke right medial rectus. This increases the amount of esotropia measured. A secondary deviation is always greater than primary deviation.
Myasthenia gravis is not likely as there was no fluctuation during the day, and ptosis was not present. A nasal orbital wall fracture could cause decreased abduction, but it was ruled out by the normal CT scan.

The figure depicts dilated and "arterialized" episcleral vessels. Other findings that may support this entity include exophthalmos and elevated IOP. A magnetic resonance angiogram is the preferred diagnostic modality to evaluate for the presence of a fistula. Q1169
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 57-year-old man reports new-onset anisocoria. His right pupil is 4.5 mm, and his left is 3.0 mm. His right palpebral fissure is 11 mm; his left is 9.5 mm. He has pain that radiates up the left side of his neck to his orbit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. dissection of the left internal carotid artery
Rationale
The presence of ipsilateral miosis and ptosis is concerning for Horner syndrome, which is caused by a lesion at any point along the oculosympathetic pathway. A painful Horner syndrome is most commonly caused by a carotid artery dissection. Pain from dissection is usually located around the temple and orbit, and may extend from the neck. This condition must be recognized because, in the acute stage, stroke is a possible complication. MRI typically shows an intramural hemorrhage, but in rare cases magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) or cerebral arteriography is needed to provide definitive evidence of dissection.
CST can also cause a Horner syndrome, but patients with this condition are typically ill and often have signs of orbital involvement, such as proptosis, hyperemia, and ophthalmoplegia. A left-sided brain stem stroke would be painless. Temporal arteritis does not cause Horner syndrome.

Q1170
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Adie tonic pupil is caused by damage to what structure?
Correct answer: C. ciliary ganglion
Rationale
Adie tonic pupil is characterized by poor reaction to light, sectoral palsy of the iris sphincter, accommodative paresis, denervation cholinergic supersensitivity, and a strong and tonic pupillary response to near vision (light-near dissociation) followed by slow redilation. It results from damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves carrying postganglionic parasympathetic fibers.
The other choices (trigeminal ganglion, cervical sympathetic ganglion, gasserian ganglion) are incorrect because they do not carry parasympathetic pupillary fibers. The trigeminal (also known as gasserian) ganglion carries synapses for the 3 divisions of cranial nerve V. The cervical sympathetic ganglion carries synapses for sympathetic fibers, damage to these fibers causes anisocoria due to miosis and dilation lag of the involved pupil, as well as ipsilateral ptosis.

Q1171
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What visual field defect is typical of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy?
Correct answer: B. cecocentral scotoma
Rationale
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is a mitochondrial disease. It is more common in males than females. The trait is not transmitted by affected males. Central or cecocentral visual field defects are typical of LHON. Arcuate field defects may be seen with papilledema and glaucoma; altitudinal fields defects commonly are associated with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy; and bitemporal hemianopia suggests a chiasmal process, such as compression from a pituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma.

Q1172
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 25-year-old woman with headache and blurred vision underwent a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan that demonstrated a pineal tumor (Figure 1). She has 20/20 acuity OU and 5 mm pupils OU with minimal reaction to light stimulus (direct and consensual). What additional pupillary finding may be detected with further testing?
Correct answer: D. pupil constriction with attempted reading
Rationale
The pineal gland is located dorsal and rostral to the pretectal nuclei and posterior commissure of the midbrain, where parasympathetic fibers mediating pupillary constriction to light are found (Figure 2). When compression from pineal gland tumors damages the dorsal midbrain, the parasympathetic light reflex pathway is disrupted, and the pupil does not constrict to light. In contrast, the fibers in the near reflex pathway approach the pretectal nucleus from the ventral aspect of the midbrain. Thus, dorsal midbrain damage can result in midsize pupils with poor light response and preserved near response. Associated findings include bilateral eyelid retraction (Collier sign), vertical gaze palsy, accommodative paresis, and convergence-retraction nystagmus (Parinaud syndrome).
Pupil constriction in a dark room (paradoxical pupils) is a clinical sign of congenital and/or inherited retinal dystrophies (eg, congenital stationary night blindness).
Poor pupillary constriction to 1% pilocarpine in a patient with fixed and dilated pupils suggests pharmacologic mydriasis.
Segmental pupil constriction with slit-lamp examination suggests segmental iris sphincter paralysis, a feature of Adie tonic pupil.

Q1173
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient has 2 mm of anisocoria that disappears in bright light. What pharmacologic agent should be used for diagnostic evaluation?
Correct answer: B. apraclonidine 0.5%
Rationale
When encountering anisocoria that is more apparent in dim light, the ophthalmologist should suspect Horner syndrome. Apraclonidine or cocaine drops may be used to assess for appropriate reaction of the affected pupil (dilates with the former, does not react to the latter). Pilocarpine may constrict an abnormally dilated pupil. Tropicamide will dilate most pupils, pathologic or not, while betaxolol has no significant effect on pupillary size.

Q1174
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Based on the contrast-enhanced MRI shown, what is the most likely finding seen in this patient?
Correct answer: A. visual field defect
Rationale
This coronal T1-weighted MRI (see photo, with call-outs) shows contrast enhancement of the optic chiasm, which would likely cause a junctional visual field defect but may or may not be associated with optic disc edema or pallor. This example highlights the importance of using contrast in patients suspected of having an optic neuropathy or chiasmal syndrome. There is no evidence of proptosis. Unless the chiasmal lesion involves the orbital optic nerve, optic disc edema would not be expected in a patient with enhancement of the optic chiasm. The cavernous sinuses appear normal, making an abduction deficit unlikely.

Q1175
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 48-year-old man has had 3 months of blurred vision OS and has been nicking the left side of his face while shaving. Visual acuity is 20/20 OD, 20/25 OS with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Sensation is reduced over the left forehead and cheek, and the left cornea has an irregular epithelium without lesion or defect. What diagnostic studies are recommended?
Correct answer: D. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, with gadolinium contrast
Rationale
There is concern that this patient may have a lesion affecting the trigeminal nerve on the left. This is causing reduced sensation of the left side of his face and a neurotrophic cornea, resulting in dryness and blurred vision. The first step in the investigation would be MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast.
Electromyography and nerve conduction velocity could be part of the workup, but only after the MRI. HSV can cause a neurotrophic cornea, but would not cause numbness of the left side of the face. Urgent orbital exploration and biopsy would only be performed after MRI.

Q1176
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What branch of the posterior cerebral artery supplies the primary visual cortex?
Correct answer: B. calcarine branch
Rationale
The distal posterior cerebral artery terminates in the calcarine branch, which supplies the primary visual cortex. The other arteries are branches of the posterior cerebral artery as well but supply different parts of the cortex.

Q1177
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Three weeks ago, a 49-year-old woman developed constant diplopia. She feels well and reports no new headache, fatigue, numbness, or weakness. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU, with equal pupils. Ductions are normal, and at distance there is a 15 PD exotropia in all positions of gaze. Stereopsis is poor even with prism correction. What is the most likely cause of her diplopia?
Correct answer: A. breakdown of a long-standing phoria
Rationale
New-onset diplopia in an adult can result from muscular, neuromuscular, or neurological causes. This patient has full ductions and no constitutional symptoms, such as weakness or headache. Her manifest strabismus is comitant. Comitant misalignment characteristically is found in patients with congenital or early-onset strabismus. Patients with this condition do not typically report diplopia, because there is suppression of the image from one eye. However, they may develop diplopia later in life. For instance, patients with a long-standing exophoria may develop diplopia in their fifth decade of life, when convergence and accommodative capacities decrease.
While there can be a spread of comitance with a sixth-nerve palsy, it does not occur within just a few weeks. She has no other symptoms to suggest increased intracranial pressure. Convergence spasm would not produce constant double vision for 3 weeks and would not produce a comitant misalignment, but it would give a larger-angle strabismus in lateral gazes.

Q1178
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 32-year-old woman has unequal pupils. They measure 4 mm OD and 3 mm OS in the light and 5 mm OD and 4 mm OS in the dark. The pupils react equally to light and dilate equally in the dark. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. physiologic anisocoria
Rationale
Anisocoria whose magnitude is equal in dim and bright light indicates that the relative function of the pupillary sphincter and dilator muscles is intact. This scenario is consistent with physiologic anisocoria. Sometimes physiologic anisocoria is more apparent in dim light than in bright light. This can make it difficult to differentiate from a Horner syndrome. In this case, physiologic anisocoria can be differentiated from Horner syndrome through pharmacologic testing.
An Adie pupil and pharmacologic dilation would show anisocoria that is greater in bright light.

Q1179
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 68-year-old man noted the acute onset of binocular diplopia. His visual acuity is 20/25 OU. He has bilateral nuclear sclerotic cataracts and normal fundi. His appearance in right gaze is shown. What is the most likely cause of his deficit?
Correct answer: B. myasthenia gravis
Rationale
The figure shows an abduction deficit on the right side from myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis may cause any ocular motility deficit, including an isolated abduction deficit. This patient appears to have a slight right upper eyelid retraction with normal eyelid position on the left; however, there is also some use of the brow, which suggests that this may actually be left upper eyelid ptosis. Thyroid eye disease should be considered in an isolated abduction deficit with eyelid retraction, but this is not an answer choice. The pupils are normal in size. Accommodative spasm (spasm of the near reflex) may cause esotropia, but this is associated with miotic pupils and this patient has normal, symmetric pupils, as shown. Duane syndrome may cause an abduction deficit but would be expected to cause narrowing of the palpebral fissure and rarely causes acute symptoms. Divergence insufficiency causes esotropia at distance but without ductional deficits.

Q1180
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 60-year-old woman presents with left-sided facial pain, which is present most of the time. She reports that when she is exposed to the cold, windy environment outside she develops electric shock-like jabs affecting the left side of her face. On examination, the ophthalmologist notes hypoesthesia in the cranial nerve V distribution on the left and is concerned for trigeminal neuralgia. What is the most likely cause in this case?
Correct answer: A. vascular compression of cranial nerve V
Rationale
Trigeminal neuralgia is caused by vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve in 80%-90% of cases. Other potential causes include demyelinating disease, infiltration, and posterior fossa mass. Trigeminal neuralgia also can be primary, with no cause demonstrated; however, the presence of abnormal sensory function on examination makes an underlying lesion more likely.

Q1181
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 50-year-old man presents with a sudden-onset and painless decrease in acuity to 20/70 in the right eye. What test would best distinguish a retinopathy from an optic neuropathy?
Correct answer: C. photostress recovery
Rationale
The photostress recovery test helps to differentiate between retinopathies and optic neuropathies by testing the amount of time it takes for vision to recover after being stimulated with a bright light. The photostress recovery test requires a corrected distance visual acuity of 20/80 or better. The patient is tested monocularly, gazing into a bright light held 2-3 cm from the eye for 10 seconds. Immediately after the light stimulus is removed, the patient attempts to read the next larger Snellen visual acuity line above the previously measured corrected visual acuity (eg, if the patient's corrected visual acuity is 20/25, the 20/30 line would be measured). Normal photostress recovery time is less than 30 seconds, but patients with maculopathy or severe carotid artery stenosis have prolonged recovery times (≥ 90-180 seconds). By contrast, patients with optic neuropathy have normal photostress recovery times.
Both retinopathies and optic neuropathies can cause relative afferent pupillary defects, contrast sensitivity abnormalities, and decreased color vision.

Q1182
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What clinical feature best distinguishes a parietal lobe lesion from an occipital lobe lesion?
Correct answer: A. abnormal optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) response
Rationale
Parietal lobe and occipital lobe lesions can have similar visual field defects (homonymous hemianopia) with normal pupil responses (no relative afferent pupillary defect). Cerebral achromatopsia is a feature of occipital lobe lesions. Pursuit and reflexive saccade movements are initiated in the parietal lobe and as such, abnormal OKN responses can be seen related to a parietal lobe lesion, but not with an occipital lobe lesion.

Q1183
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 14-year-old boy complains of intermittent binocular vertical diplopia and eye strain. Examination reveals an intermittent 15 prism diopter right hypertropia that increases in left gaze and right head tilt. Double Maddox rod testing reveals 5 degrees of extorsion of the right eye. What is the most likely etiology?
Correct answer: A. right cranial nerve IV palsy
Rationale
A cranial nerve IV palsy, also known as trochlear nerve palsy, impairs the function of the ipsilateral superior oblique muscle. It causes an ipsilateral hypertropia that is worse on contralateral gaze (adduction) and ipsilateral head tilt, with ipsilateral excyclotorsion. Therefore, a right trochlear nerve palsy would be expected to cause a right hypertropia, worse on left gaze and right head tilt, with right eye excyclotorsion.
A left cranial nerve IV palsy would be expected to demonstrate a left hypertropia, worse on right gaze and left head tilt. It would be associated with left excyclotorsion on double Maddox rod testing.
Brown syndrome is a restrictive form of strabismus producing an ipsilateral hypotropia on adduction with improvement in abduction. Forced duction testing would show restricted elevation in adduction, accentuated with retropulsion to stretch the superior oblique tendon.
A skew deviation would have a pattern different from cranial nerve palsies, such as a right hypertropia with ipsilateral incyclotorsion. Lesion origin is in the brainstem or vestibular apparatus and often has other neurologic signs.

Q1184
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An asymptomatic, otherwise healthy 38-year-old patient has small, irregular pupils that react minimally to light stimulus. With attempted reading, the pupils become even smaller. What investigation, if any, should be performed to identify the cause of this condition?
Correct answer: A. serum testing for syphilis
Rationale
The patient is demonstrating light-near dissociation with brisk near pupillary response in the absence of a good light response. The small, irregular pupils in this context raise the possibility of Argyll Robertson pupils, which are associated with advanced syphilitic infection. Similar findings can be found in widespread autonomic neuropathies, including diabetes and chronic alcoholism. In this case, testing for syphilis should be performed. If the test result is positive, referral to an infectious disease specialist for further evaluation and treatment should be made.
Orbital lesions are extremely unlikely to cause bilateral pupil findings of this sort. Apraclonidine testing is used for diagnosis of Horner syndrome and is not indicated in this case. Observation is inappropriate, since there is concern for syphilis in this case.

Q1185
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient with optic nerve drusen should be informed about what potential complication of this condition?
Correct answer: A. progressive visual field defect
Rationale
Optic nerve head drusen are refractile, often calcified nodules located within the optic nerve head. They are associated with stationary or progressive visual field defects. Visual fields should be monitored over time.
Although the segmental area of damage may become atrophic, generalized optic atrophy with subsequent central visual loss and reduced color vision is unlikely. Serous retinal detachments would not be expected.

Q1186
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A mother brings in an asymptomatic 12-year-old girl for a screening examination. The mother's forearm and hand have the abnormalities shown in the figure. What is the most common intraocular finding found in the mother or daughter?
Correct answer: A. iris melanocytic nodule
Rationale
The mother's forearm and hand demonstrate multiple neurofibromas. In this case, the mother has neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), an inherited phakomatosis. The most common ocular abnormality in NF1 is iris melanocytic nodules (Lisch nodules). Regarding other phakomatoses, diffuse choroidal hemangiomas can be found in patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome, and capillary hemangioblastomas of the retina or optic disc can be seen in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Astrocytic hamartomas are seen most characteristically in tuberous sclerosis. Although they have also been reported in neurofibromatosis, astrocytic hamartomas are less common in NF1 than iris nodules.

Q1187
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 27-year-old woman notes that her right pupil has been larger than the left since yesterday. Vision is 20/20 OU at distance, J10 OD and J1+ OS at near. Her right pupil is 8 mm and does not react to direct, consensual, or near stimulus. There is no segmental constriction of the iris. Motility is normal and there is no ptosis. What occupation puts the patient at higher risk for this problem?
Correct answer: A. intensive care nurse
Rationale
This patient has a dilated pupil and difficulty with accommodation in that eye. There is no segmental constriction of the iris to suggest an Adie pupil. There is no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia to suggest a third nerve palsy. These findings are most consistent with pharmacologic dilation.
Intensive care nurses often have to handle scopolamine patches or atropine, which if inadvertently exposed to the eye will cause pharmacologic dilation of the pupil.

Q1188
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 53-year-old woman involved in a motor vehicle accident complains of subsequent double vision. What findings would be most likely on examination, considering the imaging shown?
Correct answer: D. uncrossed diplopia in right gaze with a red lens
Rationale
This patient has diplopia from a medial wall fracture of the right orbit. The axial computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbits shows a fracture of the right medial wall adjacent to the belly of the medial rectus muscle. These fractures may result in diminished medial rectus function with or without restriction. Restriction of the medial rectus in right gaze results in esotropia that manifests as uncrossed diplopia when using a red lens (light strikes the nonfixing eye on more nasal retina, resulting in the image being seen in the temporal visual field).
Although diplopia may still be present in upgaze, it would be expected to worsen in horizontal but not vertical gaze. Excyclotorsion of less than 10° may be seen with fourth nerve palsy and V-pattern esotropia with bilateral fourth nerve palsy. None of these would be associated with the shown imaging.

Q1189
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What functional action of the superior oblique muscle contributes to the exotropia seen in a complete third nerve palsy?
Correct answer: D. tertiary
Rationale
In a complete third nerve palsy, the only functioning EOMs are the lateral rectus and superior oblique. The tertiary action of the superior oblique is abduction that exacerbates the outward position (exotropia) of the eye.

Q1190
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 20-year-old man suffered head trauma during a motor vehicle accident and has noted pulsatile synchronous tinnitus and horizontal diplopia since the accident. Examination revealed enlarged, corkscrew, arterialized conjunctival blood vessels of the left eye. He was also noted to have a left sixth nerve palsy and an audible bruit over the left eye. On neuroimaging, what vessel would be expected to be dilated in this patient?
Correct answer: C. superior ophthalmic vein
Rationale
This patient has classic signs and symptoms of a direct carotid-cavernous sinus fistula. High-flow, direct fistulas most commonly occur after severe head trauma and produce a cranial bruit. Carotid-cavernous sinus fistulas often produce elevated intraocular pressure, proptosis, and arterialization of conjunctival vessels. Compression of cranial nerve VI (CN VI) by an enlarged inferior petrosal sinus that drains the fistula can cause a sixth nerve palsy.
Abnormal connections between the carotid artery or its branches and the cavernous sinus introduce high arterial pressures into the normally low-pressure venous circulation of the cavernous sinus. Such a high-pressure connection may reverse blood flow within the superior ophthalmic vein, leading to an enlarged and dilated superior ophthalmic vein.
The other vessels listed (vein of Galen, superior sagittal sinus, ophthalmic artery) would not be expected to be enlarged from a carotid-cavernous sinus fistula.

Q1191
Neuro-Ophthalmology
When describing perceptual derangements in a patient following demyelinating optic neuritis, what is the term for the illusion of an object that moves in an elliptical path rather than a straight line?
Correct answer: B. Pulfrich phenomenon
Rationale
Due to the relative conduction delay within an optic nerve that has been affected by demyelinating optic neuritis compared with the contralateral unaffected optic nerve, an object moving in a single plane might be perceived as tracing an elliptical rather than straight path. This illusion is called the Pulfrich phenomenon. Riddoch phenomenon refers to the ability to see moving, but not static, objects in a blind hemifield (staticokinetic dissociation). Palinopsia is the preservation of a visual image after removal of the original stimulus. Optic ataxia is the inability to perform visually guided movements.

Q1192
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A pupil-involving complete third cranial nerve palsy presenting in a patient with simultaneous onset of contralateral weakness localizes to what brainstem structure?
Correct answer: A. ipsilateral midbrain third nerve fascicle in the territory of the cerebral peduncle
Rationale
Fascicular ocular motor cranial nerve palsies are caused by lesions of the nerve distal to the nerve's nucleus but within the confines of the brainstem. Involvement of the third nerve fascicle can produce 1 of 4 different syndromes:
  1. Weber syndrome = third nerve palsy + contralateral hemiparesis. This occurs due to damage to the ventral midbrain in the territory of the cerebral peduncle.
  2. Benedikt syndrome = third nerve palsy + contralateral ataxia/tremor. This occurs due to damage to the red nucleus and substantia nigra.
  3. Claude syndrome = third nerve palsy + contralateral ataxia. This occurs due to damage to the dorsal midbrain, involving the superior cerebellar peduncle.
  4. Nothnagel syndrome = nuclear third nerve lesion with features of supranuclear eye movement dysfunction + ataxia. This occurs due to damage in the dorsal midbrain.

Q1193
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For 2 weeks, a healthy 44-year-old woman reports photopsias and painless visual blur in her left eye. One month ago, she had a mild upper-respiratory infection. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OD and 20/25 OS. She has a left-relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) and no obvious fundus abnormalities. What part of the visual pathway is most likely affected?
Correct answer: A. retina
Rationale
Enlargement of the blind spot/temporal scotoma with associated photopsias in the setting of a normal-appearing fundus is suggestive of a retinal process such as acute idiopathic blind-spot enlargement (AIBSE) syndrome, multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS), or acute zonal outer occult retinopathy (AZOOR). Photopsias are a prominent symptom thought to reflect disease of the outer retina. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (OCT) line scans of the peripapillary retina reveal attenuation of the outer layers. Although AIBSE, MEWDS, and AZOOR represent outer retinal disorders, patients with these conditions can have an RAPD.
An optic nerve condition would be unlikely to present with such a large enlargement of the blind spot without significant papilledema. Theoretically, compressive optic neuropathy could cause a similar visual field defect with a normal-appearing optic nerve, but a cecocentral scotoma is much more common with compressive optic neuropathy. In addition, the photopsias point toward a retinal etiology. A lesion affecting the optic tract or occipital cortex would cause a homonymous visual field defect.

Q1194
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents with binocular vertical diplopia after noncontact whiplash injury from a motor vehicle accident. What would be the most useful clinical test to determine the etiology of the diplopia?
Correct answer: B. Parks-Bielschowsky 3 test
Rationale
A patient complaining of diplopia after noncontact trauma most likely has injury to one of the 3 motor cranial nerves (CN) supplying the extraocular muscles (III, IV, VI). Binocular vertical diplopia suggests that there is strabismus involving the vertical extraocular muscles (eliminating CN VI injury as a possibility), rather than monocular diplopia (which could be tested with pinhole).
Of the 3 motor cranial nerves, the oculomotor is the most robust and has the most direct route from the brainstem to the orbit. It is therefore least likely to be injured in a noncontact trauma. Traumatic CN III paresis or palsy typically requires severe head trauma and is usually associated with basal skull fractures and intracranial bleeding.
In contrast, the IV and VI nerve follow circuitous routes from the brainstem into the orbit and are therefore quite vulnerable to injury, even after seemingly trivial head trauma. Furthermore, the trochlear nerve is the smallest cranial nerve, containing a mere 1500 axons.
The Bielschowsky head tilt test is used as part of the "3-step test" to diagnose a CN IV palsy. In CN IV palsy, the mantra for diagnosis is a vertical deviation that manifests "a hypertropia on the same side that gets worse on opposite gaze and same head tilt."
In noncontact trauma, forced ductions would be expected to be negative, as there would not be any reason for muscle entrapment or scarring. While CN IV palsies may have torsional effects that can be measured with double Maddox rod testing, the Bielschowsky 3-step test is more helpful in the diagnosis of acute vertical diplopia from CN IV palsy.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1195
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents with unilateral upper eyelid retraction on ipsilateral attempted adduction. What is the most likely cause of this finding?
Correct answer: B. aberrant regeneration of cranial nerve (CN) III
Rationale
Cranial nerve III palsies displaying aberrant regeneration have a variety of clinical presentations, one of which is upper eyelid retraction on attempted adduction. Other common findings are pupillary miosis with attempted eyelid elevation, adduction, or infraduction. These findings are caused by nerve axon damage, such as compression from a slowly expanding mass in the cavernous sinus, leading to nerve fiber misrouting that produces several synkinetic phenomena (ie, co-contraction of muscles that normally are not activated together).
Thyroid eye disease is the most common cause of upper eyelid retraction but is not triggered by adduction. Dorsal midbrain syndrome is a bilateral condition where upper eyelid retraction (Collier sign) occurs due to compression of the posterior midbrain, but it manifests with convergence insufficiency and impaired upgaze, and is not triggered by adduction. Lastly, Duane syndrome produces a narrowed, not widened, interpalpebral fissure on adduction, due to anomalous co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles of the involved eye or eyes, which causes globe retraction.

Q1196
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 62-year-old hypertensive woman with a chronic right red eye has been treated with topical antibiotics and steroids, but has not had relief. She also reports pulsatile tinnitus. As shown, she has 3 mm of proptosis and redness in the right eye that does not blanch with phenylephrine. What abnormality might an ophthalmologist expect to find on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of her brain and orbits?
Correct answer: D. dilation of the right superior ophthalmic vein
Rationale
Abnormal connections between the carotid artery or its branches and the cavernous sinus introduce high arterial pressures into the normally low-pressure venous circulation of the cavernous sinus. Such a high-pressure connection may reverse blood flow within the superior ophthalmic vein and produce venous congestion within the orbit. Arterialization of conjunctival vessels is a classic sign of this fistula, which can be high-flow, characterized by a direct communication between the internal carotid artery and the cavernous sinus, or indirect, involving connections mediated by small arterial feeders off the internal or external carotids. T1-weighted axial MRI of the orbits (both with and without gadolinium) and axial computed tomography (CT) with contrast of the orbits can reveal an enlarged, dilated superior ophthalmic vein.

Q1197
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 55-year-old woman with a history of migraine with visual aura, who is also followed as a glaucoma suspect, developed a persistent visual field defect after a migraine headache. She had no other neurologic symptoms. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). Cup-to-disc ratio was 0.7 OU. The Goldmann visual fields are shown below. What is the most likely cause of the visual field defect?
Correct answer: A. ischemic stroke
Rationale
Patients with migraine aura are at a mild increased risk of ischemic stroke compared to the general population and also those who have migraines without aura. This patient suffered a persistent right homonymous visual field defect, indicating a lesion affecting the left post-chiasmal visual pathway. Given her history of migraines with aura, ischemic stroke is the most likely cause for her persistent visual field defect.
The other answers are less likely, given her history. A CNS infection would be unlikely in an otherwise healthy individual and would not cause an isolated visual field defect without other neurologic symptoms.
Demyelinating disease rarely affects the cortex to cause homonymous visual field defect. (However, demyelinating disease can affect the optic tract and cause a homonymous visual field defect, but it was unlikely in this patient because there was no RAPD.)
Progression of primary open-angle glaucoma would be an unlikely cause of such a congruous homonymous visual field defect.

Q1198
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What imaging technique may be contraindicated in some patients with cochlear implants?
Correct answer: A. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Rationale
Cochlear implants historically are contraindicated in MRI because the majority of implants have a magnet that can interact with the MRI. However, it should be noted that there are safe ways of obtaining MRI in many patients with cochlear implants (taking into account whether the magnetic component of the cochlear implant is removable, as well as the Tesla strength of the MRI being used). In the clinical setting, the specific manufacturer recommendations for the patient's device must be examined on an individual basis.
Table 2-1 in the American Academy of Ophthalmology's publication, Basic and Clinical Science Course, Section 5. Neuro-Ophthalmology, lists the advantages, disadvantages, and contraindications to various imaging modalities.

Q1199
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 62-year-old man with Parkinson disease is having difficulty opening his eyes. The examination shows no eyelid spasms, and he often stimulates eyelid opening by pressing on his brows. He has no ptosis once the eyelids are open. What ocular condition does he have?
Correct answer: B. apraxia of eyelid opening
Rationale
This patient has apraxia of eyelid opening, which can occur in isolation but also as part of Parkinson disease. Patients with this motor abnormality appear to be unable to generate a voluntary stimulus to activate the levator subnucleus in the midbrain, and they may use tactile stimuli to the face to overcome this problem. Levator muscle function is normal, and patients do not develop ptosis from the condition. Botulinum toxin injection to the pretarsal orbicularis oculi may be effective, although the mechanism is not entirely clear.

Q1200
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An 18-month-old infant presents with mild upper eyelid ptosis, lower eyelid elevation, and an ipsilateral miotic but reactive pupil with iris heterochromia. This child should be evaluated for what possible tumor?
Correct answer: A. neuroblastoma
Rationale
This child's clinical features are characteristic of Horner syndrome. A child with acquired Horner syndrome (ie, without a history of birth trauma) should be screened for neuroblastoma, which often presents as an acquired Horner syndrome. Neuroblastoma is one of the most common childhood cancers and usually originates in either the adrenal gland or the sympathetic ganglion chain in the retroperitoneum or mediastinum, a location that leads to interruption of papillary sympathetic innervation or Horner syndrome. Neuroblastoma is the most frequent source of childhood orbital metastasis. Retinoblastoma most commonly presents as leukocoria, while other signs may include strabismus, hemorrhage, hyphema, ocular or periocular inflammation, glaucoma, proptosis, or hypopyon. Rhabdomyosarcoma commonly presents with proptosis, ptosis, or strabismus. Wilms tumor originates in the kidney and rarely metastasizes to the orbit.

Q1201
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient is seen with asymptomatic visual field loss and bilateral elevated optic nerves. The left optic nerve is shown in the figure. What workup is necessary?
Correct answer: D. Humphrey visual field and observation
Rationale
The figure shows refractile drusen causing elevation of the left optic nerve. The correct workup is a Humphrey visual field. Most patients with disc drusen are asymptomatic, but visual field defects are common, including inferior nasal defects and enlarged blind spots. These patients have elevated discs that show calcified drusen as hyper-echoic or highly reflective on B-scan or computed tomography (CT) scan. Papilledema would require MRI/MRV to rule out intracranial mass lesions causing increased intracranial pressure and to rule out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Infection can cause papilledema including Lyme, Toxocara, and Bartonella, but this figure does not show papilledema.

Q1202
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What magnetic resonance imaging  (MRI) sequence is best for detecting periventricular white matter changes in multiple sclerosis?
Correct answer: D. fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR)
Rationale
FLAIR imaging provides T2-weighted images without the bright cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signal, which can obscure adjacent pathology. Therefore, FLAIR is ideal for detecting periventricular white matter lesions.
DWI is ideal for identifying recent infarctions. T1-weighted images are optimal for demonstrating anatomy. STIR provides T1-weighted images without the confounding bright fat signal and can be useful for orbital and spinal cord evaluation.

Q1203
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the primary reason that patients with demyelinating optic neuritis should not be treated with oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day alone?
Correct answer: D. This treatment increases risk of recurrence.
Rationale
Patients in the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) were randomized to treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone (250 mg IV q6hr for 3 days) followed by 1 mg/kg/day prednisone for 11 days then a quick taper, oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day only for 14 days, or placebo. Patients in all groups had excellent visual recovery with no difference in visual outcome at 6 months.
Steroid side effects between the 2 treated groups were similar. Steroid treatment (regardless of route) reduced the risk of MS in the first 2 years after treatment, but not thereafter. However, patients treated only with oral prednisone had a higher rate of optic neuritis recurrence than both the high-dose IV and placebo-treated patients. Therefore, oral prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day is not recommended as a treatment for optic neuritis.

Q1204
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 73-year-old woman developed frequent episodic left-sided spasms involving her orbicularis oculi and facial muscles, lasting a few seconds to minutes at a time. What is the most common cause of her symptoms?
Correct answer: B. neurovascular compression
Rationale
The patient's symptoms are consistent with hemifacial spasm. The pathogenesis of hemifacial spasm is most commonly compression of the seventh nerve root exit zone by an aberrant vessel. Less commonly, tumors within the cerebellopontine angle or previous injury to cranial nerve (CN) VII may lead to the spasms; therefore, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is typically performed to exclude a compressive lesion.
Neurodegenerative conditions, such as Parkinson disease, and basal ganglion infarction can be associated with blepharospasm, not hemifacial spasm.

Q1205
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 75-year-old woman presents for a routine examination. In bright light her pupils measure 3.5 mm OD and 3 mm OS, and in dim light they measure 5 mm OD and 4.5 mm OS. She has 1 mm ptosis OD, normal levator function, and normal ocular motility. What is the most appropriate next step?
Correct answer: A. reassessment in 1 month
Rationale
This patient has physiologic anisocoria with the same pupil disparity between bright and dim lighting conditions. Despite mild ptosis, the normal motility and levator function strongly suggest that the anisocoria is not due to a CN III palsy. Even if the ptosis were on the side of the smaller left pupil, the findings are not consistent with Horner syndrome (anisocoria should be worse in dim light). Absent evidence for an urgent process, imaging and/or hospitalization are not indicated at this time.

Q1206
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents for evaluation of diplopia. With a simple occluder in front of the right eye, the diplopia goes away; with the occluder in front of the left eye, the diplopia persists. With the left eye occluded, placing a pinhole occluder over the right eye resolves the diplopia. The manifest refraction is plano sphere in each eye. Corneal topography is normal. Ductions and versions are full. Nuclear cataracts with vacuoles are noted in each eye. There is intermediate dry macular degeneration present in the right eye and early dry macular degeneration in the left eye. The optic nerves are normal. What is the most likely cause of this patient's double vision?
Correct answer: A. cataract
Rationale
Inhomogeneous cataracts frequently split the incident light into 2 or more divergent paths, resulting in monocular diplopia. Dry age-related macular degeneration may reduce retinal sensitivity to the diminished retinal illumination seen through a pinhole, but it does not cause double vision. (Macular edema may cause monocular diplopia, however.) Recently acquired strabismus frequently causes binocular diplopia, but this resolves if either eye is covered. This patient does not have any astigmatism, as evidenced by no refractive error and normal corneal topography.

Q1207
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 58-year-old man was recently diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. He also has a past medical history of hypertension, gout, and stroke. His medications include allopurinol, furosemide, prednisone, and warfarin. Which of those medications may be causing or worsening the myasthenia gravis?
Correct answer: D. prednisone
Rationale
Myasthenia gravis (MG) can be caused, unmasked, or worsened by antiarrhythmics, statins, antibiotics, chemotherapeutic drugs, antiepileptic drugs, quinolones, penicillamine, corticosteroids, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers. Allopurinol has not been shown to worsen symptoms of myasthenia gravis. Furosemide is a diuretic, and warfarin is a blood thinner.

Q1208
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What clinical test best localizes monocular diplopia to an optical etiology?
Correct answer: A. pinhole acuity
Rationale
Monocular diplopia most commonly results from abnormalities in the refractive media, though less commonly retinal pathology and cerebral monocular diplopia (very rare) may cause monocular diplopia. Monocular diplopia that resolves with pinhole establishes that the diplopia is a result of an optical aberration and obviates the need for a neurological workup. Though corneal topography and optical coherence tomography may help evaluate monocular causes of monocular diplopia, they do not prove an optical etiology. A manifest refraction may help resolve many forms of monocular diplopia but is not always successful (irregular astigmatism, dry eyes, cataracts are just some examples in which a manifest refraction may not completely resolve monocular diplopia from an optical cause).

Q1209
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Chronic, progressive visual field loss with persistent headaches in a patient with pseudotumor cerebri despite weight loss and maximal oral medical therapy is an indication for what treatment?
Correct answer: C. ventriculoperitoneal shunt
Rationale
In a patient unresponsive to medical therapy, surgical intervention is warranted. If headaches are a significant component, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is probably the most appropriate procedure. If a patient were to have progressive vision loss without headaches, an optic nerve sheath fenestration would be most appropriate. However, sometimes the most appropriate procedure is the one that is the most easily available for the patient.
Orbital decompression is not used for pseudotumor cerebri. Intravenous prednisone is used for optic neuritis. Intravenous mannitol is used to lower intraocular pressure.

Q1210
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 3-year-old boy presents with involuntary, large amplitude, multidirectional eye movements. What underlying neoplasm is most concerning in this patient?
Correct answer: A. neuroblastoma
Rationale
This patient has opsoclonus, which sometimes can occur along with myoclonus and ataxia. Etiologies include paraneoplastic syndromes, encephalitis, drug intoxication, multiple sclerosis, environmental toxins, and hyperosmolar coma. Workup includes searching for an underlying tumor and associated paraneoplastic syndrome. In children, neuroblastoma is the primary consideration. In adults, small-cell lung carcinoma, breast cancer, and ovarian cancer are of the most concern.

Q1211
Neuro-Ophthalmology
During the 17th week of pregnancy, a 41-year-old woman developed sudden-onset, painless diplopia. She has a right abduction deficit that varies from ET 20 PD in primary position to ET 30 PD in right gaze and ET 8 PD in left gaze. Afferent function, pupils, and facial sensation are normal. Given the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings shown, what is the most likely cause of her diplopia?
Correct answer: A. tumor growth because of increased hormone levels in pregnancy
Rationale
The T1-weighted axial MRI image without contrast shows a lesion in the right cavernous sinus and sphenoid wing that is relatively isodense to brain parenchyma, with a dural tail. This lesion is most consistent with a sphenoid wing meningioma. In this case, it produced a right sixth nerve palsy due to enlargement into the right cavernous sinus. Meningiomas are commonly responsive to estrogen and related hormones, and if present prior to pregnancy, commonly enlarge during this period of increased hormone circulation.
The other answer options (thyroid eye disease, right sixth nerve palsy from raised intracranial pressure, Sheehan syndrome) do not explain the imaging finding of right sphenoid wing mass.

Q1212
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 55-year-old woman was recently started on a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and then developed severe recurrent headaches with hemianopic field loss. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) showed a “string-of-beads” appearance of the cerebral arteries. What is her most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome
Rationale
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) is characterized by severe recurrent headaches with or without focal neurologic deficits and/or seizures, as well as segmental constriction of cerebral arteries that resolves within 3 months. Visual complaints are frequent and include light sensitivity, blurred vision, and hemianopic visual field loss. This syndrome mainly affects middle-aged women, and more than one-half of RCVS cases occur during the postpartum period or after exposure to vasoactive substances (eg, SSRIs). MRA may demonstrate the characteristic “string-of-beads” appearance of the cerebral arteries.
Cerebral vasculitis and cerebral arterial dissection can cause similar symptoms, but would not typically show the classic “string-of-beads” appearance of segmental constriction of the arteries that is seen in RCVS. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome causes T2 signal abnormalities and is not typically associated with severe headaches.

Q1213
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 34-year-old woman with a metallic foreign body has head and neck pain and notes new left upper eyelid ptosis. Her right pupil is larger than the left and redilates more briskly after direct or consensual stimulus. What is the most appropriate imaging test to obtain first?
Correct answer: D. CT angiogram of the neck
Rationale
The patient has signs and symptoms to suggest a painful left-sided Horner syndrome with recent onset. Cervical carotid dissection must be excluded, and either CT or MR angiography of the neck should be performed as the initial test. Brain/head studies are not adequate to evaluate the area of concern. Catheter angiography may be done if the CTA or MRA is abnormal but is not the first test to be ordered. In fact, it may be less sensitive for initial diagnosis.

Q1214
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A hypertensive adult experienced onset of complete left ptosis 2 days ago. There is anisocoria and partial limitation of ductions in the left eye. What is the most appropriate initial management strategy?
Correct answer: C. imaging to rule out intracranial aneurysm
Rationale
The description is of a patient with pupil-involving third nerve palsy, and the usual causes are intracranial aneurysm, microvascular infarction, and diabetes. An aneurysm may be fatal and must be ruled out. Observation is not appropriate. A Tensilon test may be indicated if the initial workup is negative, and if there is variability of ptosis and strabismus on examination. Hypertension should be controlled, but an aneurysm needs to be ruled out first.

Q1215
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 50-year-old man complains of painless binocular vertical diplopia. He presents with a left head tilt and has an 8 prism-diopter (PD) right hypertropia in primary position. This hypertropia measures 12 PD in left gaze and 3 PD in right gaze. On right head tilt his hypertropia measures 13 PD and on left tilt it is 2 PD. What would suggest a congenital right fourth nerve palsy in this patient?
Correct answer: C. the patient's denial of diplopia in primary position
Rationale
If the patient denies diplopia in primary position; this indicates that he has a vertical fusional amplitude of at least 8 prism diopters (normal is 1-3 PD). Patients with a long-standing fourth nerve palsy have a relatively large vertical fusional range (>3 prism diopters). Most patients maintain a chronic head tilt. The long-standing nature of the head tilt may cause facial asymmetry and can often be confirmed by reviewing old photographs.
A right fourth nerve palsy will increase in left gaze and right head tilt. Hypertropia when the patient is looking up and to the right would be expected to be less in any right fourth nerve palsy, and therefore does not help distinguish a congenital fourth nerve palsy from other causes of a fourth nerve palsy. A left hypertropia on downgaze and right hypertropia on upgaze would not be expected in a right fourth nerve palsy of any etiology.

Q1216
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What additional physical finding would be expected for an infarct involving the fascicle of the sixth nerve?
Correct answer: B. ipsilateral facial nerve paralysis
Rationale
The seventh nerve loops around the sixth nerve nucleus within the pons. Therefore, a lesion affecting the fascicle of the sixth nerve can affect the ipsilateral seventh nerve, causing ipsilateral facial paralysis. The fascicle of the sixth nerve extends ventrally and passes adjacent to the corticospinal tract before leaving the ventral pons.
Involvement of the corticospinal tract will cause contralateral weakness (Raymond syndrome), not ipsilateral weakness. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is seen in dorsal midbrain syndrome, which would not cause an abduction deficit. Contralateral homonymous hemianopia indicates a postchiasmal lesion within the visual pathway, which would not be caused by a lesion involving the fascicle of the sixth nerve.

Q1217
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 41-year-old woman develops sudden vision loss in her right eye. Visual acuity is 20/50 in the right eye associated with a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) and an inferior visual field defect on confrontation. Visual acuity and confrontation field in the left eye is normal. Optic discs and fundi appear normal in both eyes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. retrobulbar optic neuritis
Rationale
Patients with optic neuritis and compressive optic neuropathy can have normal appearing optic nerves despite vision loss. According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), the optic disc appears normal in 65% of cases of optic neuritis. In this patient, however, the acute onset argues for optic neuritis because compressive etiologies, especially from a slow-growing meningioma, typically present with slowly progressive vision loss.
Acute vision loss in the presence of a normal optic nerve and macula is unlikely to be anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or branch retinal vein occlusion.

Q1218
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient with normal visual fields undergoes pattern-reversal visual evoked potential (VEP) testing. In one eye, the P100 wave has a preserved amplitude, but it is markedly prolonged. The other eye has a normal amplitude and latency. What condition should be suspected?
Correct answer: B. multiple sclerosis
Rationale
Visual evoked potential (VEP) testing measures electrical signals produced in response to a visual stimulus; the signals are recorded at the scalp overlying the occipital cortex. Damage anywhere along the afferent visual pathway can reduce the amplitude or speed of the signal. Because the central visual field predominates in the occipital cortex, isolated peripheral vision loss may yield normal VEP results. A common cause of delayed latency on VEP with normal visual fields is a prior bout of recovered demyelinating optic neuritis. Multiple sclerosis is the most common cause of optic neuritis. Demyelination of the optic nerve results in increased latency of the P100 waveform without significant effect on amplitude, whereas ischemic, compressive, and toxic damage reduce amplitude primarily, with less effect on latency.
Glaucoma would not cause a delayed VEP unless there was significant visual field loss. Cortical blindness can cause delayed VEP, but it would affect both eyes.

Q1219
Neuro-Ophthalmology
While shaving, an otherwise asymptomatic 34-year-old man noted that his left pupil was larger than on the right. The ophthalmologist finds that his visual acuity is 20/20 OU, and that the anisocoria (shown in the figure) is greater in the light. What evaluation is most likely to reveal the cause of his findings?
Correct answer: D. slit-lamp examination
Rationale
This patient has Adie pupil in the left eye, a likely possibility in an asymptomatic man with anisocoria, and no ptosis, asymmetric lower lid position, or strabismus (the corneal light reflex looks symmetric). From a diagnostic standpoint, the cause of anisocoria can often be determined by comparing pupil disparity in light and dark. Since his anisocoria is greater in the light, he has a problem with miosis, so the problem pupil is the larger one on the left side and the iris sphincter is dysfunctional. In the absence of ptosis or an ocular misalignment (third cranial nerve palsy), unilateral dilation of the pupil is most commonly from pharmacologic dilation, mechanical problems of the iris (sphincter trauma or synechiae), or a tonic pupil (Adie pupil). Slit-lamp examination would be most helpful to examine the iris for evidence of mechanical damage (synechia or sphincter rupture) or vermiform sectoral movements of a tonic pupil. A swinging flashlight test is most helpful to detect or measure a relative afferent pupillary defect, which is rarely useful in evaluating anisocoria. Cocaine eyedrops are helpful for evaluating anisocoria that is greater in the dark when iris dilator dysfunction (Horner syndrome) may be present. Apraclonidine is also useful for evaluating possible Horner syndrome (supersensitivity) but is not applicable here.

Q1220

A person presents with ptosis and horizontal gaze palsy associated with ataxia and areflexia. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome
Rationale
Areflexia, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia characterize Miller Fisher syndrome, a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Any pattern of ophthalmoplegia can be seen in Miller Fisher syndrome. Patients can also have bilateral ptosis, facial diplegia, and respiratory and swallowing difficulties.
Myasthenia gravis, giant cell arteritis, or an infarction to the abducens nucleus can cause horizontal gaze palsy but would not cause ataxia or areflexia.

A 56-year-old woman presents for evaluation of right eye irritation. She additionally reports a 3-day history of altered taste sensation and right-sided facial weakness, and is noted to have dense interpalpebral keratopathy, incomplete blink, and orbicularis oculi weakness on the right. Five (5) days later she presents with similar findings affecting the left side. Infection with what organism is most likely the cause of these findings?
Correct answer: B. Borrelia burgdorferi
Rationale
Borrelia burgdorferi

The patient in this case presents with bilateral sequential facial nerve palsy. The tick-borne spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative organism of Lyme disease, and can be associated with unilateral or bilateral facial nerve palsy. As many as 25% of cases of new-onset facial nerve palsies may be attributed to B burgdorferi infection in endemic areas.
Actinomyces israelii is associated with canaliculitis. Staphylococcus aureus causes staphylococcal infection, and Bartonella henselae causes cat-scratch disease.

Q1222
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 58-year-old woman noticed blurred vision, off to the right. Her visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. Her brain MRI is shown below. What clinical test is most likely to confirm the cause of her blurred vision?
Correct answer: D. alternate cover testing
Rationale
The contrast-enhanced coronal T1-weighted MRI shows an enhancing lesion involving the right cavernous sinus without involvement of the optic chiasm, which would most likely cause subtle motility disorders that may be diagnosed by performing an alternate cover test. "Blurred vision" may be used by patients to describe a variety of symptoms, including double vision, suppression, or visual field loss. Structures that pass through the cavernous sinus include cranial nerves III, IV, and VI. Cranial nerve VI passes through the cavernous sinus itself, whereas cranial nerves III and IV pass through the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. Slow-growing cavernous sinus lesions may cause subtle motility problems (such as a subtle sixth nerve palsy) so that in primary position, patients may be asymptomatic and only develop symptoms in certain positions of gaze (such as ipsilateral gaze). Ocular misalignments can be detected with alternate cover testing. Examination of the pupils may occasionally reveal anisocoria if the third nerve is involved or if there is an ipsilateral Horner syndrome; however, no relative afferent pupillary defect would be expected. Measures of afferent visual function such as Amsler grid testing and color vision testing would not be affected by a cavernous sinus lesion.

Q1223
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 57-year-old man developed severe left orbital pain, decreased vision in the left eye, and a vesicular rash involving the left upper face and eyelid. On examination, he had ophthalmoplegia. Visual acuity was 20/400 OS and there was a left afferent pupillary defect (APD). Dilated fundus examination showed mild optic disc swelling without hemorrhages in the left eye, normal in the right. Where does this constellation of findings localize?
Correct answer: C. orbital apex
Rationale
The presence of a vesicular rash involving the V1 distribution is highly suggestive of herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Zoster can affect any part of the eye and can rarely cause an orbital apex syndrome. This patient has ophthalmoplegia and an optic neuropathy, which localizes to the orbital apex. Cavernous sinus involvement would lead to ophthalmoplegia without optic neuropathy. An optic chiasm lesion would cause a bitemporal hemianopia. Scleritis would cause pain without vision loss or ophthalmoplegia.

Q1224
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient presents with continuous unilateral undulating contraction of the orbicularis oculi and most of the facial muscles. What is the most common cause of these symptoms?
Correct answer: C. pontine glioma
Rationale
Facial myokymia is usually the result of a pontine glioma or demyelination (ie, MS). It is characterized by continuous unilateral contraction of facial muscle bundles and typically signifies intramedullary disease of the pons involving the CN VII nucleus or fascicle. Compression of the CN VII root exit zone by an aberrant vessel is the most common cause of hemifacial spasm, which is characterized by a unilateral episodic spasm involving the facial musculature. Excessive caffeine intake can cause isolated eyelid myokymia. Aberrant regeneration after facial palsy is typically not continuous.

Q1225
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 7-month-old infant develops conjugate horizontal nystagmus with a null point. The infant maintains attention on a fixation target and follows it well, aside from the noted nystagmus. Testing with an optokinetic drum shows a reversal of the normally expected optokinetic nystagmus. The eye examination is normal and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is normal. What is the most likely underlying etiology?
Correct answer: A. genetic mutation
Rationale
Infantile nystagmus syndrome (INS), also called congenital nystagmus, is classically described as a binocular conjugate horizontal nystagmus that presents within the first 2 years of life. It is categorized as either congenital motor nystagmus (CMN) or congenital sensory nystagmus, depending on the etiology. Congenital motor nystagmus (CMN) is not associated with afferent pathway disease, is often associated with normal or near-normal vision, has a normal ocular examination and normal neuroimaging, and does not produce oscillopsia. In contrast, sensory nystagmus arises when central visual acuity is too poor to develop a stable fixational mechanism. Sensory nystagmus is associated with conditions that cause bilateral, pregeniculate vision loss in children younger than 2 years. Because congenital motor and congenital sensory nystagmus can present and appear identical, workup of a patient with early-onset nystagmus should include a search for clinical manifestations of pregeniculate vision loss. In the absence of obvious ocular causes such as cataract, the patient should be evaluated for the following conditions, which can be subtle and difficult to detect in uncooperative children: optic neuropathy, foveal hypoplasia, and retinal dystrophy.
Approximately two-thirds of CMN patients exhibit a paradoxical inversion of the optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) response, which is unique to CMN. Normally, when a patient with right-jerk nystagmus views an optokinetic drum rotation to the patient's left (eliciting a "pursuit left, jerk right" response), the intensity of the right-jerk nystagmus increases. However, patients with CMN exhibit a damped right-jerk nystagmus or possibly even a left-jerk nystagmus when viewing an optokinetic drum rotation to the left.
X-linked mutations in the FERM domain-containing-7 gene (FRMD7) underlie many cases of typical CMN. Intracranial brain tumors do not cause CMN. Poor fusion in a child causes fusion maldevelopment nystagmus. Chiasmal/suprachiasmal tumors such as optic pathway gliomas can result in a nystagmus identical to spasmus nutans.

Q1226
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What type of nystagmus is characterized by reversal of the normal pattern of optokinetic nystagmus?
Correct answer: D. congenital nystagmus
Rationale
Congenital nystagmus, or infantile nystagmus syndrome, is often recognized in the first few months of life. It is usually conjugate and horizontal in all positions of gaze.
There are 2 characteristic signs of congenital nystagmus:
  1. Reversal of the normal pattern of optokinetic nystagmus (OKN), characterized by slow-phase eye movements in the direction opposite that of the rotating OKN drum.
  2. Pattern in which the velocity of slow-phase movement increases exponentially with distance from fixation. Identification of this pattern requires eye movement recordings.
Latent nystagmus is an early-onset, conjugate, horizontal jerk nystagmus that is accentuated when one eye is occluded.
Spasmus nutans is a childhood nystagmus characterized by asymmetric, small-amplitude, high-frequency, shimmering eye movements. It often is associated with head nodding and torticollis.
Gaze-evoked nystagmus develops due to inability to maintain fixation in eccentric gaze, leading to the eyes drifting back to the midline. A corrective saccade is then generated to reposition the eyes on the eccentric target, meaning that the fast phase is always in the direction of gaze.

Q1227
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 66-year-old woman has repeated transient vision loss in her right eye lasting for 10-15 minutes. She is otherwise well. Her ophthalmic examination is normal, as are erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C‑reactive protein results. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain shows a focus of diffusion-weighted imaging abnormality in the right parietal area. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
Correct answer: B. immediate evaluation in a hospital stroke unit
Rationale
Transient monocular vision loss (TMVL) may herald cerebrovascular disease, usually of the ipsilateral internal carotid artery, that can place the patient at risk for hemispheric stroke. Data from the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial (NASCET) suggested that TMVL was less likely to result in stroke than other types of transient ischemic attacks (TIA). More recent data suggest that patients with TMVL should be evaluated with urgent brain MRI to look for diffuse-weighted imaging (DWI) abnormalities, as their presence indicates that cerebral ischemia has occurred recently. Such patients may be at high risk for stroke, and they may benefit from rapid surgical treatment of vascular disease. Having such patients seen in a hospital stroke unit is the most effective way to ensure they receive immediate evaluation.
Giant cell arteritis must be considered as a cause of TMVL as well, but in this patient, the normal ESR and CRP, along with absence of symptoms, as well as the DWI abnormality, indicates that she needs stroke evaluation. Scheduling routine carotid ultrasonography or simply prescribing aspirin is not adequate.

Q1228
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What diagnostic test is most helpful in the workup of a 12-year-old boy with right-sided proptosis and chronic unilateral optic disc edema?
Correct answer: D. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Rationale
While IVFA and OCT can help characterize the presence and severity of optic disc edema, proptosis with chronic optic disc edema suggests an orbital mass, which is proven only with imaging behind the globe. Magnetic resonance imaging, especially with intravenous gadolinium contrast and fat-suppressed views of the orbits, offers coronal and axial soft tissue views of the optic nerve and its sheath. This imaging modality shows intrinsic and extrinsic lesions of the optic nerve with high resolution. Optic nerve biopsy is too invasive as a first diagnostic test and is often unnecessary to diagnose the characteristic fusiform lesion morphology of optic nerve glioma, which is the most common optic nerve tumor of this age group.

Q1229
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 36-year-old male presents with binocular horizontal diplopia following a severe head injury with left medial orbital trauma. He is noted to have 20 prism diopters of esotropia in primary gaze, worse in left gaze, improving in right gaze. He has a large left abduction deficit. He has left upper and lower eyelid edema and ecchymosis. There is no enophthalmos or proptosis. His eye examination is otherwise unremarkable. What test is most appropriate for determining whether his ocular motility deficit is a result of a paretic or restrictive etiology?
Correct answer: A. saccadic velocity test
Rationale
This patient has an incomitant esotropia following trauma. Given the pattern of esotropia (worse in left gaze, improved in right gaze) and the left abduction deficit, this could represent either a paresis of the left lateral rectus muscle (left CN6 palsy from a closed head injury) or a restriction of the left medial rectus (which can occur with left medial orbital trauma).
Saccadic velocities are a simple method for helping to distinguish between a paretic and restrictive etiology. Paretic etiologies typically result in decreased saccadic velocities, whereas restrictive etiologies typically have a normal saccadic velocity. However, in cases where the saccadic velocity may not be easily ascertained (for example, a near-ophthalmoplegic eye), forced duction testing may be useful. A doll's eye test is useful in differentiating between supranuclear and nuclear/infranuclear causes of limited eye motility. A double Maddox rod test is used to quantify torsional strabismus.

Q1230
Neuro-Ophthalmology
An 88-year-old female presents for evaluation of diplopia following a brainstem stroke. What clinical finding would suggest a nuclear right cranial nerve (CN) III palsy?
Correct answer: C. left superior rectus palsy
Rationale
The CN III nuclear complex consists of paired subnuclei for the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles, as well as paired subnuclei for the pupillary constrictor muscles and a single subnucleus for the levator palpebrae muscles. The subnuclei for the superior rectus supply the contralateral superior rectus muscle; as such, a right nuclear CN III may have a left superior rectus palsy. A nuclear CN III lesion could either spare or affect both eyelids; a unilateral ptosis in the setting of a CN III palsy would suggest an infranuclear lesion. A right nuclear CN III lesion would cause right pupil dilation, not left pupil dilation. A right medial rectus palsy may be present but is not specific to a nuclear CN III palsy.

A 37-year-old man reports poor peripheral vision in both eyes for 6 months, and perimetry shows severe field constriction to less than 10 degrees in both eyes. He makes accurate saccades in all directions. Tangent screen testing at 1 meter shows a larger field than at 2 meters. Pupils are briskly reactive. What is the most likely finding on fundus examination?
Correct answer: B. normal funduscopic examination
Rationale
This patient has nonphysiological visual field loss (ie, it is not consistent with neurologic or ophthalmic disease), as demonstrated by his smaller tangent screen field at 2 meters vs 1 meter. Patients with severe visual field constriction from organic disease should have visual field expansion, as they are positioned farther away from the tangent screen. Thus, his fundus examination should be normal.

Rationale
12 supplementation

Gastric bypass patients are susceptible to intestinal malabsorption syndrome, including vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency results in a bilateral, insidious, nutritional optic neuropathy that causes central vision loss with cecocentral scotomata on visual field testing and eventually bilateral temporal optic nerve pallor. Treatment is parenteral B12 supplementation.
Intravenous corticosteroids for 3 days followed by an 11-day oral taper is the treatment for acute optic neuritis, not nutritional optic neuropathy.
The oral soluble form of vitamin A is the treatment for vitamin A deficiency, which causes nyctalopia and retinal dysfunction.
Immediate optic nerve sheath fenestration, both eyes, would be a treatment option in extreme cases of fulminant idiopathic intracranial hypertension with severe papilledema.

What supranuclear structure, if damaged, can be associated with diplopia and strabismus?

Rationale
Most supranuclear disorders affect both eyes equally and therefore do not cause diplopia. However, certain supranuclear lesions do not result in a symmetric effect and thus may produce ocular misalignment and diplopia.

Q1235
Neuro-Ophthalmology
In a patient with Horner syndrome, what is the expected effect of apraclonidine on each pupil?
Correct answer: B. dilation of the affected pupil and no effect on the normal pupil
Rationale
Apraclonidine reverses the anisocoria. It causes dilation of the affected pupil but has no effect on the normal pupil. It will dilate the affected pupil regardless of whether the lesion is pre- or postganglionic. The proposed mechanism for this asymmetric response is denervation supersensitivity; apraclonidine has weak alpha-1-adrenergic agonist properties. Denervation supersensitivity is thought to arise after 2-5 days of injury.
Though its use in acute Horner syndrome remains debatable, there was a case report of acute Horner syndrome caused by a carotid dissection in which apraclonidine was effective in diagnosis within 3 hours of symptoms.

Q1236
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 45-year-old woman has episodic right eye visual loss in right gaze. Vision returns rapidly with primary or left gaze. What test is most likely to reveal the cause of her vision loss?
Correct answer: B. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) orbits with contrast
Rationale
Gaze-evoked amaurosis is an infrequent but highly characteristic symptom of a posterior orbital mass causing optic nerve compression that worsens acutely (and temporarily) when eye movement increases the amount of compression. Vision returns rapidly when the eye returns to the neutral position. MRI orbits will delineate the mass and its extent. While CT also could be used to look at the orbital contents, MRI (with fat saturation sequences for better visualization of the orbital structures) is preferred in this case since it provides better visualization of soft tissue structures, including the optic nerve. Carotid and cardiac disease also cause amaurosis, but it is not gaze-evoked. Vertebral artery disease may cause transient homonymous vision loss with head rotation.

Q1237
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Stenosis of the carotid artery causes what visual symptom in its early stages?
Correct answer: B. transient visual loss in bright light
Rationale
Hypoperfusion from severe carotid artery stenosis leads to transient monocular vision loss (TMVL) in several situations. Ocular ischemic syndrome is characterized in part by a hypotensive, ischemic retinopathy with low retinal artery pressure, poor perfusion, and midperipheral retinopathy. In the early stages, there may be transient or persistent blurred vision or transient visual loss on exposure to bright light.
Binocular diplopia is incorrect because it is not likely to occur in ocular ischemia, but instead is due to cranial nerve palsy and other forms of strabismus.
Vision in ocular ischemic syndrome would be expected to improve, not worsen, in the supine position.
Gaze-evoked visual loss is associated with increased intracranial pressure, such as in idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), due to compression of the optic nerve within an edematous sheath on lateral gaze.

Q1238
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Four days ago, a 47-year-old hypertensive smoker developed acute constant binocular oblique diplopia and headaches. His visual acuity and visual fields are normal, as are anterior and posterior segment findings. Pupils are 4 mm OD, 6 mm OS, with no reaction to stimuli OS. Neither eye moves with attempted upgaze. The left eye is abducted and can depress slightly. A single responsible lesion is discovered on magnetic resonance imaging. Where is the location of this lesion?
Correct answer: A. midbrain
Rationale
The patient has a partial left cranial nerve III (CN III) palsy and upgaze deficit. He has stroke risk factors and clinical features of midbrain infarction with damage to the left third nerve nucleus and fascicle. Because the subnucleus to the right superior rectus sits on the left side, it has been injured as well, and neither eye can elevate.
The pons contains the nucleus and fascicle of the sixth cranial nerve and the centers for horizontal gaze. Therefore, pontine lesions can result in horizontal gaze palsies and internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Cerebellar lesions can cause nystagmus, saccadic dysfunction, and skew deviation. Wallenberg syndrome occurs with lateral medullary stroke and is associated with ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature sensation, contralateral loss of hemibody pain and temperature sensation, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, ipsilateral first-order Horner syndrome, ipsilateral ocular tilt reaction, and ocular lateropulsion.

Congenital ocular motor apraxia is an abnormality in the initiation of what type of eye movement?
Correct answer: D. horizontal saccadic eye movements
Rationale
Congenital ocular motor apraxia is a syndrome with failure of the initiation of horizontal saccades. Changes in fixation are accomplished by a head thrust that overshoots the target, followed by a rotation of the head back in the opposite direction once fixation is established. The vertical saccadic movements and both vertical and horizontal smooth pursuit movements are preserved in this condition.

Q1240

A 69-year-old woman has intermittent diplopia after reading. Extraocular movements show a slight deficit of right eye depression and adduction with no manifest strabismus. After she reads for 1 minute, she shows a 20 PD right hypotropia that resolves slowly after 45 seconds. What prior medical treatment is most likely to have resulted in this condition?
Correct answer: C. radiotherapy for skull base tumor
Rationale
The patient has characteristic findings for ocular neuromyotonia, with sustained inferior rectus contraction for 30-60 seconds after downgaze and return to primary gaze (from reading position to primary). The most common cause of ocular neuromyotonia is prior skull base radiotherapy with presumed damage to the affected cranial nerve (CN III in this case). Ocular neuromyotonia may affect any of the ocular motor nerves or their divisions.
Botulinum toxin does not cause this condition. First-generation antipsychotic use may cause tardive dyskinesia, which can involve facial spasms but is not known to produce ocular neuromyotonia. Microvascular decompression is a treatment option for patients with hemifacial spasm. It does not cause ocular neuromyotonia.
Patients may be treated with antiepileptic agents such as carbamazepine if symptoms are bothersome.
