Q1241
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 24-year-old female presents with complaints of decreased vision in her right eye and pain with eye movement for the past 3 days. On examination her visual acuity is 20/200 in her right eye, 20/20 in her left eye. She has a right afferent pupillary defect. MRI shows enhancement of the right optic nerve and 3 periventricular white matter lesions. According to the results of the Optic Neuritis Treatment  Trial, what effect is expected from a dose of oral prednisone as the initial treatment?
Correct answer: D. more likely to have a recurrence of optic neuritis
Rationale
This patient is more likely to have a recurrence of optic neuritis if she is treated with oral steroids alone. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) assessed the role of both oral and IV steroid treatment for initial episodes of unilateral optic neuritis. In essence, patients were randomized to either oral prednisone for 14 days, high-dose IV methylprednisolone for 3 days followed by oral steroids, or oral placebo for 14 days. Treatment with IV steroids accelerated visual recovery, but did not yield a better end point of vision compared to placebo. Treatment with oral steroids did not improve visual outcome and was actually associated with an increased rate of recurrence of optic neuritis. In addition to a more rapid recovery of vision, IV steroids yielded a decreased rate of progression to multiple sclerosis in patients with 2 or more white matter lesions on MRI studies, from 36% of untreated patients to 16% of patients treated with IV steroids. However, this effect was only present for the first 3 years of follow-up.

In a patient with ptosis but no extraocular motility limitation, what finding, aside from fatigability, should prompt a workup for myasthenia gravis?
Correct answer: B. orbicularis oculi weakness
Rationale
Ptosis is a common problem whose etiology varies from benign involutional changes to serious neurologic disease. A thorough examination is critical to determining the workup.
Unilateral or bilateral ptosis is the most common sign of myasthenia gravis. In addition to fatiguability and improvement with ice testing, myasthenic ptosis is often accompanied by orbicularis oculi weakness on examination. This is tested with the patient squeezing both eyes shut and the examiner manually applying pressure around the eyes to attempt to reopen them.
Myasthenia gravis never involves the pupil or sensory nerves, and it does not cause aberrant regeneration/synkinesis of other extraocular muscle nerve fibers.

Q1243

A patient is asked to fixate in downgaze for a few seconds and then look straight ahead. When this happens, there is an upward overshoot of the eyelid before the eyelid settles back to the baseline position. What is this sign called?
Correct answer: B. Cogan lid-twitch
Rationale
This patient has a classic Cogan lid-twitch sign, which is a feature of myasthenia. This can be identified by having the patient fixate in downgaze for a few seconds and then rapidly refixate straight ahead. The sign appears as an upward overshoot of the eyelid followed by fluttering as the eyelid settles into position. Lid lag is present when the upper eyelid is higher than normal in downgaze, which is seen in thyroid eye disease or a result of aberrant regeneration of CN III. Apraxia of eyelid opening is characterized by the inability to open the eyelids voluntarily.

Q1244
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Three weeks ago, a 37-year-old woman was in a motor vehicle accident. She had no immediate visual problems but now has binocular diplopia and an intermittent sound in her right ear. Vision in each eye is normal. What additional findings on examination would support her likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. dilated subconjunctival vessels that do not blanch with epinephrine
Rationale
Patients may develop intracranial vascular injury after a motor vehicle accident, and rupture of dural arteries or even the cavernous internal carotid artery may result in arteriovenous fistula formation. As the arterial blood enters the venous system, changes in flow can occur over several weeks, and symptoms may not start immediately. Arterialized blood enters the venous system and may drain anteriorly into the orbit, which causes episcleral venous dilation and arterialization. Posterior draining of this blood through the inferior petrosal sinus can compress cranial nerve (CN) VI, where it passes beneath the petroclival ligament and causes diplopia. Turbulent flow in this vessel may be transmitted to the inner ear through the petrous bone, and the patient can have pulsatile tinnitus. Orbital fracture with enophthalmos would not cause this tinnitus, and diplopia usually occurs immediately or within days, as swelling evolves.
While traumatic visual field loss from post-chiasmal visual pathway injury can occur, it is unlikely to present with the symptoms here. Ocular trauma would be more likely to cause immediate symptoms, and it would not result in binocular diplopia with tinnitus.

Q1245
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 36-year-old female with a history of migraines reports after images when looking at moving objects. What is she describing?
Correct answer: D. illusory palinopsia
Rationale
Palinopsia is visual preservation after removal of the original stimulus (multiple afterimages) and can be divided into 2 categories: illusory and hallucinatory. Illusory palinopsia is triggered by contrast and/or motion; the visual afterimage or trails appear in the same location as the original stimulus. Migraine, hallucinogenic drugs, such as LSD, and some medications can cause illusory palinopsia. In contrast, hallucinatory palinopsia is not affected by environmental conditions, and the perseverated imaged can occur in a different location than the original stimulus. Hallucinatory palinopsia typically has associated homonymous visual field loss and is caused by cortical lesions, whereas illusory palinopsia is not neurologically dangerous.
Visual snow is also often seen in patients with migraine and is described as snowy, pixelated vision, similar to television static. It is not uncommon for a patient to have both visual snow and illusory palinopsia. Visual aura is also common in migraineurs and is classically described as homonymous scintillating scotoma that lasts 5 to 60 minutes and is often followed by headache. Riddoch phenomenon is a rare condition wherein a patient with cortical blindness can see moving objects, but not static objects.

Rationale
Bartonella henselae

This patient presented with signs and symptoms consistent with neuroretinitis, which is a clinical entity characterized by acute loss of vision associated with disc edema and a star pattern of exudates in the macula. Bartonella henselae is the most common cause of neuroretinitis.
HCV is not associated with neuroretinitis. However, treatment with interferon is associated with development of retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots.
HIV-associated retinopathy is a microangiopathy characterized by cotton-wool spots, hemorrhages, and aneurysm formation.
Sarcoidosis can present with neuroretinitis, but is a less common presentation than Bartonella species. Sarcoidosis is more commonly associated with posterior uveitis.

The answer is the nasociliary nerve. The postganglionic sympathetic fibers enter the cavernous sinus via the internal carotid artery and exit into the orbit with the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.

Correct answer: D. perimetry
Rationale
The fundus photo demonstrates small optic nerves with nasalization of the retinal vessels and no discernible cup. There is no pallor noted. These findings are consistent with optic nerve hypoplasia, which can be unilateral or bilateral. They can be associated with visual field defects, but in the setting of normal visual acuity are typically not associated with color vision or contrast sensitivity abnormalities. Q1249
Neuro-Ophthalmology
In what anatomical pathway does damage cause Balint syndrome?
Correct answer: C. dorsal occipitoparietal
Rationale
The dorsal occipitoparietal pathway is the "where pathway"; it is responsible for visuospatial analysis, localization of objects, and visually directed movements toward objects. Balint syndrome results from bilateral occipitoparietal lesions and consists of the triad of simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, and ocular motor apraxia. Lesions of the medial longitudinal fasciculus produce internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The ventral occipitotemporal pathway is the "what pathway"; it is responsible for color, shape, and pattern recognition. Lesions of the bilateral ventral occipitotemporal pathway cause object agnosia. Lesions of the optic tract cause complete or incomplete homonymous hemianopia.

Q1250
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What additional findings might be found in a patient with vestibular imbalance due to lateral medullary syndrome?
Correct answer: B. ipsilateral lateropulsion, ipsilateral loss of facial pain, and contralateral hemibody loss of temperature sensation
Rationale
Vestibular imbalance is common with lesions of the caudal brainstem (lower pons and medulla) because of disruption to the CN VIII nuclei or their interconnections. One of the better-known stroke syndromes involving this area is the lateral medullary syndrome (or Wallenberg syndrome). In general, damage to a lateral region of the brainstem disrupts the sensory pathways; therefore, Wallenberg syndrome is a type of “stroke without paralysis.” Patients can present with these signs and symptoms:
  • ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature sensation (involvement of the descending tract of CN V)
  • contralateral loss of hemibody pain and temperature sensation (involvement of the lateral spinothalamic tract)
  • ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia (damage to spinocerebellar tracts)
  • ipsilateral first-order Horner syndrome
  • ipsilateral ocular tilt reaction (head tilt toward the side of the lesion)
In addition, patients can have dysarthria, dysphagia, vertigo, or persistent hiccups; there is no extremity weakness.
Although the lateral medulla is in the distribution of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), Wallenberg syndrome usually results from occlusion of the more proximal vertebral artery. Consequently, patients may experience lateropulsion, the sensation of being pulled toward the side of the lesion, which results from damage to the CN VIII nuclei. Patients may also manifest ocular lateropulsion; this effect can be tested by examination of horizontal pursuit and saccadic movements, which will reveal a bias that produces hypermetric movements toward the side of the lesion and hypometric movements away from the side of the lesion. Vertical saccades may follow an elliptical path as the eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion during the vertical movement. Finally, this directional bias also can be observed by noting that the eyes turn toward the side of the lesion after visual fixation is removed for a few seconds.

Over the past week, a 23-year-old woman developed episodes of transient and progressive visual loss, headaches, and eye pain. Her visual acuity is 20/200 OU, with sluggishly reactive pupils. Both optic discs are swollen. Her magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is shown. What pathology best explains her presentation?
Correct answer: D. inflammation
Rationale
This patient has optic neuritis. The axial T1-weighted MRI shows enhancement of both intraorbital optic nerves. The use of fat suppression is important to eliminate high signal from the orbital fat on T1-weighted imaging. This optic nerve enhancement is most commonly seen with inflammatory optic neuropathies, which would most commonly be associated with eye pain (on movement particularly) and may be associated with headaches. Increased intracranial pressure and toxic injury do not result in optic nerve enhancement. Unless there are coincidental vascular sequelae, such as anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or retinal vascular occlusion, calcific deposits typically spare central visual function and are not associated with enhancement in the optic nerves.

Q1252

Eight days ago, a 63-year-old woman had a right-sided anterior occipital stroke. She reports being startled by people coming from behind her on the left. She is slow to detect fingers in her left peripheral visual field but has normal standard automated perimetry. What test will best define the suspected field defect?
Correct answer: B. kinetic (Goldmann) perimetry
Rationale
The anterior occipital lobe subserves the far temporal visual field of the contralateral eye. In patients with anterior occipital lobe stroke involving the parieto-occipital artery, the resulting contralateral visual field defect is crescent-shaped and starts about 60 degrees temporal of fixation. Of the above choices, only Goldmann kinetic perimetry tests the outer edge of peripheral vision: temporally to 90 degrees; superiorly, inferiorly, and nasally to 60 degrees. Using several isopters (lights of standardized size and brightness), one can map a far temporal defect that would be missed on central vision testing.
Tangent screen testing is another type of kinetic perimetry wherein the patient is tested with a stimulus at 1 m. The areas of patient response are marked and the patient is moved back to 2 m. The test is then repeated using an 18-mm white stimulus. It is most useful in revealing "tubular" field defects typical of nonorganic visual loss and is not the first-choice option for stroke detection.
Frequency doubling threshold (FDT) perimetry is usually used as a screening test of the central 20-30 degree visual field and would not be adequate to pick up defects in the far periphery.
Computerized microperimetry with scanning laser ophthalmoscope (SLO) guidance tests the central macular visual field by allowing the real-time functional study of retinal sensitivity by direct ophthalmoscopy of the retinal surface at each test location. It is an appropriate method for analyzing central visual field defects but will miss peripheral depression outside 10-15 degrees.

A 70-year-old man complains of ocular pain in the right eye, as well as transient monocular visual loss. Correct answer: B. ocular ischemic syndrome
Rationale
This clinical scenario demonstrates several typical clinical features of ocular ischemic syndrome. IOP is usually low because ciliary body hypoperfusion decreases aqueous humor production. Carotid cavernous fistula is associated with elevated, not low, IOP. Orbital inflammatory disease is in the spectrum of uveitic disorders and may have ocular inflammation as a feature, but iris neovascularization is rarely seen. Thyroid orbitopathy also does not produce iris neovascularization and is associated with normal or elevated IOP.

A 73-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute onset diplopia and ptosis. In addition, the patient has a weakness of her left extremities that started at the time of the diplopia and ptosis. Based on the clinical findings, where is the lesion?
Correct answer: B. midbrain
Rationale
The finding of ptosis with an adduction, elevation, and depression deficit is highly suggestive of a third nerve palsy. The addition of a contralateral weakness is indicative of a midbrain lesion affecting the third nerve fascicle and the cerebral peduncle, resulting in an ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral weakness (Weber syndrome).
A lesion within the interpeduncular cistern, cavernous sinus, or orbital apex can cause a third nerve palsy, but it would not be expected to cause contralateral weakness.

Q1255
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 75-year-old hypertensive female presents for evaluation of sudden-onset diplopia. Her vision is 20/20, with normal color vision in each eye. She has a left relative afferent pupillary defect. She has a left hypertropia that is worse in right gaze and improves with right head tilt. Where is the most likely causative lesion?
Correct answer: D. right brainstem
Rationale
This woman has a left cranial nerve (CN) IV palsy with a left relative afferent pupillary defect without any visual loss. This would suggest that the lesion is in the brainstem near the right CN IV nucleus and affecting the pupillary fibers near the right superior colliculus, which would result in a left relative afferent pupillary defect (similar in effect to a right optic tract lesion due to the extra nasal fibers that decussate at the optic chiasm). Orbital apex lesions would result in decreased visual acuity and most likely affect other cranial nerves. The optic nerve is usually not affected in cavernous sinus lesions unless they expand to affect the optic canal. The afferent pupillary fibers do not course along the skull base.

Q1256
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Acquired cases of prosopagnosia typically result from stroke affecting what region(s) of the brain?
Correct answer: D. bilateral inferior occipitotemporal lobes or right inferior occipital lobe
Rationale
Prosopagnosia is a disorder of recognition involving visual-visual disconnection; it is characterized by the inability to recognize familiar faces. It is usually congenital, but acquired cases can result from stroke in the bilateral inferior occipitotemporal lobes or right inferior occipital lobe. The ventral occipitotemporal pathway is responsible for the processing of physical attributes of an object. Examination typically shows superior homonymous visual field defects. By contrast, the dorsal occipitoparietal pathway is responsible for visuospatial processing. enabling guidance of movement towards an object. Alexia without agraphia (patient cannot read but can write) results from damage to the splenium of the corpus callosum and the left occipital lobe.

Q1257
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most appropriate treatment for trochleitis?
Correct answer: A. local injection of corticosteroids into the trochlear region
Rationale
Trochleitis is typically an idiopathic inflammation of the trochlea, although it has been associated with systemic autoimmune disease. It causes pain on palpation of the trochlea and pain with extraocular movement. Treatment with local injection of corticosteroids in the trochlear region or high-dose nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) is recommended.

Q1258
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For what condition is anisocoria greater in light than dark and unchanged in response to pilocarpine 1%?
Correct answer: C. pharmacologic pupillary dilation
Rationale
A patient with pharmacologic pupillary dilation will present with anisocoria that is greater in the light that does not respond to full strength pilocarpine (1% or more). Mydriasis due to Adie pupil or CN III palsy is overcome with installation of dilute or full-strength pilocarpine, respectively.

Q1259
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most sensitive imaging study for detecting calcified optic disc drusen?
Correct answer: A. B-scan ultrasonography
Rationale
B-scan ultrasonography is very useful in detecting optic disc drusen. B-scan ultrasonography is more sensitive than autofluorescence or CT in detecting optic disc drusen. On B-scan, drusen appear hyperechoic (bright) with posterior shadowing. On fluorescein angiography, there is no leakage from optic disc drusen, unlike the leakage seen in true disc edema.
There are some papers that suggest that non-calcified optic disc drusen are better seen with fluorescein angiography.

Q1260
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the correct route of fibers that control the pupillary response to light?
Correct answer: A. retina to pretectal nuclei to Edinger-Westphal nuclei to ciliary ganglion to pupilloconstrictor fibers
Rationale
The pupillary response to light is mediated by parasympathetic neurons and involves midbrain pretectal nuclei that send fibers to the Edinger-Westphal subnuclei of the CN III nucleus. The parasympathetic fibers synapse in the ciliary ganglion before projecting in the short ciliary nerve to the iris sphincter.

Q1261
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A woman with headache is seen to have spontaneous venous pulsations on fundus examination. She returns 3 months later with worsening headache, and the pulsations are no longer present. What diagnostic and management plan should be followed?
Correct answer: B. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) of the brain/head, followed by lumbar puncture (LP)
Rationale
Most patients with normal intracranial pressure (ICP) have spontaneous venous pulsations. Although some patients with normal ICP may lack those pulsations, their disappearance in a patient with worsening headache and who previously was noted to have them indicates possible intracranial pressure elevation and impending papilledema. In this case, MRI and MRV should be performed to exclude a mass lesion or venous sinus thrombosis, and an LP should then be performed to measure the opening pressure and evaluate cerebrospinal fluid composition.
Lowering the IOP either acutely or chronically is not beneficial. There is no inflammation and thus no role for steroids. Observation can be appropriate when there are no venous pulsations if the patient never had them and is not exhibiting signs/symptoms of possible ICP elevation. However, this patient has worsening symptoms, and investigation of possibly elevated ICP is the better approach.

Q1262
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What diagnostic test is the most sensitive for myasthenia gravis?
Correct answer: D. single-fiber electromyography
Rationale
Electromyographic repetitive nerve stimulation shows a characteristic decremental response in patients with systemic myasthenia gravis (MG). Single-fiber electromyography is most sensitive for myasthenia gravis.
The ice-pack test is often helpful for diagnosing MG, but only if the patient has ptosis. An ice pack is placed over the patient’s lightly closed eyes for 2 minutes. Improvement of ptosis occurs in most patients with MG; however, the cooling effect may be insufficient to overcome the severe weakness in patients with complete myasthenic ptosis.
Edrophonium chloride tests are not commonly performed in eye clinics, because rare but serious adverse effects from administration of the drug can occur, including bradycardia, bronchospasm, cholinergic crisis, respiratory arrest, or syncopal episodes. Atropine sulfate (0.4–0.6 mg) should be available immediately in case it is needed. When the ocular symptom is marked (eg, complete ptosis), the endpoint (eyelid elevation) is often dramatic. However, a subtle deficit, such as minimal diplopia, may require use of other means to better define the endpoint. Maddox rod tests with prisms or diplopia fields may be performed before and after edrophonium. False-positive responses are rare. A negative test result does not exclude a diagnosis of MG, and repeat testing at a later date may be needed.
There are 3 types of commercially available acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody tests: binding, blocking, and modulating. Tests for binding antibodies are usually requested first, because these highly specific antibodies (near 100% specificity) are detected in approximately 90% of patients with generalized MG and in 50%–70% of patients with ocular MG.

Q1263
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What is the most likely cause of acute-onset unilateral brow ptosis, lagophthalmos, and drooping of the mouth?
Correct answer: C. Bell palsy
Rationale
Acute facial paralysis affecting the upper (brow) and lower (eyelid/cheek/mouth) musculature is indicative of a peripheral neuropathy. The most common acute peripheral neuropathy affecting the facial nerve is a Bell palsy. With central vascular causes (including CVAs and TIAs), brow function is typically spared because the upper face axons synapse bilaterally in the pons. Although MG can affect the facial musculature, it would be an unlikely cause of an acute facial palsy.

Q1264
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What systemic evaluation should be performed on a patient with suspected oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy?
Correct answer: D. genetic testing
Rationale
Making the diagnosis of oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (OPMD) is based on clinical criteria; however, the diagnosis may be confirmed by evaluating the gene, PABPN1, which encodes for the polyadenylate binding protein nuclear 1. PABPN1 is the only gene known to be associated with OPMD. Confirmatory molecular diagnosis of both autosomal dominant and/or autosomal recessive OPMD depends upon detection of an expansion of a GCN trinucleotide in the first exon of PABPN1. This genetic testing is now widely commercially available. Muscle biopsy is warranted only in individuals with suspected OPMD who have normal PABPN1 alleles and is performed on accessible proximal muscles such as the deltoid. Electrocardiogram, Tensilon testing, and pharyngeal biopsy are not helpful in confirming the diagnosis or evaluation of its complications.

Q1265
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 61-year-old woman has noted slowly progressive painless visual loss OD over the last 6 months. Her visual acuity is 20/80 OD and 20/20 OS. She has a right relative afferent pupillary defect. She correctly identified 5 of 10 color plates OD and 10 of 10 OS. She has a central scotoma OD and normal perimetry OS. Fundoscopy shows a diffusely pale optic disc OD; the left disc is normal. Given the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan with fat suppression and contrast shown, what diagnosis most likely accounts for her findings?
Correct answer: C. optic nerve sheath meningioma
Rationale
The patient's history of a slowly progressive painless unilateral vision loss with decreased visual acuity, relative afferent pupillary defect, decreased color vision, central scotoma, optic nerve pallor, and retinochoroidal (optociliary) shunt vessels is highly suggestive of a compressive optic neuropathy. The sagittal T1-weighted MRI with contrast and fat suppression shows fusiform enhancement of the superior optic nerve sheath (black arrow) and linear enhancement of the inferior optic nerve sheath (red arrowhead) in the right orbit with a thin nonenhancing optic nerve between the enhancing optic nerve sheath, consistent with an optic nerve sheath meningioma.
Distensible venous malformations of the orbit, previously known as orbital varices, are best visualized with MRI or contrast-enhanced rapid spiral computed tomography (CT) during a Valsalva maneuver, showing characteristic enlargement of the engorged veins. Phleboliths may also be present on imaging.
Cavernous venous malformations, previously known as cavernous hemangiomas, are the most common primary orbital lesion in adults which are described as a well-circumscribed (not fusiform) lesion within the muscle cone that may have heterogenous enhancement.
Optic nerve gliomas are very rare in adults (more common in children) and are best visualized with MRI as a heterogenous mass in the orbital apex with fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve (not the optic nerve sheath).

Q1266
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 12-year-old boy presents with sudden vision loss in the right eye. His visual acuity was no light perception (NLP) in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD); nonorganic vision loss is suspected. What test performed in clinic may help demonstrate normal 20/20 vision in the right eye in this patient?
Correct answer: B. fogging test
Rationale
Although all of the listed techniques may help uncover functional visual loss in a patient claiming monocular NLP vision, only the fogging test can demonstrate 20/20 vision in the eye with suspected nonorganic vision loss.
To perform the fogging test, the clinician employs a trial frame with plus and minus cylinder (6 diopters), which have their axes aligned; these are placed in front of the patient's "good" eye. The patient is then asked to read the Snellen chart while one of the cylinder lenses is rotated. The cylinder rotation will severely blur vision as the 2 axes are rotated out of alignment. If the patient continues to read the 20/20 line, he or she is doing so with the "bad" eye.
The fogging test is a form of confusion testing, which requires the patient to be unaware of which eye is actually tested. Other confusion tests including the duochrome test (in which the patient wears duochrome/Worth 4-dot glasses and attempts to read letters through the red/green filter on the Snellen chart; if all the letters are read, then vision is normal in both eyes) and the polarized lens test (in which the examiner uses the Snellen chart projected through polarized filters; if all the letters are read, then vision is normal in both eyes).
The mirror test can demonstrate at least light perception vision, but it would not help prove he has 20/20 vision.
Movement on optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) drum indicates 20/400 vision, but it cannot determine if the vision is any better than 20/400.
A base-out prism test showing movement when the prism is placed over the "bad" eye indicates some vision in that eye, but it cannot prove 20/20 vision.

Q1267
Neuro-Ophthalmology
During ocular motility testing, a patient develops episodic diplopia lasting 30 to 60 seconds at a time, seen as transient right exotropia in primary gaze after maintaining both eyes in extreme right gaze for several seconds. If this is a sequela of past disease, what historical event would explain these findings?
Correct answer: D. tuberculum sellae meningioma treated with radiation therapy
Rationale
Ocular neuromyotonia, in which episodic diplopia lasting 30–60 seconds develops after sustained activation of a cranial ocular motor nerve, is usually associated with a history of radiation therapy for a skull-based neoplasm.

Q1268
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient develops a Horner pupil, an ipsilateral impairment of pain and temperature sensation on the face, and a contralateral impairment of pain and temperature sensation over the trunk and limbs.  In what location is the causative lesion?
Correct answer: A. lateral medullary area
Rationale
Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) produces an ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ipsilateral impairment of pain and temperature sensation over the face (involvement of the descending tract of CN V), contralateral impairment of pain and temperature sensation over the trunk and limbs (involvement of the lateral spinal thalamic tract), ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia (damage to spinocerebellar tracts), and the ocular tilt reaction.
In addition, patients with lateral medullary syndrome might have dysarthria, dysphagia, vertigo, persistent hiccups, lateropulsion, and ocular lateropulsion. A cavernous sinus lesion, an internal carotid artery dissection, or a congenital brachial plexus injury might cause Horner syndrome, but they would not cause the crossed impaired sensation of pain and temperature of the face and rest of the body.

Q1269
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Within the cavernous sinus, what cranial nerve do the sympathetic fibers run with?
Correct answer: B. VI
Rationale
Within the cavernous sinus, sympathetic fibers destined for the dilator muscles leave the carotid in conjunction with CN VI for a few millimeters. Further anteriorly in the cavernous sinus, the sympathetic fibers join the nasociliary branch of CN V1. The sympathetic fibers do not join any of the other cranial nerves within the cavernous sinus.

Q1270
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient reports 3 months of oscillopsia. A moderate amplitude, low-frequency nystagmus is seen in which 1 eye elevates and rotates toward the nose while the fellow eye depresses and rotates outward. What afferent visual disturbance might be found with additional testing?
Correct answer: D. bitemporal hemianopia
Rationale
See-saw nystagmus is a form of disconjugate nystagmus in which 1 eye elevates and intorts while the other eye depresses and extorts, movement reminiscent of that of a see-saw. The eye movements are typically pendular and slow in frequency. It is most commonly observed in patients with large tumors of the parasellar region, which can compress the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal hemianopia. The other scotomas and visual field defects would not be expected for a parasellar lesion causing see-saw nystagmus.

Q1271
Neuro-Ophthalmology
In a patient who claims to see nothing from both eyes, but is suspected to have nonorganic vision loss, what test finding establishes the existence of some vision?
Correct answer: D. eye movement with rotation of an optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) drum
Rationale
The OKN drum test is perhaps the easiest test to perform and can help document the presence of some vision in patients who claim total bilateral blindness. In a patient with nonorganic blindness, some vision can also be confirmed via documentation of eye movements during the mirror test and abnormal responses to proprioceptive tests such as the finger-touching test. Because a relative afferent pupil defect can be absent in bilateral disease, it does not prove nonorganic vision loss.

Q1272
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 6-month-old boy presents with the findings shown in the photograph. His history is significant for a delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia. What pupillary abnormality is expected?
Correct answer: D. anisocoria greater in dim light
Rationale
This infant's heterochromia, ptosis, and reverse ptosis of the left eye in conjunction with a birth history complicated by shoulder dystocia is suggestive of a Horner syndrome due to a brachial plexus injury. Disruption of the oculosympathetic pathway at birth or early in life, as in this case, can lead to heterochromia due to abnormal development of iris melanocytes (hypochromia of affected iris). Because sympathetic innervation to the iris dilator is disrupted, there is a relative miosis of the affected eye, along with a ptosis from denervation of the Müller muscle in Horner syndrome. Dilation subsequently results only from iris sphincter relaxation, as the iris dilator muscle is denervated, causing an anisocoria greater in dim light. For the same reason, there is also ipsilateral dilation lag with Horner syndrome.
Anisocoria equal in dim and bright light refers to physiologic anisocoria. Anisocoria greater in bright light encompasses conditions such as iris sphincter damage, Adie tonic pupil, pharmacologic mydriasis, and third nerve palsy, in which the pupil does not constrict as well as the contralateral eye in response to light stimulus.

Q1273
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Over 3 months, an 8-year-old boy has developed worsening diplopia. His visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye with 10 prism diopters of exotropia in primary gaze and the motility findings shown below. What other symptoms or findings may also be present in this patient?
Correct answer: D. contralateral tremor
Rationale
This patient has a partial, pupil-involving third nerve palsy, with right adduction deficit and ipsilateral mydriasis. Although partial third nerve palsies can occur with lesions anywhere along the course of the third nerve, certain associated neurological findings can be associated with brainstem lesions that involve the third nerve nuclear complex, the third nerve fascicles, and the surrounding structures. Because these surrounding structures (which include the red nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle, and cerebral peduncle) may cause contralateral tremors, contralateral ataxia, or contralateral hemiparesis, respectively, it is helpful to look for evidence of associated neurological deficits.
Intra-axial involvement of the CN III fascicle can produce 1 of 4 syndromes, each of which includes an ipsilateral CN III palsy:
  1. Damage to the ventral midbrain and the cerebral peduncle can cause a contralateral hemiparesis (Weber syndrome).
  2. Involvement of the red nucleus and substantia nigra may produce contralateral ataxia or tremor (Benedikt syndrome).
  3. Damage to the dorsal midbrain may involve the superior cerebellar peduncle and produce contralateral ataxia (Claude syndrome).
  4. Dorsal lesion with a slightly different configuration can produce the same type of ataxia plus a CN III nuclear lesion and features of supranuclear eye movement dysfunction (Nothnagel syndrome).

Q1274
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What cause of Horner syndrome is likely to be associated with heterochromia?
Correct answer: B. congenital
Rationale
Congenital Horner syndrome is a manifestation of an interrupted sympathetic nervous chain and may cause mild ptosis associated with miosis, anhidrosis, and decreased pigmentation of the iris on the involved side. Patients with typical cluster headaches may develop Horner syndrome of the ipsilateral side during an acute attack. The Horner syndrome often resolves, but it may become permanent after repeated attacks. Patients with spontaneous dissection of the internal carotid artery may present with ipsilateral head pain and Horner syndrome. Such patients may also have amaurosis fugax and dysgeusia (distortion of sense of taste). Stroke or death are possible complications. Some patients, usually middle-aged men, have Horner syndrome and daily unilateral headaches not characteristic of cluster, and no underlying pathology can be identified. The term Raeder paratrigeminal syndrome has been used to describe these patients.

Q1275
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient is suspected to have functional vision loss in the right eye. The examination indicates a visual acuity of 20/400 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. What test would be most helpful to confirm functional vision loss in this patient?
Correct answer: C. vertical prism dissociation test
Rationale
The vertical prism dissociation test is a good examination technique for monocular vision loss. A 4 prism diopter lens is placed base-down in front of the eye with better vision (“good eye”) of a patient who reports monocular vision loss. If the subject has symmetric vision in both eyes, 2 images should be seen, 1 above the other. If the subject is able to see the letters only with the “good” eye, only 1 image should be seen. The vertical prism dissociation test can be used to obtain visual acuity in the “bad” eye, because if the patient can read the upper and lower images of a vertical-prism–dissociated 20/20 line, it can prove normal visual acuity.
An optokinetic drum test can demonstrate 20/400 vision, and the mirror test can demonstrate light perception, but would not be helpful in a patient who already has 20/400 vision. Finger-touching test would likely be normal in a patient who has monocular vision loss.

Q1276
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 44-year-old woman has a slowly progressive worsening of right facial weakness over a year. Empiric treatment with high-dose steroids led to no improvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. neoplasm
Rationale
This patient has a slowly progressive seventh cranial nerve (CN VII) palsy, which is highly suggestive of a neoplastic etiology. Neoplasms may involve the seventh nerve in the cerebellopontine angle (eg, acoustic neuroma, meningioma), within the fallopian canal, or in the parotid gland. Bell palsy represents the most common type of facial neuropathy, but presents with sudden onset of facial paresis and not a gradual onset. Herpes zoster involving the seventh nerve is called Ramsay Hunt syndrome and also presents with an acute onset of facial paralysis. Sarcoidosis can affect the seventh nerve, but often responds to steroids.

Q1277
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 45-year-old woman presents for a routine eye examination. She has no visual complaints and no headaches. Her weight is 125 lbs. Acuity is 20/20 in both eyes. Humphrey visual field testing shows arcuate defects bilaterally. Her disc appearance is shown. She has spontaneous venous pulsations in both eyes. What is the likely cause of her arcuate visual field defects?
Correct answer: C. optic disc drusen
Rationale
Optic disc drusen can lead to arcuate visual field defects similar to glaucoma. These visual field defects either remain stable or worsen very slowly. The optic nerve heads of patients with disc drusen appear elevated and small in diameter, with indistinct or irregular margins and associated anomalous vascular branching patterns. The optic nerve head does not show hyperemia or dilation of the surface microvasculature (as it might in true papilledema).
Although arcuate visual field defects also are typical of glaucoma, a glaucomatous disc would be expected to show increased cup-to-disc ratio, possible focal rim notching, and a lack of pallor of the neuroretinal rim. Macular scar causes central visual defect. Vitamin B12 deficiency results in central or cecocentral scotomas.

Q1278
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Forty-five minutes ago, the patient shown had pilocarpine 1% instilled into both eyes. What is the most likely diagnosis, given the appearance of the left pupil?
Correct answer: D. pharmacologic dilation
Rationale
Following instillation of pilocarpine 1% in both of this patient's eyes, the left pupil remains dilated. When mydriasis is pharmacologically induced by a drug, such as atropine, instillation of full-strength pilocarpine (1% or more) will not overcome the mydriasis. Mydriasis due to neurologic disease such as tonic (Adie) pupil or third nerve palsy is easily overcome with instillation of 1% pilocarpine. In the case of tonic pupil, even 0.1% (dilute) pilocarpine will result in pupillary constriction.

Q1279
Neuro-Ophthalmology
The right eye fundus of a patient is shown in the figure. The left fundus has a similar appearance. A visual field test in this patient may show what finding?
Correct answer: B. bitemporal hemianopia
Rationale
The figure shows a tilted disc. A tilted disc appears as a disc with the superior portion elevated and the inferior portion displaced posteriorly. In addition, the disc may be horizontally rotated. Situs inversus (vessels initially go nasally before turning temporally off the disc) may be observed. Visual field may reveal superotemporal defects or a bitemporal hemianopia that does not respect the midline. Patients often have myopic astigmatism. Tilted disc syndrome is associated with X-linked congenital stationary night blindness.

Q1280
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 47-year-old otherwise healthy woman has 3 mm right eye ptosis and diplopia. Adduction and depression are 50% of normal in her right eye, and her left eye moves normally. Pupils are symmetric. What initial diagnostic testing should be performed?
Correct answer: C. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain, with magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)
Rationale
Unilateral ptosis with a motility deficit, especially in a pattern matching partial cranial nerve III palsy, should raise concern for a compressive lesion. This is in contrast to a complete third nerve palsy without pupil involvement, which is usually secondary to microvascular ischemia. In a 47-year-old patient, aneurysm is the most serious potential cause and must be excluded by noninvasive angiography. The patient's symptoms are not consistent with increased intracranial pressure, nor would exotropia and ptosis likely be caused by thyroid eye disease. Giant cell arteritis is not a major consideration with this presentation in a patient under age 50.

Q1281
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A patient with superior oblique myokymia (SOM) is having more frequent symptoms of oscillopsia. She is concerned that she has a dangerous disease that needs treatment. What information can the ophthalmologist provide regarding the long-term management and prognosis of this condition?
Correct answer: C. SOM can wax and wane and can remit spontaneously.
Rationale
Superior oblique myokymia (SOM) is a generally benign disorder that produces paroxysmal, monocular, high-frequency bursts of contraction of the superior oblique muscle. It produces vertical or torsional oscillopsia, occurring spontaneously or immediately after a downward eye movement. The clinical course is highly variable, including both spontaneous recovery or a chronic relapsing course.
The course of SOM is not relentlessly progressive, and while medical treatment with carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, or topical beta-blockers shows success, not every patient is cured.
SOM is very rarely associated with serious neurologic disease, although there are rare reports of association with multiple sclerosis or posterior fossa tumor.
SOM neuroimaging findings sometimes suggest a neurovascular compressive etiology, but vascular decompression results are variable.

Q1282
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 75-year-old man has 4 months of worsening night vision and photopsias. Visual acuity is 20/25 OU, perimetry shows mild generalized constriction, and his posterior chamber intraocular lenses are in good position. The optic discs and maculae appear normal. What medical condition is most likely to be associated with his visual disturbance?
Correct answer: C. small-cell lung cancer
Rationale
Night vision problems with photopsias raise concern for a process that is destroying photoreceptors, and in a 75-year-old patient, a paraneoplastic retinopathy must be considered. While this condition mimics retinitis pigmentosa, the presence of photopsias would not be expected in that condition, and the age of onset is unusual. Uncontrolled hypertension may cause choroidal infarction and scattered visual field defects. Phenobarbital and/or seizures do not cause night vision difficulties, and remote occipital strokes could cause bilateral vision loss but not the photopsias or night vision problems.

Q1283

A 53-year-old man has transient vision loss in the right eye, lasting 15 minutes. Fundus examination showed a calcified plaque in an arteriole adjacent to the optic disc. Where is the likeliest source of the calcified plaque?
Correct answer: D. aortic valve disease
Rationale
Calcified plaques are typically caused by heart valve or aorta calcification. Carotid stenosis typically predisposes patients to Hollenhorst plaques. Aortic arch atheroma can lead to Hollenhorst plaques or platelet-fibrin plaques. Giant cell arteritis can cause transient vision loss, but it would not cause a plaque.

Q1284
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 66-year-old woman with Parkinson disease complains of binocular diplopia when reading. What finding is expected on ocular motility examination?
Correct answer: D. convergence insufficiency
Rationale
Patients with Parkinson disease can have diplopia at near and, thus, difficulty reading due to convergence insufficiency. Other ocular symptoms of Parkinson disease include dry eye from decreased blink rate, apraxia of eyelid opening, and blepharospasm.
Divergence insufficiency often results from involution of the connective tissue band between the superior rectus and lateral rectus muscles, causing inferior displacement of the lateral recti. This condition is referred to as sagging eye syndrome. Conjugate upgaze palsy may occur in the dorsal midbrain syndrome, of which convergence insufficiency also is a feature. However, Parkinson disease is not typically associated with upgaze palsy. Lateral gaze palsy may occur due to a sixth nerve nuclear lesion in the brain stem but not due to Parkinson disease.

Q1285
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 78-year-old man develops a desensitized cornea and lagophthalmos following a stroke. After managing his lagophthalmos for 6 months with copious lubrication and taping closed his eyelids, what would be the preferred surgical treatment to avoid corneal ulceration?
Correct answer: C. gold weight implantation
Rationale
Poor blinking and eyelid closure secondary to CN VII injury can lead to chronic ocular surface irritation from corneal exposure, as well as poor tear film replenishment and distribution. Lubricating drops, viscous tear supplementation, ointments, taping of the temporal half of the lower eyelid, or moisture chambers may be used alone or in combination for temporary paralysis. For cases of long-term or permanent paralysis of the eyelid, additional procedures are necessary. Placement of a weight in the upper eyelid remains the most commonly performed procedure for the treatment of paralytic lagophthalmos.
Although a complete tarsorrhaphy will reduce corneal exposure, patients dislike the permanent tarsorrhaphy from a functional and cosmetic perspective. This procedure should be avoided, except in patients with recalcitrant corneal disease from exposure. A Müller muscle resection would cause worsening of symptoms with more upper lid retraction and exposure of the ocular surface, and it is not indicated for this patient with lagophthalmos. Eyelid springs have less long-term success and greater risk of extrusion.

Q1286
Neuro-Ophthalmology
Constant oscillopsia is most frequently observed in what type of nystagmus?
Correct answer: C. acquired nystagmus
Rationale
Oscillopsia is a visual disturbance in which stationary objects are oscillating, or swaying back and forth. It occurs after the visual system has matured and is constant, with an acquired loss of oculomotor control. Temporary oscillopsia can exist in latent nystagmus with monocular disruption of fusion or in voluntary nystagmus. Patients with congenital nystagmus (infantile nystagmus syndrome) do not appreciate oscillopsia.

Q1287
Neuro-Ophthalmology
In the intensive care unit, an ophthalmologist examines a patient who has flaccid paralysis and facial weakness, bilateral ophthalmoplegia, and ptosis. Near vision is blurred. Both pupils are large and nonreactive. What serologic test is most likely to be diagnostic?
Correct answer: D. antiganglioside (anti-GQ1b) antibodies
Rationale
The Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome is the clinical triad of acute ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia, often causing facial diplegia as well. A high percentage of patients have anti-ganglioside Q1b (anti-GQ1b) IgG antibodies in their serum. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals an elevated protein level with a normal cell count, and deep tendon reflexes are generally absent. Tonic pupils, with impairment of accommodation, can also be seen in widespread autonomic dysfunction from Miller Fisher syndrome.
Acetylcholine–receptor-binding antibodies are positive in a subset of patients with ocular myasthenia gravis, which is in the differential diagnosis of ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and weakness. However, pupils are not affected in myasthenia.
Thyrotropin-receptor antibodies are markers for thyroid disease, which is in the differential diagnosis of diplopia and ptosis (although more commonly causing eyelid retraction). Thyroid disease does not cause flaccid paralysis, facial weakness, or efferent pupil dysfunction (afferent pupillary defect can be present, however, with compressive optic neuropathy from thyroid eye disease).
Anti-Müller cell antibodies target Müller glial cells, which form a structural backbone to the retina. These antibodies are markers for antiretinal antibody diseases, and thus would be associated with vision loss and abnormal b-wave electroretinogram (ERG), not with ophthalmoplegia and tonic pupils.

Q1288
Neuro-Ophthalmology
For 6 weeks, a 51-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has had frequent falls and difficulty reading. Her oncologist found serum anti-Ri (ANNA-2) antibodies and recommended treatment with oral corticosteroid. What eye movement abnormalities may be found on examination?
Correct answer: B. rapid, conjugate eye movements that are both vertical and horizontal, without pause
Rationale
This patient has breast cancer and antibodies known to be associated with a paraneoplastic syndrome that may manifest with opsoclonus. Opsoclonus is characterized by multidirectional eye movements with high frequency and amplitude without intersaccadic intervals.
Ocular flutter can also be seen in paraneoplastic syndromes. It presents with fast horizontal movements (not slow, pendular oscillations). Tonic outward deviation of the left eye for 1 minute after sustained left gaze can be seen in ocular neuromyotonia, which is typically seen months to years after radiation treatment for skull-based tumors. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is seen in dorsal midbrain syndrome.

Q1289
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 72-year-old man presents with a 1-year history of slowly progressive facial numbness, blurred vision, binocular double vision, and difficulty chewing food. His slit-lamp examination is shown below. What is the next appropriate step in management?
Correct answer: A. magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Rationale
This patient has neurotrophic keratopathy associated with facial numbness, binocular double vision, and difficulty chewing food. This would suggest that he has multiple cranial nerve palsies, which is concerning for a brainstem lesion or cavernous sinus lesion, with cavernous sinus lesions more characteristic of a slowly progressive history. This would best be evaluated with an MRI of the brain, with and without contrast.
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies would help evaluate for myasthenia gravis, which could cause double vision and difficulty chewing food but not facial numbness or neurotrophic keratopathy.
Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) levels and chest X-ray is an appropriate screening for sarcoidosis, which could cause band keratopathy and may cause facial nerve palsies. Although sarcoidosis may affect multiple cranial nerves, this presentation would be very unlikely.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are appropriate for the evaluation of giant cell arteritis, which can cause decreased vision due to ischemic optic neuropathy or retinopathy, jaw claudication, and double vision; however, giant cell arteritis typically causes scalp tenderness or headache, not facial pain.

Q1290
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 22-year-old man presents with ptosis, frontal balding, and wasting of the temporalis and masseter muscles. When the clinician shakes the patient's hand, what confirmatory finding might be expected?
Correct answer: A. has difficulty releasing grip
Rationale
This patient's external findings suggest the diagnosis of myotonic dystrophy. Myotonic dystrophy is a dominantly inherited (chromosome 19) disorder that also produces ophthalmoplegia that may mimic chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia. It usually starts in late childhood or early adulthood with myotonia that is worsened by excitement, cold, and fatigue. One might expect that this patient will not be able to quickly release grip when shaking hands. This myopathy is unusual in that distal rather than proximal muscles are affected first. The myopathic facies, frontal balding, and ptosis cause a distinct appearance. The ocular findings include pigmentary retinopathy, polychromatic lenticular deposits ("Christmas tree" cataracts), and sluggish miotic pupils. Systemic features may include low intelligence, insulin resistance, hearing loss, cardiomyopathy, cardiac conduction abnormalities, testicular atrophy, and uterine atony. Electromyography demonstrates typical myotonic discharges. Grip strength is usually normal.

Q1291
Neuro-Ophthalmology
A 49-year-old man presents with 4 days of constant diplopia. With a left face turn, his diplopia resolves. What ocular motor problem is most likely causing the double vision?
Correct answer: C. left sixth nerve palsy
Rationale
Patients with diplopia adopt head postures to take the eyes out of the affected field of gaze. Because a patient with a left sixth nerve palsy has worse double vision on left gaze, a left face turn puts the eyes in right gaze and minimizes diplopia.
Both a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia and right medial rectus fibrosis would cause double vision that worsens on right gaze/left face turn. Patients with fourth nerve palsy adopt a compensatory head tilt to take the eyes out of the field of action of the paretic superior oblique muscle.

Q1292
Neuro-Ophthalmology
What ancillary test best diagnoses Leber congenital amaurosis?
Correct answer: D. electroretinography
Rationale
Leber congenital amaurosis is a group of hereditary retinal dystrophies that affect both the rod and cone photoreceptors. It is characterized by severe vision loss in infancy, nystagmus, and poorly reactive pupils. An electroretinogram is typically used to make the diagnosis, showing extinguished waveforms. A-scan ultrasonography, fluorescein angiography, and optical coherence tomography would not be helpful in making the diagnosis.
